sens: Without payment, for free
Without reason, without motive, unjustly
In vain, without effect, uselessly
H2600.detail:
1. Without payment, for free: the word refers to what is done or given without any cost. Laban asks Jacob if he will serve him "for nothing" (Genesis 29:15), meaning without wages. Similarly, Israel was "taken away for nothing" by its oppressors (Isaiah 52:5): no one paid the price for this captivity; it was unjustified and without compensation.
2. Without reason, without motive, unjustly: the word emphasizes the absence of a legitimate foundation. Job "holds fast to his integrity" even though Satan incites him to lose it "without cause" (Job 2:3): there is no valid reason for his suffering. The psalmists complain of being hated "without cause" (Psalms 69:5) or being attacked "without motive" (Proverbs 3:30) — the aggression is gratuitous, undeserved, devoid of foundation.
3. In vain, without effect, uselessly: the word expresses the absence of result or achieved purpose. Shedding blood "uselessly" (1 Samuel 25:31) means shedding it without justification and without benefit. It is to act or suffer without anything justifying or redeeming that act or suffering.
H2600.origine: The Hebrew word חִנָּם (chinnam) comes from a root that expresses the idea of gratuity and absence of cause. It is related to words expressing freedom and detachment. In the Greek Old Testament, it translates the Hebrew with the Greek δωρεάν (dorean, "freely"). The starting image is that of something that costs nothing, that requires no exchange or reason.
H2600.emploi: The word appears 31 times in the Old Testament, concentrated mainly in the Poetic books (Psalms, Proverbs, Job) and the Prophets. It is first used in the literal sense: working without pay (Genesis 29:15), receiving a servant "for free" meaning without payment (Exodus 21:11). But its primary usage is moral and spiritual: being hated, attacked, killed "without cause" (Psalms 35:19, 69:5, 109:3; Proverbs 1:11). It is also to suffer or act "in vain," "uselessly" (Job 2:3, 1 Samuel 25:31). The word carries particular weight in the Psalms: it cries out the injustice of the persecution of the righteous who have done nothing to deserve it.
H2600.portee: This word reminds the Christian that God sees the difference between what is just and what is unjust, between what has a cause and what is devoid of one. It comforts those who suffer innocently: their sufferings are never "for nothing" in God's eyes, even if they seem gratuitous and unjustified in the eyes of men. It is also a warning: acting without cause against others invites God's judgment.

sens: Cousin of Jeremiah, son of Shallum
H2601.detail: Hanameel is a man living during the time of the divided monarchy, cousin of the prophet Jeremiah (his father Shallum is the brother of the prophet's mother). He appears in the account of Jeremiah 32, at the time when the prophet is imprisoned in the courtyard of the prison in Jerusalem. He is the seller of a field in Anathoth: according to Israel's law, the right of redemption belongs first to the nearest relative, which explains why Hanameel comes to propose to Jeremiah to buy his field (Jeremiah 32:7-8). Jeremiah recognizes in this unexpected visit a sign from God and buys the field for seventeen shekels of silver, an act that symbolizes his hope in the restoration of Israel after the exile (Jeremiah 32:9).
H2601.origine: The name Hanameel means "God is gracious" or "God has shown His grace," formed from "El" (God) and a root that expresses divine mercy. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, expressing trust in the goodness of the Lord.
H2601.emploi: Hanameel appears only four times in the Bible, all in Jeremiah 32:7-12, during the episode of the siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar. He is presented solely as the cousin selling the field in Anathoth. His role is discreet but crucial: he embodies the instrument through which God confirms to Jeremiah that life and economy will continue after the exile, despite the imminent disaster. This act of purchase, carried out in the midst of the prophet's future captivity, has become a prophetic sign of restoration and hope.
H2601.portee: The presence of Hanameel reminds the Christian reader that God often acts through ordinary means and simple people to fulfill His promises. The purchase of the field illustrates how faith in God is manifested through concrete actions, even when everything seems lost. It is a call to maintain hope and to recognize God's hand in the circumstances of daily life.

sens: Meteorological phenomenon that destroys crops: frost, hail, or other climatic calamity
Destruction of plants caused by cold or a natural disaster
H2602.detail: 1. The word refers to a devastating meteorological phenomenon — frost, hail, or perhaps hail mixed with snow — that ravages crops and fruit trees. It is an image of natural destruction. In Psalm 78:47, God sends this frost against the sycamores of Egypt to punish Pharaoh and force his heart to yield. 2. More broadly, it is the climatic scourge that ruins harvests and starves a people. The frost here figures as one of the plagues of Egypt, a divine weapon to manifest God's power and His judgment. It shows that nature itself obeys God and can become an instrument of His action.
H2602.origine: The Hebrew word חֲנָמֵל comes from a root that probably means "to strike" or "to burn," referring to the devastating effect of intense cold or the mixture of hail and snow on crops. The exact etymology remains uncertain, but the image is one of rapid and violent destruction. This term belongs to the vocabulary of catastrophic natural phenomena, a domain where biblical Hebrew has several words to designate different types of calamities.
H2602.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalm 78:47, in the poetic account of the ten plagues of Egypt. It is used to describe the scourge that annihilates the Egyptian sycamores, that is, the wild fig trees that produced a valuable fruit. The context reveals that this frost is sent by God in judgment against Egypt and its Pharaoh. It is an example of the epic and theological style of Psalm 78, which celebrates God's miracles on behalf of Israel.
H2602.portee: This word reminds us that God has control over all creation, including natural forces, to accomplish His will and punish injustice. It invites the reader to recognize that earthly calamities are never absurd: they can be calls to repentance or signs of divine sovereignty. For Israel, this passage reinforces trust in the God who protects His people and humiliates His enemies through supernatural means.

sens: Show kindness, compassion towards someone who does not deserve it
Grant a gift, a favor without it being earned
Implore someone to obtain their pity, their clemency
Act with mercy towards one who suffers or is in need
H2603A.detail:
1. To show kindness or compassion: it is to look at someone with favor and goodness, often despite their guilt or misery. Esau, in Genesis 33:5, acknowledges that the children and women Jacob has with him are gifts "granted" by God — an expression of His grace towards Jacob. It is the opposite action of judgment: instead of condemning, one chooses to bless.
2. To grant a gift or favor without the recipient having earned it: God "grants" His blessings out of pure goodness. Job cries, "Have pity on me" (Job 19:21), pleading to be treated with clemency rather than according to his faults. It is a freely given act, not owed.
3. To implore, to beg someone to show pity: in 1 Kings 8:47, the captives "address supplications" to God — they plead for Him to look upon them with pity and to free them. This meaning emphasizes the request, the imploring of one who recognizes their weakness.
4. To act with mercy towards those who suffer or are in need: in Proverbs 14:21, he who "has pity on the needy" is happy — it translates compassion into concrete action of help and support for the poor and oppressed.
H2603A.origine: The verb חָנַן comes from a root that expresses the idea of leaning towards someone, turning one's face towards them with favor. The underlying image is that of a gracious gaze: the one who "shows grace" looks at the one in need with kindness. The different forms of the verb in Hebrew (active, passive, reflexive) show that grace can come from God towards man, or from one person to another, or be implored by the one in need. The word is very ancient and fundamental in Hebrew religious vocabulary.
H2603A.emploi: This verb appears 72 times in the Old Testament, especially in the Psalms (where it is very frequent) and in the historical books. It is mainly used in two ways: first, God showing His grace towards Israel or towards an individual (Exodus 33:19, Numbers 6:25, Psalms 67:2), which is at the heart of biblical covenant theology; secondly, humans imploring this grace (Psalms 6:3, 25:16, 86:16) or showing it to one another (Proverbs 14:21, 14:31). The contexts vary: forgiveness after sin (1 Kings 8:33), protection in affliction (Psalms 57:2), generosity towards the poor (Proverbs 14:21). The term always carries the idea of an unmerited favor, freely given by the one who has the power to grant it.
H2603A.portee: This word reveals the very heart of the relationship between God and His people: God does not act according to strict justice, but according to His grace — He looks favorably upon the one who does not deserve it. For the Christian, it is a promise that their prayers and laments do not go unanswered. It is also a call: since God has shown us grace, we must in turn be compassionate towards those who suffer or are in need. Grace is contagious: it creates a chain of kindness.

sens: Expression of discontent or suffering
Words that displease and hurt
Cry that provokes disgust or aversion
H2603B.detail: 1. A complaint is the expression of the pain or discontent of someone who suffers and manifests it through their words. It is a voice that comes from inner pain. 2. The complaint can also be a word or a groan that displeases the one who hears it, that hurts or repels them: it creates distance, tension between the one who complains and their surroundings. 3. More broadly, it is any expression of pain that provokes disgust or aversion in the one who receives it — something that becomes unpleasant to bear. In the text of Job, the patriarch says: "My complaint to the sons of my womb" (Job 19:17), meaning that even his children find his groans unbearable, so deep is his suffering and heavy his voice to hear.
H2603B.origine: The Hebrew word חָנַן (chanan) has a root that first evokes the idea of rejection or disgust: something that becomes abominable or repulsive. In this specific context, it designates less a gracious request than a word or sound that provokes aversion. The translation as "complaint" emphasizes this meaning: the complaint is the audible manifestation of suffering, one that often produces discomfort in those who listen.
H2603B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible (in Job 19:17). It describes Job's painful complaint, afflicted by leprosy and isolation: neither his wife nor his children can bear to hear his groaning voice. It is a rare word that paints the extremity of distress, the moment when suffering becomes so visible and audible that it even repels close ones. Job is alone with God in the face of his complaint.
H2603B.portee: This word shows the depth of the isolation of the sufferer: the complaint, while natural, can become an obstacle to communion with others. It invites the reader to attentive compassion: a heard complaint is the beginning of consolation. It also reminds us that suffering, when expressed, disturbs and requires from those who listen a courageous and patient ear.

sens: show favor, kindness to someone
show compassion towards the unfortunate
implore someone's grace, beg them
H2604.detail:
1. To show favor to someone is to grant them free kindness, without them having earned it. King Nebuchadnezzar is invited to show compassion towards the unfortunate, to grant them favor by treating them justly (Daniel 4:27).
2. To show compassion means concretely to demonstrate pity and gentleness towards those who suffer or are in need. It is the image of a hand reaching down to lift up the weak.
3. To implore grace is to beg someone to treat you kindly. Daniel prayed and called upon his God, that is, he begged Him to show him grace, to treat him favorably (Daniel 6:11).
H2604.origine: The Hebrew verb חֲנַן (chanan) fundamentally expresses the idea of leaning towards someone with gentleness and kindness. It belongs to the family of חֵן (hen, grace), and its image is that of a person who leans or bows with favor. The word designates both the one who gives grace and the one who earnestly requests it.
H2604.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the transmitted texts. In both cases, it is found in the book of Daniel, which dates from the late period of the Old Testament. First, it describes the action of showing compassion to the unfortunate (Daniel 4:27), an act of justice and mercy. Then, it expresses the act of begging God, invoking His grace (Daniel 6:11). The word thus covers two realities: giving freely what is not owed, and humbly requesting that favor.
H2604.portee: This word reveals that grace is never owed. It is the expression of a freely given kindness, whether that of a master towards his subjects or that of God towards His supplicants. For the believer, it reminds us that justice must be accompanied by compassion: the one who has received grace is called to show it to others. It is also a word that teaches the humility of heart: to implore grace is to recognize one's need and the superiority of the one from whom it is requested.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the divided monarchy
H2605G.detail: Hanan is a man of the tribe of Benjamin mentioned in the royal genealogies. He appears in 1 Chronicles 8:23 as the son of Shashak and brother of several other Benjaminites including Ishpan, Eber, and Eliel.
H2605G.origine: The name Hanan means "he is merciful" or "he is gracious." It comes from the Hebrew root that expresses grace and divine pity, a virtue highly esteemed in biblical culture.
H2605G.emploi: Hanan is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:23, in the genealogical list of the tribe of Benjamin. He is a member of this tribe during the time of the divided monarchy (after Solomon's reign). Other characters bear this name in the Old Testament (notably Levites and officers of Nehemiah), but this one is distinguished by his specific place in the Benjaminite family tree.

sens: son of Azel, of the tribe of Benjamin
man from the time of the divided monarchy
H2605H.detail: Hanan is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned in the genealogies during the time of the divided monarchy (when Israel was split between the Northern and Southern kingdoms). He is the sixth and last son of Azel, a descendant of Saul. His five brothers are named Azrikam, Bocru, Ismaël, Schéaria, and Abdias (1 Chronicles 8:38 and 9:44 provide the same list).
H2605H.origine: The name Hanan means "he is merciful" in Hebrew, derived from the root חנן (hanan) which evokes grace and compassion. It is a common theophoric name among the Israelites, expressing a divine quality.
H2605H.emploi: Hanan appears twice in the Bible, in the same parallel verses of 1 Chronicles 8:38 and 9:44, which list the sons of Azel. These two genealogical passages serve to trace the lineage of Saul and confirm Hanan's place in the tribe of Benjamin. The repetition of his name in these two lists emphasizes the importance of genealogies for Israel after the exile.

sens: Son of Maacah, warrior of David
H2605I.detail: Hanan is a man living during the time of the divided monarchy of Israel. He is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:43, where he is presented as the son of Maacah and one of David's mighty warriors — a man who served the king in his battles and military campaigns.
H2605I.origine: The name Hanan comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to be merciful" or "to show grace." It expresses the idea of active kindness, of a tender heart. This name was quite common in Israel, borne by several important figures throughout the history of Israel and Judah.
H2605I.emploi: Hanan is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in 1 Chronicles 11:43. He is listed among David's "mighty men" or "valiant warriors" (the "gibborim"), these renowned fighters who accompanied the king in his military expeditions. This brief but honorable mention shows that he was a renowned warrior during David's reign, somewhere around the 10th century B.C.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned during the exile and return
H2605J.detail: Hanan is a name borne by several important men during the time of the exile and the return to Jerusalem. The name means "he is merciful" in Hebrew. In the two passages where he appears in the Bible (Ezra 2:46 and Nehemiah 7:49), he is mentioned as an ancestor of families returning from exile: his sons ("the sons of Hanan") are counted among those who rebuild Jerusalem with Zerubbabel. These genealogical lists testify to the survival of God's people despite the Babylonian captivity.
H2605J.origine: The name Hanan comes from the Hebrew root חָנַן (chanan), which means "to show grace," "to have mercy." It is a theophoric name (containing a reference to divine action) that expresses the belief that God is merciful. Several biblical characters bear this name, all linked to key moments in the history of Israel.
H2605J.emploi: Hanan is the name of several important men in the Old Testament. The two most explicit biblical occurrences mention him as an ancestor of families returning from Babylonian captivity with Zerubbabel (Ezra 2:46 and Nehemiah 7:49). These parallel genealogical passages show that Hanan's house survived the exile and participated in the rebuilding of the temple and the community of Jerusalem. His name, meaning "merciful," reflects God's grace toward His people in their return from exile.

sens: Levite who assisted Ezra in explaining the Law to the people
Leader of the people who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah
H2605K.detail:
1. Hanan is a Levite mentioned in Nehemiah 8:7 among those who "explained the law to the people" during a great assembly after the return from exile. He was part of the religious leaders tasked with making the teaching of the Torah understandable to the gathered Israelites.

2. The same Hanan is also cited in Nehemiah 10:10 among "their brothers" who sealed the solemn covenant of the people with God, as Nehemiah engaged them. He thus represents one of the religious leaders who publicly committed to uphold the commandments.
H2605K.origine: The name Hanan means "he is merciful" or "he has had pity," derived from the Hebrew root חָנַן (hanan), which expresses God's grace or compassion toward His people. It is a theophoric name that reflects a divine characteristic — free goodness. Several men bore this name during the time of the return from exile, showing how central the concept of mercy was in Israel's faith.
H2605K.emploi: Hanan refers to a character or a small group of characters of the same name in Israel during the Exile and Return period. The two certain uses drawn from the Segond 1910 place him at the heart of the religious work under the leadership of Nehemiah and Ezra: first as a teacher of the Law, then as a signer of the restored covenant. He embodies the role of the Levites, those mediators between God and the people, particularly in the transmission of the Torah and the people's commitment to the Covenant.
H2605K.portee: Hanan reminds us that understanding God's Word requires faithful men and women who dedicate themselves to teaching and living it. His very name — meaning "mercy" — emphasizes that those who serve God must be driven by grace and transmit that grace to others. For the Christian, Hanan illustrates how authentic spiritual leaders personally commit to obedience to God before calling others to obey.

sens: Leader of the people of Judah at the return from exile
H2605L.detail: 1. Hanan is one of the leaders of the people who returned from Babylonian captivity under Nehemiah's leadership. He appears in the list of those who sealed the covenant with the Lord, thus testifying to his commitment to observe God's law and live according to the renewed covenant (Nehemiah 10:22).
H2605L.origine: The name Hanan means "he is merciful" or "he is compassionate," formed from the Hebrew root חנן (hanan) which expresses divine grace and compassion. This root evokes the idea of showing favor and kindness, particularly in relations with those who are weak or needy.
H2605L.emploi: Hanan appears only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 10:22, where he is listed among the leaders of the people who signed the renewed covenant under Nehemiah's leadership after the return from exile. His name appears alongside other notable figures, indicating his role as a recognized leader in the restored community. The context suggests that he represented a portion of the people and that his signature committed his group to uphold the commitments outlined in this solemn document.
H2605L.portee: Hanan's presence among the signers of the covenant reminds us of the importance of personal and communal responsibility in the covenant with God. His act of signing the covenant symbolizes the conscious decision to submit to divine law and participate in the spiritual restoration of the people after the judgment of exile.

sens: Leader of the people who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah
H2605M.detail: 1. Hanan is a name borne by several important men during the time of the return from exile. In the provided usage (Nehemiah 10:26), it refers to one of the leaders of the people who affixed his seal to the solemn covenant made with Nehemiah to commit to observing the Law of God. This was a solemn act showing the leaders' adherence to the renewal of the covenant.
H2605M.origine: The name Hanan comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to show mercy" or "to be gracious." It expresses the idea of active grace, of compassionate action. The name carries with it the promise of an attitude of kindness towards others.
H2605M.emploi: Hanan appears only once in the Segond translation, in Nehemiah 10:26. At this time of return from exile, several men bore this name: sons of Azel (descendants of Saul), warriors of David, Levites who helped Ezra teach the Law, and other leaders of the people. The man mentioned in Nehemiah 10:26 is one of the signatories of the covenant: he represents one of the leading families of restored Judah who solemnly committed to obeying the divine commandments.
H2605M.portee: This account of the covenant sealed with Nehemiah shows how the leaders of God's people, in the face of exile and its lessons, collectively committed to faithfulness. The name Hanan, bearer of mercy, reminds us that this covenant rested on God's grace and on the leaders' desire to guide the people with justice. For the believer, it is an invitation to examine one's own commitments to God: am I among those who seal a covenant of faithfulness, or does my faith remain lukewarm?

sens: Character from the time of Exile and Return
Son of Zaccur and grandson of Mattaniah
Levite in charge of the tithe provisions
H2605N.detail: Hanan is a name borne by several men in the history of Israel during the time of Exile and Return. The one mentioned in Nehemiah 13:13 is the son of Zaccur and grandson of Mattaniah. He is a Levite — a member of the tribe dedicated to temple service — whom Governor Nehemiah appointed as responsible for the administration of the storerooms containing the offerings and tithes (the portions due to God and His servants). His name literally means "he is merciful" or "he shows grace." The text presents him as a trustworthy man, known for his faithfulness, which explains his access to this position of financial and administrative responsibility in the service of the temple community.
H2605N.origine: The Hebrew name חָנָן (Hanan) comes from the root חנן (hanân) which means "to show grace," "to be merciful," "to have compassion." This root expresses one of God's central qualities in the Bible: His free goodness towards His people. Related names include Hanani ("the Merciful"), Hannah ("Grace" or "Favor"), and John in Greek (derived from the same Hebrew root). The name Hanan thus carries the hope that the one who bears it will be kind and just towards those he serves.
H2605N.emploi: Hanan appears only once in the Segond translation: in Nehemiah 13:13, at the time of the reconstruction of the temple and the restoration of worship after the Exile in Babylon. At that time, Nehemiah, the governor sent by the king of Persia, reorganizes the religious and financial administration of Jerusalem. He entrusts Hanan, alongside the priest Shelemiah and the scribe Zadok, with the responsibility of overseeing the storerooms of provisions. This role shows that Hanan enjoyed a high reputation for integrity and faithfulness in his time. His role was crucial: the tithes collected supported the Levites, the priests, and the poor, and if mismanaged, they could have caused disorder or injustice.
H2605N.portee: This passage reminds us of the importance God places on faithfulness in the administration of collective and sacred goods. Hanan, though a simple Levite, received a major responsibility because he was trusted. For the Christian reader, this illustrates that managing resources — whether material or spiritual — is a task that requires honesty and dedication to the service of the Lord. His name, "The One Who Shows Grace," also suggests that mercy should accompany every act of administration or judgment.

sens: Character mentioned during the divided monarchy in Israel
H2605O.detail: Hanan is a man mentioned only once in the Bible: in Jeremiah 35:4. He is presented as the son of Jigdalia, described as a "man of God." In this passage, the prophet Jeremiah brings the Rechabites to the house of the Lord and places them in a room named after this Hanan, located near that of the leaders and above that of Maaseiah, the gatekeeper. This mention indicates that Hanan enjoyed a certain prestige or particular responsibility at the temple in Jerusalem.
H2605O.origine: The name Hanan comes from the Hebrew חָנָן (chanan), which means "he is merciful" or "he is gracious." It is a theophoric name expressing mercy and grace, divine qualities. The root evokes the idea of bending down with compassion, showing favor towards someone. This name was borne by several important figures in the history of Israel.
H2605O.emploi: Hanan appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 35:4. He is designated as the son of Jigdalia and described as a "man of God," suggesting a status of religious or prophetic respectability. A room in the temple bore his name, indicating either that he owned it or that he was associated with it in a particular way. The context of the passage shows Jeremiah using this room to test the faithfulness of the Rechabites to the order not to drink wine given by their ancestor Jonadab.

sens: Fortified tower in the northeast of Jerusalem, part of its defenses
Landmark for delineating the city's boundaries
Symbol of the reconstruction of Jerusalem
H2606.detail:
1. The Tower of Hananeel is a concrete fortification in the northeast of Jerusalem, mentioned as a starting or ending point in the description of the walls. During the reconstruction under Nehemiah, this tower marked one of the key points of the walls (Nehemiah 3:1), and it served as a tangible geographical landmark for the inhabitants.
2. It appears as a territorial boundary in several prophetic visions: Jeremiah mentions it while announcing the renewal of the city (Jeremiah 31:38), and Zechariah cites it to delineate the extent of restored Jerusalem (Zechariah 14:10). It is always associated with other landmarks (Tower of Meah, Gate of Benjamin, Corner Gate).
3. The tower symbolizes the restoration and divine protection of Jerusalem: in prophetic promises, it marks the heart of the city that God raises up and preserves for His people.
H2606.origine: The name means "God has shown grace" or "God has favored," formed from two Hebrew roots: "hanan" (grace, favor) and "el" (God). This tower bears a theophoric name — that is, containing the name of God — common in Israel to express trust in divine protection. It likely derives its name from its function: a tower where God's grace was exercised in protecting the city.
H2606.emploi: The Tower of Hananeel appears four times in Scripture, always to describe Jerusalem and its boundaries. Under Nehemiah, it was rebuilt as an integral part of the defensive system of the city restored after the exile (Nehemiah 3:1 and 12:39). In later prophecies, it becomes a symbolic landmark: Jeremiah uses it to announce a renewed Jerusalem (Jeremiah 31:38), and Zechariah, in his eschatological vision, mentions it as a boundary of the transformed Jerusalem at the end of time (Zechariah 14:10). It appears only in these four passages, always linked to the reconstruction or the restored vision of the holy city.
H2606.portee: The Tower of Hananeel reminds the believer that God does not abandon His people: even after exile, even in disaster, the city is rebuilt and its boundaries are once again delineated. It embodies divine faithfulness that restores what seemed lost, and it directs the gaze towards the promises of ultimate renewal that the prophets announce for Jerusalem.

sens: A prophet and seer during the divided monarchy in Israel and Judah
H2607G.detail: Hanani is first mentioned as the father of the prophet Jehu, who delivers the word of the Lord against Baasha, king of Israel (1 Kings 16:1, 16:7). He is also a seer who appears before King Asa of Judah to rebuke him for seeking help from the king of Syria instead of trusting in God (2 Chronicles 16:7). His son Jehu also intervenes with King Jehoshaphat to warn him against supporting the wicked (2 Chronicles 19:2), and his records are documented in the book of the kings of Israel (2 Chronicles 20:34).
H2607G.origine: The name Hanani means "gracious" or "the one whom the Lord has favored." It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the divine name, expressing the idea that God grants His favor. Several men bear this name in the Old Testament, but the references primarily designate the father of the prophet Jehu.
H2607G.emploi: Hanani appears five times in the Hebrew Bible, all in the books of Kings and Chronicles. He is presented as a prophet and seer, that is, as a bearer of the divine word to the kings of Israel and Judah. His main role is to convey the warnings of the Lord: he rebukes King Asa for his lack of trust in God, and his son Jehu continues this mission by speaking harshly against the kings who stray from faithfulness to the Lord. These mentions underscore the importance of prophets in the governance of God's people during the monarchy.
H2607G.portee: Hanani illustrates the role of the true prophet: to speak courageously in the name of God, even to the powerful, to remind them of obedience and trust in Him. His example shows that true help comes from God alone, not from human alliances or earthly power. For the believer, this invites reflection on the importance of listening to the prophetic word and honoring those whom God sends to correct our paths.

sens: Son of Heman, musician of worship under David
Chief of the eighteenth division of service at the temple
H2607H.detail:
1. Hanani is a Levite, son of the famous musician Heman, mentioned among the singers and musicians attached to the service of the temple (1 Chronicles 25:4). He is part of a large family of talented musicians.
2. He is designated as the chief of the eighteenth division of the temple musicians, responsible for a team of twelve men who took turns providing musical service and sacred songs (1 Chronicles 25:25).
H2607H.origine: The name Hanani means "gracious" or "merciful" in Hebrew, derived from the root "hen" (grace, favor). This name was borne by several important men in Israel's history, all marked by a particular service to God or the people.
H2607H.emploi: Hanani is mentioned twice in 1 Chronicles 25, a text that lists the organization of the temple musicians instituted by David. He is among the thirteen sons of Heman, chief of the royal musicians. The Bible distinguishes here the order of service: the eighteenth course was that of Hanani, with his sons and brothers forming a team of twelve people. These records show the importance that David placed on liturgical music and the precise organization of the teams responsible for worship.
H2607H.portee: Hanani reminds us that the service of God, even in its musical and liturgical aspects, requires order, discipline, and family transmission. His place in the organization of the temple shows that every believer, regardless of their function, has a defined role in the worship rendered to God.

sens: A man who, during the time of Ezra, took a foreign wife
H2607I.detail: 1. Hanani is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, during the return from exile. He was among the priests who, after marrying women of foreign origin, had to send away their wives according to Ezra's decree (Ezra 10:20). His name appears in the list of the sons of Immer, an important priestly family.
H2607I.origine: The name Hanani means "gracious" or "God has been gracious" in Hebrew, formed from the root חנן ("to show grace"). It is a covenant name that expresses divine blessing. Although several Hanani lived at different times in Israel's history — including the musician during David's time, the seer who reproached Asa, and Nehemiah's brother — this one is identified solely by this passage in Ezra.
H2607I.emploi: Hanani is mentioned only once in the Scriptures, in Ezra 10:20, where he is listed among the descendants of the priests who returned from exile in Babylon. This list records the men who had entered into mixed marriages with non-Israelite women, which was considered a violation of the law and the covenant. The inclusion of Hanani in this enumeration shows that even members of the clergy had succumbed to this practice during the exile.

sens: Brother of Nehemiah and governor of Jerusalem
H2607J.detail: Hanani is a figure from the time of the Exile and the Return. He was the brother of Nehemiah and lived in Jerusalem. In Nehemiah 1:2, he comes to bring news to Nehemiah about the state of Judah and Jerusalem. Later, Nehemiah entrusts him with an important charge: in Nehemiah 7:2, he appoints him governor of the citadel of Jerusalem, alongside Hananiah. Nehemiah chooses him for this responsibility because he considers him superior to others due to his faithfulness and fear of God. Hanani thus represents the trustworthy man, worthy of governing the holy city at the crucial time of reconstruction after the Exile.
H2607J.origine: The name Hanani means "gracious" in Hebrew, formed from the root "hanan" which means to show grace, to show kindness. It is a name that expresses divine favor or grace. Several men bear this name in the Bible: a musician son of Heman during David's time, a prophet who rebuked King Asa, a priest during Ezra's time, and this one, brother of Nehemiah.
H2607J.emploi: Hanani appears twice in the book of Nehemiah. First in Nehemiah 1:2, where he arrives from Judah with others to bring news to Nehemiah about the situation of the survivors and Jerusalem. Then in Nehemiah 7:2, where Nehemiah places him in a position of authority, designating him as governor of the citadel of Jerusalem. The text emphasizes that Nehemiah chose Hanani precisely for his faithfulness and fear of God, essential qualities in governing the holy city during a time of reconstruction.
H2607J.portee: Hanani embodies faithfulness and fear of God as criteria for true leadership. Nehemiah does not choose this man solely for his administrative abilities, but for his moral and spiritual integrity. This account reminds the believer that true responsibilities are only entrusted to those who sincerely fear God and live in accordance with His will.

sens: Chief musician during the time of Nehemiah
Son of the musician Heman
Levite serving in the temple of Jerusalem
H2607K.detail:
1. Hanani is a chief musician who served in the temple of Jerusalem under the leadership of Nehemiah. His name means "the one to whom God has shown grace." He appears in the account of the dedication of the walls of Jerusalem, walking in the praise procession with his brothers and musical instruments (Nehemiah 12:36).
2. He is the son of the musician Heman, one of the great chief musicians of David during the time of the Exile and the Return. This genealogy shows that he comes from a family of Levites dedicated to the musical service of the temple.
3. Hanani was one of the many Levites responsible for praise and sacred music, using the traditional musical instruments passed down by David for generations.
H2607K.origine: The name Hanani comes from the Hebrew root meaning "to show grace" or "to be gracious." It is a theophoric name — that is, a name that contains the idea of divine grace. In Israelite tradition, names expressed God's action or blessing towards the bearer of the name. This name was borne by several important figures in Israel's history, including a seer who rebuked King Asa and a brother of the governor Nehemiah.
H2607K.emploi: Hanani appears only once in the Bible in the sense we present here: in Nehemiah 12:36, during the ceremony of dedication of the walls of Jerusalem after the return from exile. He is mentioned as a chief musician walking in procession with his brothers Schemaiah, Azareel, Milalai, Gilalai, Maai, Nethaneel, and Judah, all armed with the musical instruments of David. This passage shows the importance of music and praise in the restoration of temple worship. The name Hanani in the Bible also refers to other figures — a son of Heman, a seer who reproached King Asa, a priest during the time of Ezra, and the brother of Nehemiah — but the only usage provided concerns this musician of Nehemiah.
H2607K.portee: This passage reminds us that musical praise was at the heart of the restored temple worship. Hanani and his brothers represent the commitment of the Levites to honor God through music, and the fact that Nehemiah mentions their role shows that the return to God was expressed not only through material reconstruction but also through the restoration of joyful and orderly worship.

sens: False prophet of Judah who opposed Jeremiah during the reign of Zedekiah
H2608A.detail: Hanania is a historical figure from the kingdom of Judah, a prophet from Gibeon who appears during the time of King Zedekiah. He is best known for his conflict with Jeremiah: while Jeremiah proclaimed that Judah would remain subject to Babylon, Hanania prophesied a quick liberation from the yoke of King Nebuchadnezzar within two years (Jeremiah 28:3-4). He even went so far as to remove the symbolic yoke that Jeremiah was wearing on his shoulders and break it before the people (Jeremiah 28:10), publicly affirming that God would break the Babylonian yoke. However, God contradicted Hanania by condemning him to death for speaking false words (Jeremiah 28:15-17), revealing him as a false prophet.
H2608A.origine: The name Hanania means "God has favored" or "God has shown grace," composed of the Hebrew root "hanun" (gracious, merciful) and the divine name Yah. It is a beautiful name, borne by several faithful men in the Old Testament — notably Shadrach, Daniel's friend, who refused to defile himself and was saved in the fiery furnace. But this Hanania from Gibeon proved unworthy by usurping the title of prophet.
H2608A.emploi: Hanania appears only in chapter 28 of Jeremiah, where he is mentioned in at least 6 verses. He is presented as a prophet from Gibeon, son of Azzur. At the beginning of Zedekiah's reign, he publicly rises in the temple to contradict Jeremiah's prophecy regarding captivity (Jeremiah 28:1-4). He dialogues with Jeremiah, who responds to him with dignity (Jeremiah 28:5-9), then he performs his symbolic act by breaking the yoke (Jeremiah 28:10-11). But Jeremiah then receives God's order to announce his judgment (Jeremiah 28:12-16), and Hanania dies shortly after (Jeremiah 28:17), confirming that he was indeed a false prophet.
H2608A.portee: The story of Hanania warns every believer of the danger of false prophecies. Even when a message seems more encouraging or pleases public opinion, only the true word of God matters. It also teaches us that God defends the truth of His word and judges those who counterfeit it. For us, it is a call to test every teaching in the light of Scripture and to remain faithful to the true message of God, even when it is difficult or unpopular.

sens: companion of Daniel at the court of Babylon, also called Shadrach
young man from Judah taken into exile
faithful friend who refused to defile himself
H2608B.detail: 1. Hanania is a young Judean of noble lineage, deported to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar during the conquest of Jerusalem. He is among the young men chosen to serve at the king's court (Daniel 1:3-4). 2. He is one of Daniel's three close companions: together, they refused to eat the royal food, as these foods violated the purity laws given by God to the Jews (Daniel 1:8). 3. Hanania is best known for his heroic act of faith: with his two companions Mishael and Azariah, he refused to bow down before the golden statue erected by Nebuchadnezzar and was thrown into the fiery furnace, from which God miraculously saved them (Daniel 3). The Babylonian king gave him the name "Shadrach" to erase his Jewish identity.
H2608B.origine: The name Hanania means "God has shown favor" or "God has been gracious," formed from two Hebrew elements: "Hanan" (favor, grace) and "Ya" (abbreviation of Yahweh, the name of God). This name expresses the belief that this child was the fruit of divine mercy. Several other biblical characters have borne this name, but this one is the most famous for his spiritual courage.
H2608B.emploi: Hanania primarily appears in the book of Daniel (chapters 1 to 3), where he is mentioned by his Hebrew name in Daniel 2:17, when Daniel informs him of the king's mysterious vision. In chapter 3, he is referred to by his Babylonian name "Shadrach." Along with Daniel and his other companions, he embodies faithfulness to God and the Law amidst a hostile pagan culture. His story shows how a young believer can remain true to his religious convictions in the face of political power pressures, refusing both moral corruption and idolatry.
H2608B.portee: The story of Hanania encourages the Christian who must live out his faith in a hostile or secular environment. His example shows that refusing to "defile" oneself — that is, compromising one's moral and spiritual principles — does not bring divine punishment, but rather deliverance. His courage in the face of the furnace reminds us that faithfulness to God, even at the cost of mortal risks, is honored by God Himself.

sens: Priest who restored a section of the wall of Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah
H2608G.detail: Hanania is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, during the reconstruction of the walls of Jerusalem under the leadership of Nehemiah. He is identified as the son of Shelemiah and participated in the restoration of a portion of the wall, thus contributing to the collective effort of rebuilding the city after the exile (Nehemiah 3:30). His name appears among the list of workers who labored on this great communal project.
H2608G.origine: The name Hanania means "God has shown favor" or "God has been gracious." It comes from the Hebrew root חנן (hanan), which expresses the idea of grace, compassion, and kindness. This name was borne by several important figures in biblical history, notably Daniel's friend who was renamed Shadrach, one of the three young men miraculously saved from the fiery furnace.
H2608G.emploi: Hanania appears only once in the Scriptures, in Nehemiah 3:30, as one of the many restorers of the wall of Jerusalem. He is presented as the son of Shelemiah and works alongside other laborers in this great rebuilding effort that took place after the Babylonian exile (around 445 B.C.). This usage shows that Hanania was an ordinary yet faithful man, participating in the work of restoring the holy city.
H2608G.portee: The mention of Hanania reminds us that God used anonymous and humble people to accomplish His great purposes. Although nothing else is known about this man, his work on the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem gives him a place in the history of God's people and shows how every contribution, even that of those forgotten by history, is significant in God's eyes.

sens: Chief of the citadel of Jerusalem under Nehemiah, brother or close associate of Hanani
H2608H.detail: Hanania is the head of the citadel (fortress) of Jerusalem during the time of Nehemiah, governor of Judah upon the return from the Babylonian Exile. He is presented as a man of remarkable character, distinguished by his faithfulness and fear of God — essential qualities for guarding the holy city. His name means "God has favored" in Hebrew.
H2608H.origine: The name Hanania comes from the Hebrew root חנן (hanan), which means "to favor," "to show grace." It is a theophoric name — it proclaims the action of God: "Yah (God) has favored." This type of name was common in Israel to confess divine goodness towards a family. Several biblical figures bear this name, each in a different context.
H2608H.emploi: The only certain usage of this Hanania in the Bible is Nehemiah 7:2, where he is named chief of the citadel of Jerusalem. He appears alongside Hanani (possibly his brother) as one of the trusted officials that Nehemiah appointed to guard the gates of Jerusalem and ensure the city's security during its reconstruction after the Exile. His administrative and military role, combined with his reputation for faithfulness and fear of God, illustrates the importance Nehemiah placed on moral integrity in public office.
H2608H.portee: The portrait of Hanania reminds the reader that the reconstruction of Jerusalem and the restoration of God's people required men of character — faithful, God-fearing, and trustworthy. This illustrates the biblical maxim that a community prospers when its leaders first seek to honor God.

sens: Biblical character from the time of exile and return
Man whose name means "God has shown favor"
H2608I.detail: Hanania is a name borne by several men in biblical history, from the time of exile in Babylon and after the return to Jerusalem. The most famous is Daniel's companion, whom Nebuchadnezzar renamed Shadrach: he is the one who refused to defile himself by eating the king's food and was thrown into the fiery furnace for refusing to bow down to the idol, before being miraculously delivered by the angel of the Lord. But the name also refers to other men: one of the sons of Heman and leader of a choir in the temple, a general in King Uzziah's army, the father of Zedekiah, a false prophet from Benjamin during the time of Zedekiah, and several others, including a priest who helped rebuild the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah (Nehemiah 10:23).
H2608I.origine: The name Hanania comes from Hebrew and literally means "God has shown favor" or "the Lord has been gracious." It is composed of the divine name (Yah) and a verb meaning "to show grace." It is a theophoric name, meaning it carries the name of God, expressing the belief that the child is a gift of divine favor.
H2608I.emploi: The name Hanania appears several times in the Old Testament, from the time of the Babylonian exile to after the return. The Bible mentions at least thirteen people bearing this name. The most well-known remains Daniel's young friend, also known by the Aramaic name Shadrach. Nehemiah 10:23 mentions him among the signers of Nehemiah's covenant after the return from exile, as a priest involved in the reconstruction of Jerusalem and in organizing worship.

sens: Man of Judah at the time of the return from exile, head of a priestly family
H2608J.detail: Hanania is a man's name that appears in the records of the Judean community after the Babylonian exile. He is mentioned as the head of a house of priests during the time of the high priest Jehoiakim (Nehemiah 12:12), where his name appears among the heads of priestly families responsible for organizing the worship of the rebuilt temple. This Hanania embodies the restoration of Israel's religious life after the return from exile.
H2608J.origine: The name Hanania means "God has shown favor" or "God has had mercy." It comes from the Hebrew root that expresses divine grace and mercy. It is a theophoric name (bearing the name of God) very common in biblical Israel, borne by several important figures: Daniel's companion known as Shadrach, a leader of the Levites, a general of King Uzziah, and others. The name expresses the faith of the parents in the compassion of the Lord.
H2608J.emploi: Hanania is a name borne by at least thirteen different people in the Hebrew Bible, from the time of exile to the post-exilic period. This Hanania of Nehemiah 12:12 belongs to the generation that restored the temple and the religious life of Jerusalem after the return from captivity. He is identified as a priest and head of a family, indicating a position of responsibility in the priestly hierarchy. His inclusion in the official register of priestly family heads shows the importance of clergy organization for the rebuilt Judean community.
H2608J.portee: The name Hanania reminds us that God never abandoned His people, even in exile. This character, recorded in the registers of the rebuilt temple, symbolizes the faithfulness of the Lord that allows for the return and restoration of worship. For the believer, this name evokes that divine grace persists through trials and judgments.

sens: Character from the time of exile and the return of Israel
H2608K.detail: Hanania is a name borne by several men in the history of Israel. In Nehemiah 12:41, he is a priest who participated in the consecration of the wall of Jerusalem, probably during the time of Nehemiah, after the return from the Babylonian exile.
H2608K.origine: The name Hanania means "God has shown grace" or "God has favored," composed of two elements: "Han" (grace) and "Yah" (God). It is a typical name of the people of Israel, expressing trust in divine goodness. Several biblical figures have borne this name at different times.
H2608K.emploi: In Nehemiah 12:41, Hanania is one of the priests who, to the sound of trumpets, participated in the solemn ceremony of consecration of the rebuilt wall of Jerusalem. He represents one of the priestly families that played a central role in the worship at the Temple after the return of the people of Israel from the Babylonian exile.
H2608K.portee: This passage shows us how, upon the return from exile, worship of the Lord was restored with solemnity and joy. Priests like Hanania had the honor of leading Israel in worship, marking the restoration of the religious life of the people after a period of desolation.

sens: Son of Zerubbabel, from the tribe of Judah, living during the time of the divided monarchy.
Father of several sons including Pelatiah and Isaiah.
H2608L.detail:
1. Hanania is a man from the tribe of Judah mentioned for the first time in 1 Chronicles 3:19 as the son of Zerubbabel (who himself was the leader who restored the temple after the exile). He belonged to the royal lineage of David and lived after the return from exile in Babylon.
2. Hanania had several sons: Pelatiah, Isaiah, Rephaiah, Arnan, Abijah, and Shecaniah, according to 1 Chronicles 3:21. His descendants connect him to the continuity of the people of Israel after the exile.
H2608L.origine: The name Hanania means "God has shown favor" or "God has been gracious." It comes from the Hebrew root "hanan" (to be gracious, to show kindness) and "Yah" (God, an abbreviation of the divine name). It was a name borne by several important figures in Israel's history, notably the companion of Daniel (also called Shadrach) who refused to defile himself by eating the king's food and was thrown into the fiery furnace.
H2608L.emploi: This particular Hanania, son of Zerubbabel, is mentioned only in 1 Chronicles 3:19-21, where his genealogy is given. These verses are part of the genealogical record of the royal house of David, established after the return from exile. The attention given to his descendants highlights his importance in the continuation of the messianic royal lineage. This Hanania is distinct from other Hananiahs named in the Bible (the companion of Daniel, the temple musician, the false prophet Hananiah son of Azzur, etc.).
H2608L.portee: This Hanania represents God's faithfulness to His promise made to David: despite the exile to Babylon, the royal line continued, and through Hanania and his descendants, God preserved the generation that would lead to the Messiah. Hanania reminds us that God keeps His commitments through the generations and that divine grace extends even after the judgment of exile.

sens: Father of Zedekiah during the reign of King Jehoiakim
H2608M.detail: 1. Hanania is a figure from the Old Testament whose name means "God has favored." He appears only once in the Bible, as the father of Zedekiah, an officer of King Jehoiakim. The text of Jeremiah 36:12 mentions him in the list of officials who gathered at the king's house to hear the reading of the scroll of Jeremiah by the secretary Baruch.
H2608M.origine: The Hebrew name Hanania (חֲנַנְיָהוּ) literally means "God has favored" or "God has shown grace." It comes from the root חנן (hanan), which means "to be gracious" or "to show mercy." This name reflects a trust in God's kindness toward the one who bears it.
H2608M.emploi: Hanania appears only once in the Bible, in Jeremiah 36:12, where he is identified as the father of Zedekiah. In this passage, Zedekiah is one of the officials who were in the chamber of the secretary Elishama when the scroll of Jeremiah was read there. This event takes place during the reign of King Jehoiakim, at a time when Judah was threatened by Babylon.

sens: Father of Shelemiah, grandfather of Jireiah
H2608N.detail: Hanania is a man who appears only once in the provided biblical text: he is the grandfather of Jireiah, commander of the guard at the Benjamin Gate. Jireiah is the one who stops the prophet Jeremiah, accusing him of deserting to the Chaldeans (Jeremiah 37:13). It is through this genealogy — Hanania, then his son Shelemiah, then the grandson Jireiah — that he is mentioned in biblical history.
H2608N.origine: The name Hanania means "God has shown favor" or "God has been gracious." It comes from the Hebrew root that expresses grace and divine kindness. It is a common theophoric name in Israel, borne by several men at different periods in biblical history.
H2608N.emploi: Hanania is named only once in the recorded uses: in Jeremiah 37:13, where he is identified as the grandfather of Jireiah, the commander of the guard at the Benjamin Gate. This context is at the end of the siege of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar, when the prophet Jeremiah attempts to leave the city and is arrested. Although the text does not recount anything about Hanania himself, his presence in the genealogy shows that he was a man of power: his grandson holds an important military position.

sens: Man from the tribe of Benjamin during the time of the divided monarchy
H2608O.detail: 1. Hanania is a man from the tribe of Benjamin mentioned only once in the Bible, during the time when the kingdom of Israel was divided between the North and the South. He appears in a genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin (1 Chronicles 8:24), where he is listed among the descendants of Shashak.
H2608O.origine: The name Hanania comes from Hebrew and means "God has shown grace" or "God has favored." It is composed of two elements: "Han" which relates to grace, and "Yah," the shortened divine name. This same name has been borne by several other important figures in biblical history — notably the companion of Daniel in the fiery furnace (renamed Shadrach by Nebuchadnezzar) and a false prophet during the time of Zedekiah — but this passage from 1 Chronicles 8:24 refers to a simple man from the tribe of Benjamin of whom we know nothing else.
H2608O.emploi: Hanania appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 8:24, in a genealogical list of the descendants of Benjamin. His only role is to be listed among the sons or grandsons of Shashak, alongside his brothers Ishpan, Eber, Eliel, Abdon, Zichri, Hanan, Elam, Anthothijah, Iphdia, and Penuel. This very brief mention, without any detail about his life or deeds, reminds us that many righteous and forgotten Israelites contributed to the life of their people without history retaining their names.

sens: Son of the musician Heman, leader of a division of the Temple musicians
H2608P.detail: 1. Hanania is one of the fourteen sons of the Levite Heman, a high-ranking musician serving in the Temple during the divided monarchy (1 Chronicles 25:4). He is designated as the leader of the sixteenth division or "course" of the Temple musicians, meaning he led a group of singers and musicians who took turns for worship (1 Chronicles 25:23). His name literally means "God has shown grace" or "God has been favorable."
H2608P.origine: The name Hanania comes from the Hebrew root חנן (chanan), which means "to be gracious" or "to be favorable." This same root has given rise to several biblical names carrying the same idea of divine grace (Hanani, Hannah, Jochanan). The suffix -iah or -yahu denotes God (Yahweh), so Hanania literally means "Yahweh has shown grace" — a name that expresses gratitude for the blessing received at birth.
H2608P.emploi: Hanania appears only in 1 Chronicles 25, where the musicians of Heman's family are counted during the time of David. He is first named among the thirteen sons of Heman listed in verse 4, and then the organization of the Temple service rotations is described in verse 23, where we learn that Hanania led the sixteenth course, assisted by his brothers. This detail underscores the importance of well-ordered religious offices in Israel's worship: the Temple musicians did not serve randomly, but according to an established schedule and clearly defined responsibilities.
H2608P.portee: Hanania's role in the service of the Temple reminds the reader that worship rendered to God must be organized with order and responsibility. Everyone has their place and function, and even a task that may seem secondary — leading a division of musicians — is part of the grand project of Israel's communal worship. It also shows that faith is lived out in daily life: each quarter, during the sixteenth week, Hanania and his men took their turn to praise God with their instruments.

sens: General of the army of King Uzziah (2 Chronicles 26:11)
Israeli military leader of the 8th century BC
H2608Q.detail: 1. Hanania is a significant military officer in the kingdom of Judah in the 8th century BC. He serves under King Uzziah and commands part of his army — that which goes to war in organized bands. He is one of the 'chiefs of the king,' a prestigious position that demonstrates his authority and the trust placed in him by the sovereign.
H2608Q.origine: The name Hanania comes from Hebrew and means 'God has shown grace' or 'God has favored,' composed of two elements: 'hanan' (grace, favor) and 'Yah' (the name of God). It is a common theophoric name in Israel — several Hananiahs appear at different times — expressing the parents' trust in divine benevolence towards their child.
H2608Q.emploi: Hanania appears only once in the Segond 1910, in 2 Chronicles 26:11, where he is presented as one of the military leaders of King Uzziah of Judah. He acts alongside the secretary Jeiel and the commissioner Maaseiah to organize the royal army into numbered companies. His role shows the administrative and military importance of his function in managing the Judean army at the time when Uzziah consolidates his power.

sens: Man who returned from Babylonian exile with Ezra
H2608R.detail: Hanania is an Israelite among the sons of Bebai who returned from Babylon with Ezra (Ezra 10:28). His name means 'God has shown favor.' Although not well known, he appears in the list of exiles who returned and committed to uphold God's covenant, particularly by renouncing their mixed marriages.
H2608R.origine: The Hebrew name חֲנַנְיָהוּ (Hananiah) is composed of two elements: חָנַן (hanan, 'to show grace, to show favor') and יָהּ (Yah, abbreviation of the divine name Yahweh). It literally means 'Yahweh has shown favor.' This name was common in Israel and borne by several important biblical figures, including Daniel's companion known as Shadrach.
H2608R.emploi: Hanania appears only once in the Bible, in Ezra 10:28, in the midst of a list of Israelites who returned from exile and had married foreign women, committing to end those unions. He is part of the sons of Bebai, a clan that had several members among the exiles. Ezra 10 documents this pivotal moment of the restoration of the Jewish people after the Babylonian captivity, when the returnees had to purify themselves and recommit to the Law.
H2608R.portee: This passage shows that even upon returning from exile, God's people had to continually struggle to remain faithful to their principles. Hanania, though anonymous, represents the thousands of ordinary Israelites who chose to return and submit to God's will rather than remain safe and comfortable in a foreign land.

sens: Priest and perfumer who participated in the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem under Nehemiah
H2608S.detail: Hanania is a man whose action is explicitly mentioned in Nehemiah 3:8: he was of the profession of perfumers (those who prepared sacred oils and incense) and he worked on the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem alongside the mason Uzziel. His name means 'God has shown favor,' which is fitting for a man who worked to restore the city's defenses and the temple worship.
H2608S.origine: The name Hanania comes from the Hebrew חָנַן (hanan), which means 'to show grace, to do favor,' and from יָהּ (Yah), a shortened form of the divine name. It expresses the belief that God has manifested His benevolence towards the one who bears this name. This name was borne by several men in the history of Israel, the most famous being Daniel's friend whom King Nebuchadnezzar called Shadrach.
H2608S.emploi: Hanania is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Nehemiah 3:8, in the context of the reconstruction of the wall of Jerusalem after the Babylonian exile. He is listed among the workers who participated in this great project under Nehemiah's leadership, around 445 BC. His profession as a perfumer indicates that he was a skilled craftsman, responsible for making the oils and incense used in temple worship. The Bible mentions him not to recount his personal life, but to honor his contribution to the restoration of Jerusalem.
H2608S.portee: The account in Nehemiah shows that the reconstruction of the wall was a communal effort: each, according to his trade and strengths, contributed his stone to the building. Hanania reminds us that ordinary work, done faithfully, contributes to God's plan for His people. The concrete commitment of this craftsman to the restoration of the holy city testifies that obedience to God is also lived out in practical action and sharing the communal burden.

sens: Young Jewish man during the Babylonian exile, also called Shadrach
One of Daniel's three companions at the court of Nebuchadnezzar
He who refused to defile himself by eating the king's food
He who was thrown into the fiery furnace for refusing to bow down to the idol
H2608T.detail:
1. Hanania is a young Jew from a noble family, deported to Babylon during the conquest of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar. His Hebrew name means 'God has shown grace.' The king gave him the Babylonian name Shadrach (Daniel 1:7).

2. Hanania is best known as the faithful friend and companion of Daniel. Along with Mishael and Azariah, he was among the most remarkable young men presented to the king: 'No one was found like Daniel, Hanania, Mishael, and Azaria' (Daniel 1:19).

3. He refused, along with his three friends, to defile himself by eating the food and wine from the king's table, which violated the dietary laws that God had given to the Jews. This courageous refusal to obey the king's orders demonstrates his faithfulness to God despite the exile.

4. His greatest act of faith was refusing to bow down before the golden statue that Nebuchadnezzar had erected. Thrown into the fiery furnace with his two companions, he was miraculously saved by the angel of the Lord, which led the king to recognize the power of the God of Israel.
H2608T.origine: The name Hanania comes from the Hebrew root 'hanan,' which means 'to show grace' or 'to show favor.' It is a theophoric name, meaning it contains the name of God (Yah, a short form of Yahweh), making it a name of trust: 'God has shown His favor.' This name expresses God's saving action towards His people.
H2608T.emploi: Hanania appears in four verses of the book of Daniel, all concentrated in chapter 1. He is first mentioned in Daniel 1:6 as one of the young Jews chosen to serve at the king's court. In Daniel 1:7, we learn that the king renamed him Shadrach. In Daniel 1:11 and 1:19, he is cited among the young men who refused to defile themselves and who distinguished themselves by their wisdom and appearance. These brief mentions in chapter 1 present him before the dramatic events recounted in chapter 3, where he will be among the three young men thrown into the fiery furnace.
H2608T.portee: The life of Hanania inspires Christians who, faced with the pressures of the world, must remain faithful to their convictions. His refusal to be corrupted by the riches and pleasures of Babylon shows that it is possible to live in exile while maintaining a pure conscience before God. His example teaches that true faithfulness is not without risk, but it attracts the favor and protection of the Lord.

sens: city in Egypt mentioned only once in the Bible
H2609.detail: Hanès is a city in Egypt whose exact identity remains uncertain. It appears in the context of Isaiah 30:4, where the envoys of the king of Judah go to it to negotiate with Egypt. According to ancient sources, it could be Tahpanhes, a fortified city on the eastern border of Egypt, or another locality in Lower Egypt, on an island in the Nile south of Memphis.
H2609.origine: The name Hanès would literally mean 'grace has fled' in Hebrew, although this etymology is debated. It is likely a Hebrew transcription of an ancient Egyptian name, the exact form and precise location of which archaeologists struggle to identify with certainty.
H2609.emploi: Hanès appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 30:4. The prophet mentions this city to denounce the Egyptian policy of the king of Judah: his princes went to Zoan and his envoys to Hanès, seeking support from the pharaoh. This allusion illustrates the temptation of the kings of Judah to rely on Egypt rather than on God.

sens: To be stained, defiled by a material or moral impurity
To profane, violate the sacred character of something
To make impure the one who commits evil or transgression
To corrupt morally or spiritually
H2610.detail:
1. To be stained, defiled: the word primarily describes an impurity that attaches itself to a person or a place. Numbers 35:33 speaks of blood that defiles the land: the shedding of unjustly spilled blood leaves an irreparable stain on the earth itself, as if it absorbs this guilt.
2. To profane, violate the sacred: to defile also means to transgress what is holy or protected. Isaiah 24:5 states that the land was profaned because its inhabitants transgressed the eternal covenant: one cannot live in rupture with God without polluting what surrounds Him.
3. To make impure through sin: the one who commits adultery or idolatry defiles himself. Jeremiah 3:9 asserts that Israel has defiled the land through its adultery with stone and wood (that is, with idols): sin does not remain secret; it affects the land, the people, to the point of breaking the bond with God.
4. To corrupt morally: to defile also designates internal corruption, a departure from justice. Psalms 106:38 reports that innocent blood was shed in idolatrous sacrifices, and the land was profaned: murder and apostasy together transform a nation into a guilty and impure nation.
H2610.origine: The Hebrew verb חָנֵף (chaneph) comes from a root that first evokes the idea of staining, marking with a visible defilement. It is used in a physical sense (the blood that defiles the ground) and in a spiritual sense (the sin that defiles the soul and the people). The passive form ('to be defiled') describes the state of the one or that which receives the stain; the active form ('to defile') describes the action of the one who causes it. It is a key word in biblical theology of purity and impurity.
H2610.emploi: The verb χάνηφ appears 9 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the prophetic books (Jeremiah, Isaiah) and the Psalms. It always designates a defilement caused by sin: murder (Numbers 35:33, Psalms 106:38), transgression of the covenant (Isaiah 24:5), adultery and idolatry (Jeremiah 3:1-9), apostasy (Daniel 11:32). The land or the entire people can be defiled, not just the guilty individual: the evil of one spreads to all. This spiritual pollution can only be erased by the shed blood of the guilty or by sincere repentance.
H2610.portee: This word reminds us that sin is never a private matter: it defiles not only the guilty party but spreads to all that surrounds them, their family, their people, their land. That is why confession and repentance are essential to restore spiritual purity. For the Christian, this also sheds light on why Jesus offers Himself as a sacrifice to take away the sins of the world: only the blood of a perfect innocent can purify what sin has defiled.

sens: One who rejects God and His laws
One who feigns piety while acting against it
One who profanes the sacred
The wicked and irreligious man
H2611.detail: 1. The wicked is primarily one who deliberately abandons God, who 'forgets God' as Job 8:13 says: he refuses to fear Him and obey Him. It is a conscious and voluntary refusal, not ignorance. 2. There is also the idea of deception: the wicked hides, he feigns an honest appearance to deceive. Psalms 35:16 shows him who 'sneers' in secret, 'a parasite' who grinds his teeth against the righteous while appearing respectable. 3. The wicked profanes holy things, defiling them through his contempt and unbelief. His lifestyle — that of a wicked man — contradicts divine laws. 4. In the wisdom texts of Job and Proverbs, the wicked is simply the quintessential evil man, one who lives without regard for God. His hope is vain (Job 8:13) and his house barren (Job 15:34).
H2611.origine: The Hebrew word חָנֵף (chàneph) comes from a root that means 'to defile, to be rotten.' The wicked is literally one who has defiled himself by abandoning communion with God. That is why the word also carries the idea of profanation: he contaminates what he touches. The root evokes a moral and spiritual filth.
H2611.emploi: The word appears 13 times in the Old Testament, mostly in the wisdom literature: Job (8 occurrences), Psalms (1), Proverbs (1), Isaiah (2), Isaiah (1). The writers of the book of Job use it to designate those who reject God or act against Him: their houses do not prosper, their hope is brief, their triumph is fleeting. Isaiah 9:16 associates it with the 'wicked' to describe the people who utter infamies. The word never designates a mere mistake or weakness, but a choice to turn away from God.
H2611.portee: For the Christian reader, the wicked is a call to examination: am I not pretending piety while acting against it? The word also reassures: God sees the wicked, condemns his apparent triumph, and exposes him. The hope of one who rejects God will disappear.

sens: Wicked conduct, disrespectful towards God
Moral dishonesty, absence of justice
Religious or social hypocrisy
H2612.detail:
1. Impiety is the attitude of one who rejects or despises God and His will. It is a criminal and rebellious conduct against the Lord. In Isaiah 32:6, the fool 'devotes himself' to impiety: this means that his heart is turned towards evil and that he speaks against the Lord with lies.
2. Impiety leads to injustice towards others: it is not helping the hungry, refusing to give drink to the thirsty. It is a moral revolt that also affects one's neighbor, for one who despises God does not respect men either.
3. Impiety can also designate hypocritical falsehood: telling lies against the Lord while maintaining an appearance. It is refusing to acknowledge divine truth and justice.
H2612.origine: The word comes from a root that carries the idea of soiling, profaning, or dishonoring. Impiety is not so much theoretical unbelief as a conduct deliberately turned towards evil and contrary to the holiness of God. It is the practical refusal of moral and spiritual purity.
H2612.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Isaiah 32:6. The prophet uses it to describe the behavior of the fool, one whose heart is occupied by evil. It is a prophetic judgment addressed to one who commits social injustice — not feeding the hungry, refusing water to the thirsty — and who spreads lies against God. The context shows that impiety is inseparable from injustice towards one's neighbor.
H2612.portee: This word reminds the believer that impiety is not a mere religious opinion, but an active moral reality: it is refusing to serve God and mistreating others. It highlights that respect for God and social justice are linked. One who despises the Lord also rejects the responsibility to relieve the misery of one's neighbor.

sens: State of one who rejects God and His commandments
Hypocritical behavior that pretends to serve God while dishonoring Him
Moral and religious pollution that spreads among a people
H2613.detail:
1. Impiety is the refusal to acknowledge God or obey Him. It is the attitude of one who lives as if God does not exist or has no rights over their life. In Jeremiah 23:15, the false prophets are guilty of impiety: they speak in the name of the Lord without truly fearing Him, thus deceiving the people.
2. The word also refers to religious hypocrisy — pretending to serve God while living in a manner contrary to His laws. The prophets of Jerusalem commit precisely this betrayal: they claim to be messengers of the Lord, but their hearts are far from Him.
3. Impiety has a contagious force; it "extends" and "spreads" like contamination. It corrupts not only those who commit it, but it infects the entire land, leading others into unfaithfulness to God.
H2613.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be defiled" or "to be unclean." It expresses the idea that rejecting God or acting hypocritically creates a moral and spiritual impurity. In biblical Hebrew, impiety is a stain that spreads and demands judgment.
H2613.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Jeremiah 23:15. This is a crucial moment: the prophet Jeremiah denounces the false prophets of Jerusalem who deceive the people of Israel. The impiety they manifest — this mixture of prophetic lies and indifference to divine will — has spread throughout the land like poison. This passage shows that religious impiety is particularly grave in the eyes of God because it abuses His name and leads His people away from the truth.
H2613.portee: This word reminds believers that God takes religious sincerity and authentic obedience seriously. Impiety is not just a personal sin; it has collective consequences that affect an entire community. It invites us to examine our own hearts: do we seek to please God only in appearance, or do we offer Him true obedience and sincere fear?

sens: To kill by compressing the throat or asphyxiation
To kill or injure by violent constriction
H2614.detail:
1. The verb denotes the action of killing someone by tightening their throat, suffocating their breath. Ahithophel, King David's advisor, "strangled" himself — that is, he took his own life by compressing his throat — when he saw that the king did not follow his advice (2 Samuel 17:23).
2. The word also applies to any act of killing or suffocating by violent constriction. The lion, in its ferocity, "strangled" its prey for its lionesses, killing them by squeezing tightly before devouring them (Nahum 2:13).
H2614.origine: The Hebrew verb חָנַק comes from a root that evokes the idea of asphyxiation and compression. The so-called "Niphal" form (which often expresses an action that the subject undergoes or inflicts upon themselves) denotes the suffocation of a person by themselves; the "Piel" form (which intensifies the action) marks the violent strangulation inflicted on someone else. The word appears only twice in the Bible, always to describe this violent death by asphyxiation.
H2614.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In 2 Samuel 17:23, Ahithophel, the renowned advisor of King David, commits suicide by strangling himself after the king rejects his counsel. This is an act of despair and shame. In Nahum 2:13, the prophet describes the ferocity of the lion hunting: the animal "strangled" its prey to feed its lionesses. Both usages emphasize death or suffocation by compression; the context varies, one being a suicide, the other an act of animal predation.
H2614.portee: This verb reveals the weight of despair: Ahithophel's suicide by strangulation shows how pride and the rejection of counsel can lead to a tragic and shameful end. For the Christian reader, this invites humility and trust in God rather than in one's own wisdom. The word also confronts us with the raw image of death and destruction, reminding us of the reality of sin and its consequences.

sens: City in the territory of Zebulun
H2615.detail: Hannathon is a small city located in the territory assigned to the tribe of Zebulun during the division of the promised lands. Its Hebrew name means "gracious" or "full of grace." It is mentioned only once in the Bible, in the description of the borders of Zebulun's territory, where it marks a geographical landmark (Joshua 19:14).
H2615.origine: The name Hannathon comes from Hebrew and literally means "gracious," composed of a word expressing grace or divine favor. It is a toponym — a place name — typical of Canaanite cities in northern Palestine.
H2615.emploi: Hannathon appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:14, where it is listed in the text that enumerates and describes the cities of the territory assigned to the tribe of Zebulun after the conquest of Canaan. It plays no narrative role; it simply serves as a landmark to establish the borders of this territory. Its exact location in ancient Palestine is not precisely known today.

sens: To act with goodwill and generosity towards someone
To demonstrate faithfulness and attachment in a relationship
To conduct oneself rightly and loyally in response to the righteousness of others
H2616A.detail:
1. The verb expresses the action of showing, of concretely manifesting kindness — not just an inner feeling, but an act of goodwill that is seen and experienced. In 2 Samuel 22:26, David affirms that God "shows kindness" to the one who is good, meaning He acts towards him with favor and generosity.
