2. This word carries the idea of faithful and lasting kindness, linked to attachment and loyalty in an established relationship. It is to show devotion to someone with whom one has a bond: a friend, an ally, a faithful servant.
3. The meaning often nuances into that of reciprocity: one shows kindness to the one who has shown it in the same way, responding to righteousness with righteousness. Psalm 18:26 illustrates this parallelism: God shows kindness to the good, upright with the upright — He corresponds to what one is.
H2616A.origine: The verb חָסַד (hasad) comes from a root that evokes active kindness and manifested goodwill. It is very close to the noun חֶסֶד (hèsed), which denotes faithful kindness, grace, mercy — a committed and enduring kindness that characterizes God's covenant with His people. The form here (Hithpael) literally means "to show kindness to oneself" or "to show kindness towards": it is to actively express this kindness in a relationship.
H2616A.emploi: This verb appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, in two parallel passages: 2 Samuel 22:26 and Psalms 18:26. In both contexts, it is David who praises how God shows kindness to the one who is good and upright with the upright man. The word emphasizes divine faithfulness in response to human faithfulness: God does not withhold His kindness from the one who seeks and practices it. It is less a statement of universal principles than an affirmation of trust in divine reciprocity.
H2616A.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God's kindness is not indifferent or automatic — it is expressed and lived in relation to our own path. By living righteousness and faithfulness, we do not force God: we open ourselves to His kindness, which is always ready to manifest. This word calls for a life of integrity, based on the trust that God responds to the one who sincerely seeks to please Him.

sens: Overwhelm someone with shame or dishonor by revealing their secrets
Subject someone to public contempt or guilt
H2616B.detail:
1. The verb means to cover someone with shame: it is to overwhelm them with dishonor, to load them with ignominy. This happens to someone whose secrets are betrayed — in Proverbs 25:10, the one who reports the words of a friend risks covering that friend with shame, destroying their reputation. The image is that of a garment or shroud of shame that envelops the person and exposes them to contempt.
2. This verb also expresses the result of shameful conduct: being laid bare, being exposed to public judgment. One who sees their secrets revealed feels dishonored, and their bad reputation becomes impossible to erase.
H2616B.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that carries the idea of covering or enveloping, hence the meaning of "covering with" something — in this case, shame or disgrace. The form used here (Piel) intensifies the action, marking a deliberate act of dishonor inflicted on someone.
H2616B.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Bible, in Proverbs 25:10. In this context of practical wisdom, it warns against betraying the secrets of others: the one who divulges what a friend has confided to them in secret covers them with shame and destroys their honor. It is a rare word that underscores the seriousness of the violation of trust and its lasting consequences on the victim's reputation.
H2616B.portee: This verse teaches Christians the fundamental respect for trust and secrecy. Keeping silent about the weaknesses or secrets of a friend is not just politeness: it is an act of protection of their honor and dignity. Conversely, the one who reports the secret words of others commits a sin of the tongue that destroys relationships and permanently marks the one whose trust has been betrayed.

sens: Action of treating someone well, showing them kindness
Feeling of compassion and tenderness towards one who suffers
Faithful commitment to keep promises and be loyal
Free grace given without being deserved
Concrete act of generosity and help
Favor and protection received from one who has power
H2617A.detail:
1. Goodness is primarily a disposition to do good towards others. Lot tells the Lord that He has "shown him the greatness of His mercy by preserving his life" (Genesis 19:19): it is the concrete action of one who prefers the good of another.
2. It is accompanied by compassion in the face of distress: "you deliver my soul from the depths of the grave" (Psalms 86:13) expresses a heartfelt impulse that cannot bear the suffering of one to whom one is attached.
3. Goodness is also faithfulness and constancy in covenant, in promise: one asks the Lord to "show kindness and faithfulness" (2 Samuel 15:20), as if it were not enough to do good once, but to persevere.
4. It is often free and not earned by our merits: it is a favor given freely, a grace received of which one recognizes they have not earned it.
5. Goodness is manifested in acts: it helps, protects, keeps alive (Genesis 39:21 where the Lord is with Joseph in prison).
6. It also designates the benevolence of the king or the powerful towards those who depend on him: receiving "goodness" from the Most High means being assured of the support of one from whom nothing can be demanded.
H2617A.origine: The Hebrew word חֶ֫סֶד (hesed) comes from a root that expresses the idea of inclination, of leaning of the heart. There is no common corresponding verb in the Old Testament, but the word itself designates less a vague feeling than an active disposition: that of the heart that leans towards one in need. The Lord, in the Hebrew Bible, is presented as abundant in hesed (Exodus 34:6: "the Lord, the Lord, a merciful God"), which makes it a constitutive attribute of His nature and His covenant with His people.
H2617A.emploi: The word hesed appears 239 times in the Hebrew Bible, much more often in the Psalms, the narratives of the Sword (Samuel, Kings), and the books of covenant (Exodus, Deuteronomy). Three main uses dominate: first, goodness as a trait of God towards His people, solid and inexhaustible ("His mercy endures forever," Psalms 118:4); secondly, goodness requested or rendered between men, a sign of loyalty (between David and Jonathan, between Boaz and Ruth); finally, goodness as reward or favor from the king towards his subjects. The word also carries a nuance of commitment: it is not sentimental goodness, but goodness linked to the pact, to the covenant. That is why it is said to be "eternal" or "forever."
H2617A.portee: For the Christian reader, this word reveals that God is not a distant power but a faithful ally whose goodness is the very heart of His being. It is a word of comfort: when all seems lost, one can cry out to God, "make me know Your goodness" (Psalms 143:8) and rely on Him not out of obligation, but because it is His nature. Moreover, hesed invites every believer to reflect this goodness towards others, to descend from the throne of our self-sufficiency to lean towards those in need of us.

sens: Dishonor, disgrace caused by a reprehensible act
State of a person or a nation covered with shame
Attack on honor and dignity
H2617B.detail:
1. Infamy is primarily the dishonor that attaches to a shameful action or one contrary to divine law. In Leviticus 20:17, the sexual union between brother and sister is called an "infamy": it is a transgression that sullies the one who commits it and exposes them publicly to contempt.
2. It is also the state of a person or a community that bears the weight of this disgrace. In Proverbs 14:34, sin is described as "the shame of nations": it debases and humiliates an entire nation in the eyes of all, contrasting with justice that elevates it.
3. The word finally designates the deep attack on honor and dignity that results from transgression and that is exposed to public view.
H2617B.origine: The Hebrew word חֶסֶד (hesed) is here taken in its sense of infamy or dishonor. It is a rare word in this sense; in other contexts, a similar word may designate mercy or goodness, but here the Hebrew clearly expresses the idea of a disgrace that tarnishes the guilty party. The root refers to the idea of what is visible, hence the image of public dishonor: something that is seen, that is exposed.
H2617B.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Leviticus 20:17, it qualifies the infamy of incest, an act that exposes its authors to the death penalty. In Proverbs 14:34, it characterizes sin as a source of shame for an entire people. In both cases, infamy is linked to the breaking of divine law and has visible social and spiritual consequences: it dishonors not only the individual but also the entire community.
H2617B.portee: This word reminds us that sin is never a private matter: it tarnishes the honor of the one who commits it and reflects on their family, their people, their loved ones. For the believer, it underscores the importance of justice and obedience, for the transgression of the limits that God has set brings dishonor and disgrace. It is a call to preserve one's moral integrity and that of one's community.

sens: Officer or administrative chief under the reign of Solomon
H2618.detail: Hesed is a character mentioned only once in the Bible, in the context of the administrators that King Solomon placed over the various regions of Israel. His son, Ben-Hesed, was responsible for the region of Arubboth, with authority over Soco and the land of Hepher (1 Kings 4:10). Although the text is brief, it indicates that Hesed was a trusted man of the king, belonging to the royal administration during Solomon's prosperous time.
H2618.origine: The name Hesed means "son of fidelity" or "son of goodness": it reflects an important moral virtue in Hebrew thought. The Hebrew term חסד (hesed) that composes this name designates fidelity, loyalty, and mercy — ideal qualities for a man holding a position of responsibility with the king.
H2618.emploi: Hesed appears only once in the canonical Bible, in 1 Kings 4:10. He is cited as the father of Ben-Hesed, one of the twelve commissioners or administrative prefects that Solomon had established to govern different regions of the unified kingdom and collect taxes and provisions. This passage is part of a listing showing the sophisticated administrative organization of the kingdom under Solomon, reflecting his wisdom in governance.

sens: Son of Zerubbabel, of the tribe of Judah, during the time of the divided monarchy
H2619.detail: Hasadia is a character from the Old Testament mentioned only once in the Bible. He is one of the sons of Zerubbabel, the governor of Judah who returned from Babylonian exile and restored the temple. He appears in the genealogy of Judah in 1 Chronicles 3:20, where he is listed among the five sons of Zerubbabel along with his brothers Hashubah, Ohel, Berechiah, and Jushab-Hesed.
H2619.origine: The name Hasadia means "the Lord has been faithful" or "Jehovah has been faithful" in Hebrew. It is formed from two elements: "Has" (the mercy, the faithfulness of God) and "Yah" (the Lord). This name expresses a trust in God's constant kindness towards His people, particularly appropriate for a descendant of Zerubbabel who had experienced exile and longed to return.
H2619.emploi: Hasadia is mentioned only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 3:20, in the genealogical list of David's descendants. He is listed as one of the five sons of Zerubbabel, himself the son of Shealtiel and a key figure in the return from exile. This genealogy connects the Davidic dynasty to the post-exilic period and shows the continuity of God's people despite captivity. His appearance in this genealogical context emphasizes the importance of preserving the memory of royal families and their heritage.
H2619.portee: The name Hasadia, "the Lord has been faithful," reminds the reader that God has never abandoned His people, even during the exile in Babylon. The presence of this name in the post-exilic genealogy of Judah manifests divine faithfulness to the promises made to the ancestors and encourages the believer to trust in God's constancy during trials.

sens: Flee to escape danger and find protection
Seek help from someone or something stronger
Place one's trust in God, rely on Him
Find shelter and security under protection
H2620.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a concrete flight: one takes refuge when one runs to safety, away from peril. It is seeking asylum in a protected place, like the sons of Israel who would have sought refuge with their idols (Deuteronomy 32:37).
2. The word also evokes the idea of throwing oneself into someone's arms for salvation, seeking help by imploring their strength. Those who seek refuge in God entrust their lives to His goodness and justice (Psalms 36:8).
3. Gradually, the meaning rises and becomes spiritual: taking refuge in God means placing absolute trust, hope, and expectation in Him (Psalms 5:12). It is making God the foundation of one's inner security, even amid storms.
4. The metaphor changes image: the one who takes refuge in God finds shelter under His wings, like a chick under its mother's feathers (Psalms 91:4). This shelter is impregnable—a living shield against all evils.
H2620.origine: The Hebrew verb חָסָה (chasah) literally means "to hide," "to take cover." Its root image is that of fleeing and retreating to a safe place. The word belongs to a family of ideas where the vulnerability of the fugitive finds response in the strength of a fortress or a powerful person. This root is frequent in the poetry of the Psalms, where trust in God is constantly painted in the colors of protection and refuge.
H2620.emploi: The verb appears 36 times in the Hebrew Bible, almost exclusively in the Psalms (28 occurrences) and often in parallel with other expressions of trust. Especially in David's case, the hunted and threatened man, the word recurs as a leitmotif: taking refuge in God is the response of faith in the face of enemies (Psalms 2:12, 18:31). Psalm 91, a poem of protection, uses it to describe the intimacy between God and the one who trusts (Psalms 91:4). It is also found at the heart of liturgical confessions (Proverbs 30:5) or prophetic promises (Isaiah 14:32). The meaning remains stable: it is always a movement of the soul towards security, concrete at first, then entirely spiritual.
H2620.portee: For the believer, this word reminds a fundamental truth: life is filled with dangers—material, moral, spiritual—and human beings alone are weak. But faith offers a real escape: running to take refuge in God, sheltering in His strength, is to discover a protection that reassures and liberates. This is not superstition; it is the recognition of reality: placing one's trust in the One who is greater than the threats.

sens: Fortified city in the territory of Asher, in ancient Israel
H2621G.detail: Hosa is a fortified city mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time of the land division among the tribes of Israel after the conquest of Canaan. It was located in the territory assigned to the tribe of Asher, in the northwest of the country, near the Mediterranean Sea. The text of Joshua 19:29 places it between Ramah and Tyre, as a geographical landmark defining the borders of Asher's inheritance: "It then turned toward Ramah, to the fortified city of Tyre, and toward Hosa, to reach the sea."
H2621G.origine: The name Hosa means "refuge" in Hebrew, derived from the root חסה (khassah) which expresses the idea of seeking protection or shelter. This root is the same as that of the verb "to take refuge" or "to find a refuge," common in the Psalms. The name suggests that this locality may have been a strategic place of refuge or protection on the coast.
H2621G.emploi: Hosa appears only once in the Bible, in the context of the land division after the conquest. Joshua 19:29 lists it as one of the border cities of the territory of Asher, at the northwestern edge of Israel. Its role is purely geographical: it serves as a landmark to delineate tribal possessions and situate the inheritance of the people of Israel in the promised land.

sens: Porter of the temple during the divided monarchy
Chief of a family of Levites who were gatekeepers
Member of a tribe of Merari
H2621H.detail:
1. Hosa was a Levite who served as a porter of the temple in Jerusalem during the time when the kingdom was divided between Judah and Israel. He is first mentioned alongside Obed-Edom, with whom he was responsible for guarding the entrance to the sanctuary (1 Chronicles 16:38).
2. Hosa was the father of several sons—Shimri, Hilkiah, Thebaliah, and Zechariah—and he led an important family of Levites: his descendants and brothers formed a group of thirteen gatekeepers (1 Chronicles 26:10-11).
3. In the service of the temple, Hosa was assigned to guard the Shallecheth gate on the western side, where he ensured regular surveillance with other porters (1 Chronicles 26:16).
H2621H.origine: The name Hosa means "refuge" in Hebrew, expressing the idea of protection and shelter. This name reflects the spiritual function of the Levites: guardians and protectors of God's sanctuary, they ensured that the temple remained a holy and preserved place.
H2621H.emploi: Hosa is mentioned four times in Chronicles, always in relation to his service as a porter of the temple. The usages show that he was not a mere isolated guard, but the recognized head of a Levitical family involved in the organization of worship. His name appears alongside Obed-Edom in the enumeration of temple officials under King David, indicating his status and importance in the priestly hierarchy. His sons and descendants continued this holy charge, overseeing the various gates of the temple.
H2621H.portee: Hosa reminds us that serving the Lord, even in seemingly humble tasks, requires faithfulness and dedication. The porters of the temple were not second-rate servants: they guarded access to God's house and would pass on to their descendants a holy responsibility. His example speaks to those who perform discreet yet essential services in the Church.

sens: A safe place to take cover to escape danger
Refuge, protection offered by a power or authority
Help or support one relies on, often deceptive
H2622.detail: 1. The word primarily designates a physical place to take refuge, a natural or created shelter where one can be safe from a threat — such as seeking shade to protect oneself from the sun or prying eyes. 2. It also signifies the protection conferred by a political or military power: here, the "shelter" that the Egyptians are supposed to offer to the Judeans (Isaiah 30:3). 3. By extension, it refers to any form of support or recourse one seeks from someone or something — but the text from Isaiah shows that this shelter proves to be humiliating and worthless, since Egypt cannot truly save Judah.
H2622.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that carries the idea of hiding, covering, seeking protection. It is found in other Hebrew words expressing asylum, protective covering, or the shade that conceals. The primary image is that of natural cover — branches, rocks, shade — where one shelters from sight or inclement weather.
H2622.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 30:3. The prophet addresses the Judeans who seek to negotiate with Egypt for protection from Assyria. Isaiah denounces this strategy by saying that the "shelter" under Egyptian protection will bring them only shame and humiliation. Thus, it is an illusory shelter, a misplaced trust in human power instead of relying on God.
H2622.portee: This word challenges the believer to consider the true sources of protection and security. Seeking a "shelter" among the powerful of the world rather than in God is deceptive: only divine protection is reliable. It is an invitation to examine where we place our trust in trials and threats.

sens: One who keeps the covenant with God, who remains attached to Him
One who shows kindness and mercy
One who is pious, who fears God and seeks to please Him
One whom God loves and protects
H2623.detail:
1. The faithful one is primarily one who remains attached to God and His covenant. It is a trustworthy person towards Him, as seen in 2 Samuel 22:26 where the Psalmist sings: "You show yourself faithful to the one who is faithful" — there is a reciprocity: those who remain with God receive protection and favor.
2. The word also describes concrete kindness, mercy towards others. In Psalms 116:15, "the death of those who love Him" is precious in the eyes of the Lord: these are the faithful, people with generous hearts towards God and others.
3. The faithful one is one who fears God and seeks to do His will. In Psalms 12:2, the Psalmist cries out for help upon seeing the godly men vanish: these faithful ones are rare individuals who truly maintain the fear of God in a world that forgets Him.
4. Finally, the faithful one is recognized, loved, and protected by God. In Psalms 148:14, the Lord "has raised the strength of His people": this is a subject of praise for all His faithful ones, those He has chosen and in whom He rejoices.
H2623.origine: The Hebrew word חָסִיד comes from the root חסד (hesed), which means kindness, covenantal love, mercy. A faithful one is literally one who practices or manifests this hesed towards God and others. It is a term that describes a covenant relationship: the faithful one is one who responds to the Lord's covenant love by remaining attached to Him and living according to His will.
H2623.emploi: This word appears 33 times in the Old Testament, largely concentrated in the Psalms (about 30 occurrences). It designates the members of God's people who stand out for their commitment and faithfulness to the Lord. In Deuteronomy 33:8, Moses speaks of Levi as a "saint," a man in whom God could trust in times of crisis. The Psalms repeatedly affirm this: the faithful one is one who worships Him, praises Him, and receives His protection and mercy. Its meaning oscillates between personal piety and the quality of a community, but always within the idea of a lived covenant and a response of love to God's love.
H2623.portee: This word invites every Christian to recognize themselves as a "faithful" of God — not by personal merit, but by the covenant that God offers. It is a call to constancy, to remain attached to the Lord in difficult times as Moses and the psalmists did. For the believer, being faithful means concretely living out mercy: showing kindness as it has been received, and trusting God even when the world forgets Him.

sens: Large wading bird with a long neck and long legs
Migratory bird that faithfully returns to its home
Symbol of fidelity and filial piety in biblical imagery
H2624.detail:
1. The stork is a large bird with distinctive characteristics: it has a long neck, long legs, and impressive wings. Its appearance makes it easily recognizable, especially in biblical lists of clean or unclean animals. In Leviticus 11:19 and Deuteronomy 14:18, it is listed among the birds that the Israelites must not eat.
2. The stork is famous in the ancient East for its instinct for regular migration: it leaves the land in winter and returns at the same time each year. This trait is precisely what Jeremiah 8:7 highlights by saying that "the stork knows in the heavens its season," comparing it to other migratory birds that "observe the time of their arrival."
3. In biblical and Eastern imagery, the stork symbolizes fidelity, filial piety (tradition held that it cared for its aging parents), and the connection between heaven and earth. This symbolic charge appears in the vision of Zechariah 5:9, where two women with stork wings carry away the ephah (a commercial weight): the image evokes a majestic divine intervention.
H2624.origine: The Hebrew word חֲסִידָה (hasidah) comes from the root חסד, which expresses kindness, grace, and fidelity. This etymological link is not accidental: the stork received its name precisely for its legendary fidelity, its regular return, and its filial devotion to its parents. The name thus reflects the moral qualities that this bird embodies in the eyes of biblical culture.
H2624.emploi: The word appears six times in the Hebrew Bible, exclusively in contexts where creatures are enumerated. Twice (Leviticus 11:19 and Deuteronomy 14:18), the stork is included in the list of unclean animals that the Israelites cannot consume. The other occurrences use the stork as an example or image: in Job 39:16, its wings symbolize natural beauty; in Psalms 104:17, it represents the order and harmony of creation, establishing its home in the cypress trees; in Jeremiah 8:7, it becomes a living lesson of instinctive wisdom, contrasting with Israel's unfaithfulness; in Zechariah 5:9, it appears in a symbolic vision as an expression of divine power and movement.
H2624.portee: The stork invites the reader to meditate on the instinct created by God: this bird "knows" the laws of nature without human instruction, while God's people refuse to know His Law. It also reminds that God has ordered every creature to its place and time. For the believer, the natural fidelity and order of the stork become an encouragement to be faithful to God's Word and covenant.

sens: devastating insect with long legs and wings folded on its back
swarm of locusts devastating crops
developmental stage of a locust between larva and adult insect
destruction and desolation caused by these insects
divine judgment on a rebellious people
H2625.detail:
1. The word refers to this well-known jumping insect, characterized by its long hind legs and its ability to move by leaps. In Joel 1:4, it is listed among other species of locusts (gazam, jélek, hasil) that devour crops one after another.
2. This word is also used to refer to an army of locusts, a multitude that invades a territory and destroys everything in its path. Psalm 78:46 shows how locusts devour the crops and the produce of the farmers' labor, an image of total ruin.
3. In the succession listed in Joel 1:4, this word may refer to a particular stage in the development of the locust, distinct from the other species mentioned — perhaps the young or mature insect at a specific moment in its cycle.
4. Metaphorically, the word evokes complete destruction: Isaiah 33:4 compares the plundering of the spoil to how "one harvests the locust," as the insect ravages without leaving traces.
5. In the punishments sent by God, the locust symbolizes divine judgment: in 1 Kings 8:37 and 2 Chronicles 6:28, it is among the plagues sent against the unfaithful people, alongside famine, pestilence, and rust.
H2625.origine: The Hebrew word חָסִיל (hasil) literally refers to this well-known jumping insect from Mediterranean and Near Eastern regions. Several species of locusts are mentioned in the Hebrew Bible (gazam, arbé, jélek, hasil): each may have a specific name according to its developmental stage or precise species, but all refer to harmful insects of the same order. The word evokes through its imagery the animal that ravages, eats, devours.
H2625.emploi: This word appears six times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom books and the prophets. It is especially prominent in Joel (1:4 and 2:25), where four species of locusts are listed as successively devouring the crops — this passage describes a real plague or a vision of divine judgment. In 1 Kings 8:37 and 2 Chronicles 6:28, it appears in the list of evils sent by God as punishment for unfaithfulness. In Psalm 78:46 and Isaiah 33:4, it symbolizes the destruction of crops and human labor. The word can refer to the singular insect or the devastating multitude, depending on the context.
H2625.portee: The locust in the Bible is never a mere natural detail: it embodies God's intervention, either as punishment for sin or as a demonstration of His power. It teaches the believer that God controls even the smallest creatures to accomplish His judgment, and that unfaithfulness to divine commandments leads to visible and catastrophic consequences. This image also reminds us that God can both restore and destroy (see Joel 2:25, where He promises to compensate for the years of devastation).

sens: Who possesses remarkable strength or vigor
Who exercises great authority or influence
Who surpasses ordinary forces
H2626.detail:
1. The word describes one who has considerable physical or moral strength, capable of accomplishing what others cannot. In Psalm 89:9, the psalmist addresses God, calling Him "mighty": "O Lord God of hosts! Who is like You, mighty, O Lord?" It is God's power that enables Him to reign over all and accomplish His unshakeable purposes.
2. The word can also qualify one who exercises dominion or authority, one upon whom others cannot have a hold. The power here is not only physical but expresses absolute authority.
H2626.origine: This Hebrew word comes from a root that refers to the idea of strength and solidity. It belongs to a family of Hebrew terms that evoke robustness, the ability to stand firm and resist. The basic image is that of someone or something well-established, stable, that nothing can easily shake.
H2626.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Psalm 89:9. In this context, it is applied to God to express His absolute power and unmatched dominion over all that exists. The psalmist raises a rhetorical question: who could be as mighty as the Lord? It is an affirmation of divine superiority and God's unwavering faithfulness to His people.
H2626.portee: This word reminds the reader that God is not only benevolent but possesses the power necessary to fulfill His promises and protect His people. God's power is inseparable from His faithfulness: it is because He is mighty that one can rely on Him. For the believer, recognizing God's power invites trust and surrender in the face of life's challenges.

sens: Lacking weight, insufficient in substance
Deficient, absent, or incomplete
Figuratively: lacking value, merit, or seriousness
H2627.detail:
1. The word first describes what does not weigh enough, what is insufficient in quantity or substance — this is the literal sense of weight. In Daniel 5:27, King Belshazzar is "found light" in the balance, meaning that his moral weight is insufficient, that he lacks the required weight.
2. More broadly, "light" means what is lacking or not found in its rightful place. It is the absence or incompleteness: something essential is missing.
3. Figuratively, the word evokes what lacks seriousness, value, or moral substance. A king found "light" does not have the merit, authority, or value expected of him.
H2627.origine: The Hebrew word חַסִּר comes from a root that means "to lack" or "to be missing." It describes absence or insufficiency: what does not weigh enough, what does not measure up to the expected height. The family of this word in Hebrew includes the idea of deprivation and lack.
H2627.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in the dramatic episode of the weighing of King Belshazzar. The context is that of divine judgment: during the king's feast, a supernatural hand writes on the wall "Mene, Mene, Tekel, Upharsin." The prophet Daniel interprets this message: "Tekel" means you have been "weighed in the balance, and found light" (Daniel 5:27). This weighing symbolizes the moral and spiritual evaluation of the king. The word "light" emphasizes the king's insufficiency in the face of God's judgment: he does not have the weight, substance, or value expected of a ruler.
H2627.portee: This word reminds us that God weighs the hearts and actions of men according to His justice. Being "found light" means not holding the balance against God's expectations, lacking moral or spiritual weight. For the believer, it is an invitation to examine one's own substance before God: not to be superficial in faith, but to have weight, depth, and solidity in one's relationship with God.

sens: To eat and completely consume
To destroy or annihilate quickly
H2628.detail:
1. To eat and completely consume: the word describes the action of eating something until it disappears. In Deuteronomy 28:38, the locusts will "devour" the harvest, meaning they will eat it completely, leaving nothing for the reaper.
2. To destroy or annihilate quickly: in a figurative sense, the word evokes rapid and total destruction, as when a hostile force consumes or annihilates something. The idea is one of an end that leaves nothing remaining.
H2628.origine: The Hebrew verb חָסַל comes from a root that expresses the idea of consuming, finishing, or putting an end to something. The primary meaning is to eat, to devour, which then extends to any form of complete consumption or destruction. The family of this word revolves around the image of what disappears or comes to an end.
H2628.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 28:38, in the context of the curses pronounced against Israel if it disobeys the Lord. The locusts will devour the harvest: it is a concrete image of famine and divine judgment. The word illustrates how nature itself can be an instrument of God's punishment, or how the smallest creatures can annihilate human labor.
H2628.portee: This word reminds us that nothing is guaranteed in this world and that our security rests on obedience to God rather than solely on our efforts. In the face of plagues, big or small, the believer learns that God may allow our works to be destroyed to bring us back to Him.

sens: To put a device (a muzzle or a restraint) on an animal's mouth to prevent it from eating or biting
To close, block, or obstruct a passage or opening
H2629.detail:
1. Muzzling literally means placing a muzzle on an animal's snout to prevent it from eating or acting. In Deuteronomy 25:4, the Law commands not to muzzle the ox while it treads out the grain: the animal must be able to feed while it works, as it participates in the harvest. It is a rule of justice towards the beast.
2. Figuratively, the verb expresses the idea of closing, obstructing, or blocking. In Ezekiel 39:11, the "valley that will serve as a grave" will close the passage to travelers: it will be a tomb so large and deep that it will block the way. The image is of a place that closes in on the one it buries.
H2629.origine: The root חָסַם (cha.sam) expresses the action of closing, blocking, stopping. It evokes the primary image of a muzzle or a bridle that prevents action. The word belongs to a family of Hebrew terms describing obstacles or closures: anything that blocks, interrupts a passage or a function.
H2629.emploi: The verb appears twice in the Louis Segond translation. In Deuteronomy 25:4, it is a prohibition: "You shall not muzzle the ox" — a protection granted to the working animal, based on compassion. In Ezekiel 39:11, it describes the grave of Gog: this massive tomb "will close the passage to travelers." In each case, the meaning oscillates between the action of physically immobilizing (with a muzzle) and that of blocking, obstructing a space.
H2629.portee: This law in Deuteronomy teaches the believer that even in work, even the animal deserves respect and food: the Christian faith is rooted in compassion for all creatures. Ezekiel shows that God judges and stops the plans of the wicked, who can only be "closed" in death — an image of His ultimate victory.

sens: To set aside and keep for later
To accumulate, pile up
To hoard, accumulate wealth
H2630.detail:
1. To store means to keep something precious, to set it aside or stock it for future use or possession. The word evokes the idea of not spending or dispersing, but of retaining. In Isaiah 23:18, the prophet says that the gain from prostitution will not be "stored" — it will not remain in the hands of the courtesan, nor accumulate for her.
2. To store can also mean to pile up, that is, to amass in quantity. The contrast in the same verse shows that what is not stored by the courtesan "will provide" abundantly for the faithful of the Lord: the gain will thus be redistributed, not hoarded by the one who gained it unjustly.
3. Figuratively, to store evokes the attitude of one who hoards, who accumulates goods for oneself. It is the idea of selfishly retaining, as opposed to giving or letting circulate — what the text of Isaiah implicitly condemns by announcing that dishonest money will not remain in the hands of the sinner.
H2630.origine: The Hebrew word חָסַן (chasan) comes from a root that expresses the idea of keeping, retaining, hoarding. The cognate Aramaic חֲסַן (chasan) means "to possess." The word suggests a voluntary retention, an act of setting aside. In biblical context, it is mainly used to describe the accumulation of goods or wealth, often with a moral nuance: it is found especially when it concerns what should not be amassed or what will be confiscated.
H2630.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 23:18. It is used in the passive form (niphal): the immoral gains "will not be stored." This rarity gives weight to this prophetic passage: the prophet announces that dishonesty will not enrich the one who commits it — their gains will not accumulate, nor remain in their possession. It is an implicit divine judgment: ill-gotten wealth will not be retained.
H2630.portee: This word reminds believers of a profound truth: the goods accumulated through sin or injustice will not last. Scripture affirms that God does not allow the sinner to enjoy their dishonest acquisitions, but redirects them for good. It is an encouragement to trust in divine justice and a warning against lucrative dishonesty.

sens: To take possession of something, to become the owner
To hold firmly, to keep in one's possession
To exercise control or dominion over something
H2631.detail:
1. The verb primarily means to take possession of something, to become its owner. It is the idea of seizing and holding. In Daniel 7:18, the saints of the Most High "will possess the kingdom forever": they will receive and keep the eternal kingship.

2. The word can also evoke the idea of holding firmly, maintaining something in one's power. It is less about an instantaneous act than about a firm and lasting hold.

3. In a broader sense, to possess is to exercise dominion or control. In Daniel 7:22, "the time came when the saints possessed the kingdom": they received authority and dominion over the kingdom, fulfilling the divine promise.
H2631.origine: The word is Aramaic, an intensive form (aphel) of the verb חָסַן (ḥasan, Hebrew), which literally means "to hoard" or "to accumulate." The starting image is that of someone who accumulates, who keeps precious things. From there comes the idea of holding firmly in possession, then of possessing or dominating. It is a rare word in Scripture, mainly used in the Aramaic sections of Daniel.
H2631.emploi: The verb appears only twice, both in Daniel (7:18 and 7:22), in the vision of the four beasts and divine judgment. Both uses speak of the same event: the saints of the Most High will receive and possess the kingdom forever, after the Ancient of Days has granted rights to the elect. The context is eschatological: it concerns the promise that the faithful will ultimately inherit the divine reign. The word emphasizes both the reception of the kingdom and the firm and lasting possession of this royal authority.
H2631.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that God's promise to the saints is not temporary, but eternal and unshakeable. To possess the kingdom means not only to receive it, but to hold it with assurance, forever. It is a word of victory and comfort for those who suffer: the Most High guarantees His own the supreme and lasting inheritance.

sens: Ability to exercise authority
Physical or moral strength
Royal domination, sovereign power
H2632.detail:
1. The word denotes the concrete ability to exercise authority, to impose one's will: it is the power of action, the strength that allows one to command and decide. In Daniel 2:37, the king of Babylon receives from the God of heaven "the empire, the power, the strength, and the glory" — in other words, the complete authority to reign.
2. It is also the brute force, the physical or moral vigor that supports this authority. In Daniel 4:30, the king boasts of having built Babylon "by the power of [his] strength": he celebrates both his power (his royal authority) and his strength (the concrete means that made it possible).
3. In particular, it is the sovereign power of the king, his right and ability to govern his empire. The word characterizes the exercise of royal power in all its extent.
H2632.origine: This Aramaic word comes from the same family as the Hebrew word "authority" (shilton). It denotes power as the concrete ability of one who holds authority: the king who reigns as master, the sovereign who commands. The basic image is that of strength — physical or moral — that supports and realizes the exercise of power.
H2632.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in the book of Daniel, and only in passages where the king of Babylon speaks of his own power. In Daniel 2:37, it is part of a list of divine gifts: the empire, the power, the strength, and the glory. In Daniel 4:30, it appears when the king boasts of his achievements and magnificence. In both cases, it describes the sovereign power of the king, the concrete strength that allows him to reign and build his empire. It is an Aramaic word, reflecting the historical context of the book of Daniel and the kingdom of Babylon.
H2632.portee: This word reminds us that all earthly power, even that of the most powerful king, is given by God. The power that the king of Babylon claims has been granted to him by the God of heaven — it is neither absolute nor eternal. For the believer, it is a call to recognize that God alone is the source of all true power, and that no human authority can stand outside of His will.

sens: Accumulated material goods, fortune, assets
Abundance of resources, treasures
Source of security or power
Hidden or preserved treasure
H2633.detail:
1. The word denotes the totality of material goods that a person or community possesses: it is their fortune, what they have accumulated. Jeremiah 20:5 illustrates this well: the wealth of a city is its treasures, its precious reserves, everything that has value and can be plundered or taken away.
2. It can also mean general abundance, prosperity — not just a simple quantity, but a generous fullness. Proverbs 15:6 says that "great abundance" dwells in the house of the righteous: it conveys a sense of sufficiency and blessing.
3. Sometimes the word points to what makes one secure or powerful: a source of strength or confidence. Isaiah 33:6 calls wisdom and understanding a "source" of salvation — it is what protects and saves.
4. Finally, it can designate a treasure kept precious, what one guards as valuable and capital, as Isaiah 33:6 speaks of the treasure of Zion.
H2633.origine: The Hebrew word חֹסֶן comes from a root that expresses the idea of "keeping" or "preserving" — it thus denotes what one accumulates and keeps jealously. It belongs to the family of words related to security and shelter. In biblical context, wealth is never neutral: it can be a blessing or a temptation, the wealth of the righteous or the spoils of the wicked.
H2633.emploi: This word appears five times in the Old Testament, mainly in the wisdom books and the prophets. Proverbs uses it to contrast the prosperity of the righteous with the troubles of the wicked (15:6) and to remind of the instability of earthly riches (27:24). The prophets (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel) use it in contexts of judgment: they speak of wealth plundered by the enemy, treasures taken to Babylon, resources that corrupt prophets appropriate. The word thus carries different shades depending on whether it refers to wealth as a sign of divine blessing or as an object of human greed and judgment.
H2633.portee: This word invites the believer to meditate on the true nature of security. Proverbs teaches that the wealth of the righteous does not come by chance, but from integrity; it is never definitive (27:24), only the fear of God is a stable treasure (Isaiah 33:6). This word also reminds us that material possessions can become a trap — the prophets denounce those who enrich themselves at the expense of others. Reading "wealth" in Hebrew invites us to distinguish what truly enriches from what deceives.

sens: Possessing great physical or moral power
Having vigor, solidity
Ability or power to resist, to endure
H2634.detail: 1. The word first describes a person or thing endowed with great power: the strong man of Isaiah 1:31 is one who possesses strength and dominion, but the prophet announces that this human strength, without God, is illusory and fragile, destined to burn like stubble. 2. It also evokes structural solidity: in Amos 2:9, the Amorites are strong like oaks, with deep roots — an image of stability and resistance that seems unshakeable. 3. Finally, the word can designate strength itself, this capacity for power: the Amorites possess a strength comparable to that of the strongest trees, a power that God crushes nonetheless.
H2634.origine: The Hebrew word חָסֹן comes from a root that expresses robustness and the ability to hold, to resist. It is found in the idea of what does not yield, of what has a solid foundation. Its initial image is that of physical solidity, like that of a well-rooted tree or a stable construction.
H2634.emploi: The word appears twice in the Old Testament. In Isaiah 1:31, it qualifies the "strong" man — one who relies on his own power — to show the illusion of this human strength in the face of God's judgment: it will collapse like a spark. In Amos 2:9, it designates the strength of the Amorites, compared to that of oaks, to highlight the immensity of their earthly power before God breaks it. In both cases, the strength of the world, however imposing, is fragile and temporary before God.
H2634.portee: This word invites the believer not to rely on human strength — whether it be one's own strength, wealth, or power — for it remains illusory and perishable. Only the strength and stability that God provides endure. It is a lesson against pride and for trust in God rather than in oneself.

sens: Malleable and crumbly material, shaped by the potter to make vessels
Pottery debris, broken shard
Figuratively: weakness, fragility, unstable nature
H2635.detail:
1. Clay is the raw material of the potter: moist earth that can be shaped by hand to create objects. It is easy to form but fragile once fired. In Nebuchadnezzar's dream, the clay making up the feet of the statue symbolizes this malleability (Daniel 2:33).

2. The word can also refer to a piece of broken pottery, a shard. It is the broken material, reduced to pieces, that can no longer be used.

3. In a symbolic sense, the clay mixed with iron in the statue (Daniel 2:41-2:43) represents a divided kingdom, mixing strength and weakness. The clay that does not bond with the iron shows the impossibility of a lasting union: it is the biblical image of political instability and incompatibility.
H2635.origine: The Hebrew word חֲסַף comes from a root that expresses the idea of breaking or shattering. Clay is quintessentially the material that breaks, that shatters easily. In Hebrew, there is also the word יָצַר (yatsar), "to form," which refers to the work of the potter shaping the clay. This opposition between the malleability of the clay in its fresh state and its fragility once fired is fundamental in biblical imagery.
H2635.emploi: The word appears only in chapter 2 of the book of Daniel, 6 times, always in the interpretation of the dream of the four kingdoms. Nebuchadnezzar sees a great statue made of different metals and clay at the feet. The angel Gabriel explains to Daniel that each material represents an empire: the head of gold (Babylon), the chest and arms of silver (Medes and Persians), the belly and thighs of bronze (Greece), the legs of iron and the feet mixed of iron and clay (divided Rome). Here, clay symbolizes the final division of the last empire and its inability to remain united. Each occurrence reinforces this idea of instability: the clay breaks (2:35), it does not unite with the iron (2:43).
H2635.portee: For the Christian reader, this passage teaches that human kingdoms, no matter how powerful, rest on a fragile foundation destined to disappear. The clay mixed with iron of the last empire shows that even military power cannot create true unity. Only the kingdom of God, symbolized by the stone that becomes a mountain and fills the whole earth, is enduring and invincible. This image invites us not to place our trust in the empires of this world.

sens: Having the appearance of small scales or fine detached flakes
Resembling frost or fine pellicular particles
H2636.detail:
1. The verb literally means "to peel" or "to come off in scales." In Exodus 16:14, it describes the manna that fell from heaven: it has the appearance of small scales or fine flakes, as if it were sprinkled with fine detached particles that shine on the surface — exactly what one sees when frost covers the ground.
2. The word evokes the concrete image of a surface beaded with tiny elements that detach: Moses seeks to help Israel understand what manna looks like by comparing it to something visible and familiar, the white jelly of the morning. It is a description of the outward appearance of the miraculous gift.
H2636.origine: The Hebrew verb חַסְפַּס comes from a root that expresses the action of peeling, removing the skin, or scaling. It belongs to the group of descriptive verbs that imitate by sound the action they designate — here, the dry sound of the scale detaching. The corresponding noun can also evoke fish or reptile scales.
H2636.emploi: This word appears only once in the Bible, in Exodus 16:14. Moses and Aaron describe to the Israelites what covers the ground in the morning: there is something small "like grains" and "like white jelly." The use of the term "scaly" reinforces the idea that manna does not resemble anything we truly know, but that we can relate it to natural phenomena — frost, small crystals — to recognize and gather it.
H2636.portee: This word reminds us that God feeds His people in a very concrete way, in daily life. The detailed description of the manna — its appearance, its texture — shows that it is real, it can be seen and touched, it is not an illusion. For the Christian, it is a lesson in trust: God provides for our real, visible needs every day.

sens: To be absent, not present or available
To need something, to be deprived of it
To decrease in quantity, to become less important
To deprive someone of something (causative sense)
H2637.detail: 1. The verb describes what is not there or what goes away: the waters "decreased" after the flood (Genesis 8:3), the clothes did not "wear out" in the desert (Nehemiah 9:21). It is the absence or reduction of what was expected. 2. It also expresses need, scarcity: the one who gathers the manna "did not lack" it, everyone had what they needed (Exodus 16:18); the psalmist says, "I shall not lack anything" (Psalms 23:1), confident that God provides. 3. Sometimes, the verb carries the idea of gradual decrease or failure: the belly of the wicked "experiences scarcity" (Proverbs 13:25), the oil must "not lack" on your head (Ecclesiastes 9:8). 4. In the causative form, it means "to deprive of" or "to cause someone to lack": God commands to "provide" for the needs of the poor (Deuteronomy 15:8), which amounts to not letting them lack the necessities.
H2637.origine: The Hebrew verb חָסֵר (hasêr) comes from a root meaning "to cut off, to diminish." It is related to the idea of making something absent, leaving a void. The root is also used to describe what is incomplete or damaged. In Greek, the New Testament often uses the verb "hustéreô" to translate this same idea of lack or deficiency.
H2637.emploi: This verb appears 23 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives, the Psalms, and Wisdom literature. In the simple sense (passive), it describes absence or decrease: the floodwaters decrease (Genesis 8:3), God does not let the people lack anything in the desert (Nehemiah 9:21), the psalmist affirms he lacks nothing under the Lord's guidance (Psalms 23:1). In the causative form (active), it takes the meaning of "not giving," "refusing": one must not refuse to lend to the poor (Deuteronomy 15:8). The context is often that of divine providence: God "provides" or "does not let anything be lacking" to those who trust Him.
H2637.portee: This word invites the believer to meditate on divine providence: the people in the desert lacked nothing, despite forty years of wandering (Nehemiah 9:21), the psalmist can confidently affirm, "I shall not lack anything" (Psalms 23:1). It is a word of trust addressed to those who fear God. It also calls for generosity towards the poor: not to deny them the help they need (Deuteronomy 15:8).

sens: To be deprived of something, not having it
To fail someone, to let someone down
To be devoid of a moral or mental quality
H2638.detail:
1. The word describes one who is in need, who does not have what they require. When Pharaoh asks Hadad, "What do you lack from me?" (1 Kings 11:22), he is asking what is missing for him to be happy at home. It is the absence of something or a necessary condition.
2. The word can also indicate that something is missing, that it is lacking. In Proverbs 10:21, "the foolish die for lack of sense": reason is missing for them, it is absent in them. It is the lack of a quality or moral resource.
3. It primarily designates one who is devoid of discernment, common sense, or wisdom. In Proverbs 7:7, the young man "lacking sense" is someone who has not acquired wisdom, who lacks judgment and is easily seduced. It is a lack of intelligence or morality.
H2638.origine: The Hebrew word חָסֵר (cha.ser) comes from a root meaning "to be lacking, to be incomplete." It expresses the idea of emptiness, absence, deprivation. It is mainly found in wisdom literature (Proverbs, Ecclesiastes), where it characterizes one who does not have the necessary moral or intellectual qualities to live wisely. The root evokes concrete lack and lack of wisdom or virtue.
H2638.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the Old Testament, primarily in Proverbs (14 occurrences). It first describes material lacks: one who lacks bread (Proverbs 12:9), one who lacks reason (Proverbs 10:21). But its most frequent use concerns the lack of wisdom and discernment: "the boy lacking sense" (Proverbs 7:7 and 9:16), "one who lacks heart" (Proverbs 6:32). In Proverbs, the word implicitly opposes wisdom, discernment, and prudence. It is a characteristic of the fool who runs to his ruin.
H2638.portee: This word reminds the reader that wisdom, moral intelligence, and discernment do not come automatically. One who "lacks sense" puts themselves in danger: they are easily seduced, they act without considering the consequences. For the believer, it is an invitation to actively seek wisdom rather than remain lacking, and to recognize that the fear of God is the beginning of all understanding.

sens: Lack of food, hunger
Poverty, material deprivation
Absence, shortage of essential goods
H2639.detail: 1. The word primarily denotes the lack of food and hunger. In Job 30:3, impoverished men, "dried up by misery and hunger," flee into arid deserts: it is the concrete image of people who have nothing to eat, who are perishing. 2. More broadly, it is the state of poverty and material deprivation where one lacks what is necessary. In Proverbs 28:22, one who chases after wealth out of envy ends up receiving famine — impoverishment, the lack of everything that sustains life.
H2639.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to lack," "to be reduced to nothing." It expresses the idea of emptiness, absence, exhaustion — when resources are gone and nothing remains. It is a concrete term that paints the condition of the poor in ancient Israel.
H2639.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Job 30:3, it describes the miserable condition of starving vagabonds, victims of hunger and abandonment. In Proverbs 28:22, it is a threat — the punishment of one who seeks to enrich themselves out of envy: they will receive famine instead of wealth. The Bible uses it to depict extreme poverty, not as a mere inconvenience, but as true destitution.
H2639.portee: Famine in the Bible is often linked to sin or moral abandonment. It reminds the believer that the greedy pursuit of wealth leads to emptiness, and that true good lies elsewhere — in justice, trust in God, and not in accumulation. It is also a lesson in compassion: those who suffer from famine are the objects of God's mercy.

sens: Absence or insufficiency of something necessary
Deprivation of food or essential resources
State of shortage or material distress
H2640.detail:
1. Lack is the absence or insufficiency of what is necessary for life — food, clothing, everything that allows one to survive with dignity. In Deuteronomy 28:48, God threatens Israel with "lack of all things": this is not just the loss of a possession, but total impoverishment that accompanies slavery imposed by the enemy.
2. In a more specific sense, it is famine, hunger, the absence of bread. Amos 4:6 speaks of the "lack of bread in all your dwellings" — a famine that God sends to bring His people back to Him. It is a concrete, material, and visible punishment.
3. The word can also describe one who is "lacking" in resources, deprived of what they need. In Deuteronomy 28:57, the mother "lacking everything" during a siege finds herself in extreme misery and desperate acts.
H2640.origine: The Hebrew word חֹסֶר (hoser) comes from a root meaning "to be without," "to fail." It designates the absence or deficit of something. It is a concrete and direct term: it does not speak of an abstract absence, but of a deprivation that is felt — hunger, nakedness, impoverishment. The word is mainly used in the prophetic and legislative passages of the Hebrew Bible to describe the consequences of sin or disobedience.
H2640.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible, always in contexts of curse or divine judgment. In Deuteronomy 28, it appears in the list of evils that will strike Israel if they disobey the Lord: hunger, thirst, nakedness, lack of everything (v. 48) and the mother who, lacking bread during a siege, secretly feeds her children with what she should keep for herself (v. 57). In Amos 4:6, the prophet reminds that the Lord has already sent famine — the lack of bread — in all the cities and homes of Israel, to call them to repentance. These uses show a word closely related to the practical and painful consequence of sin: material deprivation.
H2640.portee: This word reminds that God takes disobedience seriously and can strike where it hurts: hunger, nakedness, indigence. For the believer, it emphasizes the importance of obedience and faith in God for the provision of necessities. But it also invites compassion towards those who truly lack daily bread — those the Bible calls the poor and the hungry. It is a call to see in material deprivation a spiritual warning.

sens: Grandfather of Shallum, husband of the prophetess Huldah, living during the divided monarchy
H2641.detail: Hasra is a character mentioned only once in the Bible. He is the grandfather of Shallum, who was married to Huldah, a respected prophetess in Jerusalem. Shallum, son of Tokheath and grandson of Hasra, was in charge of the guardianship of the garments (in 2 Chronicles 34:22). Hasra lived during the time when the kingdom was divided into Israel and Judah. His name literally means "lack" in Hebrew, but nothing is known about his life or his particular role beyond this genealogy.
H2641.origine: The name Hasra means "lack" or "absence" in Hebrew, derived from a root that evokes the idea of what is lacking. He is also known by another form, Harhas (חַרְחַס), which appears in some manuscripts. It is a proper name blending description and personal identity, as was common in Hebrew culture.
H2641.emploi: Hasra appears only once in the Bible, in 2 Chronicles 34:22, during the account where King Josiah sends his advisors to consult the prophetess Huldah to know God's will regarding the book of the Law discovered in the temple. Shallum, Huldah's husband, is identified as being the grandson of Hasra. This moment occurs in the seventh century before Christ, during the religious reforms of King Josiah. The mention of Hasra in this genealogy highlights the respected status of Huldah's family.

sens: What is missing, what does not exist or has disappeared
What is incomplete or insufficient
What cannot be repaired or corrected
H2642.detail:
1. Lack refers to the absence of something: what should be there but is not, or what has been taken away. In Ecclesiastes 1:15, the wise man observes that "what is lacking cannot be counted" — he speaks of the absence of righteousness in the world: evil has left a void that cannot be compensated by mere enumeration.
2. Lack can also express insufficiency: when something is incomplete or lacking, it is missing a part to be whole. It is a deficit that renders it imperfect.
3. In this passage, lack especially evokes irreparability: certain things that are lacking — lost wisdom, absent justice — can never be restored. It is a permanent void, inevitable in a world marked by vanity.
H2642.origine: The Hebrew word חֶסְרוֹן (hesron) comes from the root חסר (hsar), "to lack," "to be deficient." This root is found in other words that express absence or insufficiency. The starting image is that of empty space, a lack of fullness, of what does not meet the expected measure.
H2642.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Ecclesiastes 1:15. The context of the verse — at the beginning of the great poem of vanity — shows that the Wise Man uses lack to express the constitutive imperfection of the world under the sun. It is not a simple accidental lack, but a fundamental flaw: what is bent, that is to say, distorted by evil or injustice, cannot be straightened, and what is lacking, that is to say, what has been lost or distorted, cannot be counted or compensated. The word emphasizes human powerlessness in the face of the order of the world.
H2642.portee: This word speaks to us of our limits in the face of the realities of sin and disorder. In this world, there are lacks that we cannot repair ourselves — injustices that cannot be righted, losses that cannot be restored. This teaching humbles our confidence in our own efforts and pushes us to seek beyond ourselves for redemption, which comes solely from God.

sens: Without stain, without blemish, pure
Innocent, free from guilt or evil
Pure in conscience, blameless
H2643.detail: 1. The word first evokes physical cleanliness, the absence of dirt or stain — what is clean shines with purity. 2. In moral conscience, it denotes innocence: one who is clean has not committed evil, or at least does not feel responsible for the evil attributed to them. Job uses it in Job 33:9: "I am pure, I am without sin, I am clean," meaning he proclaims his innocence before God, asserting that there is no iniquity in him.
H2643.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the absence of defect or blemish. It belongs to the family of biblical terms of purity, often paralleled with "pure" (tahor) and "without sin." In Hebrew, this root carries the idea of whiteness, a clarity that excludes any trace of defilement.
H2643.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Job 33:9. It is Eliphaz who reports Job's words affirming his innocence before God. The context is that of a theological debate: Job denies being a great sinner, defending himself by proclaiming his integrity. The word "clean" emphasizes here the total absence of guilt that Job claims.
H2643.portee: This word invites the believer to consider the weight of guilt and innocence. For Job, crying out his innocence is an act of faith, an affirmation of trust in God despite suffering. It also reminds us that true purity is a matter of conscience and sincerity before God, not just of outward appearance.

sens: To act in a hidden manner, without others knowing
To accomplish something while avoiding the gaze, the knowledge of someone
To hide one's actions, intentions
H2644.detail:
1. The verb evokes the idea of camouflaging, veiling an action: doing something without others seeing or knowing it. It is to act furtively, in secret, as if trying not to be discovered. In 2 Kings 17:9, the children of Israel acted secretly against the Lord: they committed acts of religious rebellion in hiding, wandering to build high places without admitting it openly.
2. The word also emphasizes the intention to conceal, to keep something hidden: it is less the action itself than the occult nature, the act of withdrawing from sight, that prevails. This implies a consciousness of wrongdoing, or at least of doing something that must remain unknown.
H2644.origine: The root חפא evokes the idea of covering, hiding. The context of the passage (2 Kings 17:9) shows that it is an action committed in moral as well as physical darkness: the Israelites were hiding their religious unfaithfulness. What is "secretly" is what escapes view, what is willfully hidden or concealed.
H2644.emploi: This verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Kings 17:9. It describes the behavior of the Northern kingdoms of Israel after the fall of Samaria: they acted against the Lord their God by secretly building high places and idols, seeking to conceal this religious rebellion. It is a voluntary act of camouflaged disobedience, which shows both guilt and an attempt to escape divine punishment.
H2644.portee: This word reminds us of an important spiritual truth: nothing can be hidden from God. The Israelites may have acted secretly against the Lord, but He who sees all uncovered their unfaithfulness. For the reader, it is a warning against lying and hypocrisy: no sin committed in secret escapes God. It is also a call to authenticity and sincere obedience, without double dealing.

sens: Place something over or around something to protect or hide it
Coat a surface with a material (wood, gold, etc.)
Wear a veil or fabric over the head as a sign of mourning or shame
H2645.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to cover in a physical sense: to put a garment, a sheet, or a veil over something or someone. When David flees Jerusalem during Absalom's revolt, he goes up the Mount of Olives "with his head covered" and all those accompanying him "also cover their heads," an act that expresses mourning and humiliation (2 Samuel 15:30). It is an act of protection or modesty.
2. To cover also means to apply a layer of coating on a surface to decorate or beautify it. In the temple that Solomon builds, the workers "cover the walls with cedar wood" and "overlay with pure gold" the surfaces, transforming the building into a splendid dwelling (2 Chronicles 3:5, 3:7, 3:8). The verb here describes the action of completely covering with a precious material.
3. Covering the head is a gesture of dishonor or dismay: Haman, humiliated by Mordecai, returns home "with his head covered" (Esther 6:12), showing his shame and dejection. The veil becomes the external symbol of an inner distress.
H2645.origine: The verb חָפָה (chaphah) comes from a root that evokes the idea of covering or hiding. It belongs to the family of verbs related to coating and protection. In Hebrew, it has three main forms: the simple form (Qal, "to cover"), the passive form (Niphal, "to be covered"), and the intensive form (Piel, "to cover completely, to adorn"). This root fundamentally expresses the action of placing something over, masking, or protecting by hiding.
H2645.emploi: The verb חָפָה appears about ten times in the Hebrew Bible, especially in historical narratives and temple descriptions. It is used first in a concrete and material sense: covering the walls and objects of the temple with wood and gold (2 Chronicles 3:5-9), making it a technical verb in the context of construction and decoration. It is also used for clothing the body, particularly the head, where it takes on an emotional or moral value: covering the head as a sign of mourning (2 Samuel 15:30) or shame (Esther 6:12). In these passages, covering the head is not a mere physical act but the visible expression of humiliation or sorrow.
H2645.portee: This verb reminds us that the external gestures of the body express the inner realities of the soul. Covering the head as a sign of mourning or shame is a body language that everyone understood in antiquity: it is to say without words that one is broken, dishonored, or repentant. For the Christian reader, this invites us to recognize that our actions, gestures, and appearance testify to what resides in our hearts. The verb also shows the beauty and richness of the temple, covered in gold, which speaks of the glory of God.

sens: Enclosed space where the newlyweds sleep
Protected place, shelter under cover
Figurative divine protection
H2646.detail:
1. The bridal chamber is primarily the place where the groom and bride retreat together after the wedding. In Joel 2:16, the prophet calls the groom to "come out of his chamber" and the bride from her "bridal chamber," which precisely designates this intimate space separate from the rest of the house. It is a closed place, a reserved interior.

2. The word is also used for any enclosed space that provides protection: an ordinary room, a cover (roof or shelter). In Isaiah 4:5, the Lord establishes a "smoking cloud" and "a flaming fire" as a cover over Zion, meaning a protection that covers and defends the inhabitants.

3. This notion of a protective space takes on a spiritual meaning: the chamber becomes the image of divine protection. In Psalms 19:6, the sun "comes out of its chamber" like a strong groom — an image of the Lord's power that manifests with brilliance. The chamber here evokes less a closed place than the secret from which life springs forth.
H2646.origine: The word חֻפָּה (chuppah) likely comes from a root meaning "to cover" or "to enclose." It first describes an enclosed space, then the image enriches: what covers becomes protection. In Hebrew, the same idea is found in words from the family of covering and shelter. Even today, the "chuppah" (the wedding canopy) is the covering that shelters the bride and groom in Jewish tradition.
H2646.emploi: The word appears three times in the Hebrew Bible. In Psalms 19:6, it depicts the sun as a groom joyfully coming out of his chamber to traverse the sky — a pure image of vitality and power. In Joel 2:16, on the contrary, it designates the concrete place where the newlyweds live, from which the prophet calls them to come out to join the pious assembly in the face of judgment. In Isaiah 4:5, the meaning completely spiritualizes: the cloud and fire of the Lord form a cover (a chamber) of protection over Zion. Thus, the word shifts from the particular (the house of a young bride) to the universal (divine protection over all the people).
H2646.portee: This word teaches that God does not abandon His people: He creates a covering, a safe shelter over Zion. The image of the bridal chamber, a place of intimacy and joy, transforms our understanding of divine protection — it is not a cold armor, but a space of rest and trust. It reminds believers that God's faithfulness, like that of a husband to his wife, creates a space of security and intimacy.

sens: priest during the time of David
H2647.detail: Huppah is a priest mentioned only once in the Bible, at the time when David organizes the temple service. His name literally means "canopy" or "pavilion" in Hebrew — an image that might evoke majesty or protection. He is classified among the priests of the thirteenth class of service (1 Chronicles 24:13), indicating that the priests were divided into rotating groups to ensure regular worship at the temple. Nothing else is said about him.
H2647.origine: His Hebrew name חֻפָּה (chuppah) literally means "canopy," "pavilion," or "vault" — the word designates a covered structure or awning. It is also the same word used for the traditional chuppah, the Jewish wedding canopy. For this man, the name was likely carried without connection to these concrete meanings, simply as a personal name passed down in his priestly family.
H2647.emploi: Huppah appears only once in Scripture, in 1 Chronicles 24:13. It is in the text where David organizes the 24 classes of priests, sons of Aaron, who take turns serving in the temple of Jerusalem. Huppah holds the rank of the thirteenth class. This passage establishes the order of the priestly service that likely persisted for a long time. Only his name is preserved for us; no act or word of his is reported.

sens: to act or move with haste, speed
to flee hastily, to escape
to be seized with fear or dread
the action or state of haste, panic
H2648.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to act with great haste and speed, without taking the time to think. It is to move quickly, to hurry. In 2 Samuel 4:4, the nurse "hastened her flight" while fleeing with Jonathan's son — she ran without waiting.

2. Often, this haste is that of someone fleeing from danger or an enemy. David "fled hastily" before Saul (1 Samuel 23:26), meaning he escaped urgently, without slowing down.

3. This word also denotes the fear or dread that seizes a person and drives them to act quickly. In Deuteronomy 20:3, God commands the leader not to "frighten" the warriors before battle — do not let them become panicked and frantic.

4. The word is also used as a noun to denote the state of panic or the flight itself. The Syrians, in fleeing, threw their belongings "in their haste" (2 Kings 7:15), so great was their panic. Similarly, the psalmist speaks of his "haste" in Psalms 31:23, referring to the moment when he felt pursued and terrified.
H2648.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of moving quickly, being seized by haste or fear. The same root appears in several Hebrew words that describe rapid movement or the emotion that provokes it. The word paints the image of a person overwhelmed by fear or danger, losing their calm and acting without thinking.
H2648.emploi: This verb appears 9 times in the Old Testament, mostly in historical narratives and the Psalms. It describes concrete situations of flight and panic: David fleeing Saul, the nurse escaping with Jonathan's son, the Syrians abandoning their goods in their flight. It also denotes the fear that must be prevented in soldiers before battle (Deuteronomy 20:3). In the Psalms, the word evokes the anguish of the righteous being pursued or in distress (Psalms 31:23). The word can be used literally (to run fast) and figuratively (to be seized with fear, to become frantic).
H2648.portee: This word reminds us that fear and haste lead us away from wisdom and trust in God. Deuteronomy 20:3 shows that God does not want His children to be terrified and frantic: He calls them to calmness and faith. Conversely, the psalmist discovers that even in the haste of his anguish, God listens to him (Psalms 31:23). The contrast invites the believer to seek rest in God rather than to be dominated by panic.

sens: Hasty speed, urgency that drives to act without delay
State of trouble or fear that accelerates movements
Flight or departure in disorder, without preparation
Urgency marked by agitation and anxiety
H2649.detail:
1. Haste is primarily the action of doing things quickly, pressed by time or circumstances. At Passover, the Israelites must eat "in haste" (Exodus 12:11), ready to leave at once: with their loins girded, sandals on their feet, staff in hand, like people preparing to leave a place urgently.
2. This word also denotes the inner state of agitation and trouble that accompanies a hurried action. When one goes out "with haste" (Deuteronomy 16:3), it is not just quick: it is done in fear and the disorder of flight, with the emotion gripping the one who escapes.
3. Haste can evoke a disordered flight, a departure in panic or escape. Isaiah 52:12 contrasts this anxious haste with the assured march of return: "Do not go out with haste, do not flee"—for this time, the Lord Himself guides and protects them, and they no longer need to flee in panic.
H2649.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of pressing, trembling, and fleeing. It is formed with a reinforcement (doubling) that intensifies the meaning: it is not just rapidity, but agitated rapidity, marked by fear. The Hebrew word expresses the image of someone seized by urgency or fear, who moves quickly and in a disordered manner.
H2649.emploi: This word appears three times in the Old Testament, always in contexts of departure or exit. At the Passover in Egypt (Exodus 12:11), it marks the urgent and orderly character of this flight: one must eat quickly, equipped to leave. In Deuteronomy 16:3, it refers to the same exit from Egypt, recalled each year so that the Israelites never forget the emotion and urgency of this foundational event. In Isaiah 52:12, the prophet uses the word in a context of restoration and hope: he exhorts the people not to depart "with haste," because this time God goes before them and they can advance in confidence, not in panic.
H2649.portee: This word reminds believers of God's acts of deliverance, marked by speed and urgency, but also by God's order amid trouble. It invites reflection on the difference between anxious haste, which comes from fear, and trust in God that allows one to walk without panic. It is also a call to remember how God saved His people in urgency, and to trust Him when the time comes to follow His guidance.

sens: Man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Ir
H2650G.detail: 1. Huppim is a man of the tribe of Benjamin, son of Ir, mentioned during the time of Egypt and the desert. He appears in the Benjamite genealogy as the son of Ir and brother of Schuppim and Maaca (1 Chronicles 7:12). His name means "protected" in Hebrew, evoking the idea of a person sheltered or guarded.
H2650G.origine: The name Huppim comes from a Hebrew root meaning "to protect" or "to shelter." This theophoric or protective name was common in Israelite genealogies to express divine blessing or God's protection over the bearer of the name.
H2650G.emploi: Huppim is mentioned twice in 1 Chronicles 7, which lists the descendants of Benjamin and his sons. In 1 Chronicles 7:12, he is identified as the son of Ir. In 1 Chronicles 7:15, he is mentioned again alongside Schuppim, and it is learned that Makir took a wife "from Huppim and Schuppim," suggesting that these two men gave their name to influential Benjamite families. These mentions testify to the importance of Huppim and his descendants in the tribe of Benjamin.

sens: Son of Benjamin, ancestor of an Israelite family
H2650H.detail: Huppim is the name of a man of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned only once in Genesis when Jacob presents his sons to the Pharaoh of Egypt. He is one of the ten sons listed of Benjamin. His name means "protected," suggesting divine blessing upon his birth.
H2650H.origine: The name Huppim comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of protection or covering. The same individual is referred to by variations in other passages of Scripture: "Hupham" in Numbers 26:39, and "Huram" in 1 Chronicles 8:5. These variations reflect the different ways in which ancient Hebrew texts transmitted and recorded this proper name over generations.
H2650H.emploi: Huppim appears only once in the Bible, in Genesis 46:21, where he is presented as one of the sons of Benjamin.
