This enumeration of Jacob's descendants takes place in Egypt, at the time when Joseph introduces his family to Pharaoh. The name appears in the genealogical list that establishes the foundations of the nation of Israel in a foreign land. Although Huppim himself is mentioned only once, his descendants will form a family (the Huphamites) later attested during the census in the desert.

sens: The palm of the hand, hollow and capable of holding
A quantity that the hand can contain, a handful
Figuratively, the capacity to act or to control
H2651.detail: 1. The hand primarily refers to the hollow palm, the inner part of the hand with which one grasps and holds. In Exodus 9:8, Moses and Aaron are to "fill" their hands with ashes: the image is that of the palm hollowing out to receive and contain. 2. From this hollow shape comes the meaning of "handful," a quantity measured not by weight but by what a hand can hold. In Leviticus 16:12, the priest takes "two handfuls" of fragrant incense: two full hands, not an abstract measure. 3. The hand also becomes the biblical image of the capacity to act, to control, to accomplish. In Proverbs 30:4, "gathering the wind in one's hands" and "holding the waters in one's garment" describe acts that exceed human strength — it is asking for the one who possesses the absolute power to control creation.
H2651.origine: The Hebrew word chophen comes from a root meaning "to hollow out" or "to form a hollow." The hand is first thought of by its shape: hollow, capable of receiving. This image of the hollow and the container is the key to the word. It is found in other Hebrew words of the same family that describe shapes or containers.
H2651.emploi: The word appears 6 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in contexts where one must "fill" the hands or take something "with full hands." In Exodus 9:8 and Ezekiel 10:2, 10:7, it is to grasp burning coals or ashes: a concrete and important action. In Leviticus 16:12, it is a measure of quantity for the Temple incense. In Ecclesiastes 4:6 and Proverbs 30:4, the word evokes rather the idea of possession and control: having hands full of rest, or possessing the power to control the wind and the waters. The meaning oscillates between the concrete (what one holds) and the figurative (what one possesses or controls).
H2651.portee: This word reminds us that the hand is the instrument of action and possession. For the biblical reader, it invites meditation on what we hold, what we accomplish, and what only God can control. Ecclesiastes 4:6 particularly speaks of the wisdom of possessing little but in peace, rather than much in trouble — a lesson in sobriety and trust.

sens: One of the two sons of the priest Eli at Shiloh
Priest of Israel during the time of the united monarchy
A man marked by abuse of power and moral corruption
H2652.detail:
1. Hophni is the name of a man who lived during the time of the united monarchy in Israel. He was one of the two sons of Eli, the high priest of Shiloh, as shown in 1 Samuel 1:3, where he is mentioned alongside his brother Phinehas among the priests of the Lord.

2. Hophni and his brother served in the priestly ministry at Shiloh, the great sanctuary of Israel at that time. They participated in essential religious acts, as shown in 1 Samuel 4:4, where they accompany the ark of the covenant during a battle against the Philistines.

3. However, the Bible depicts him as a man characterized by brutality and corruption. Their conduct was so wicked that it brought a curse upon their father's house (1 Samuel 2:34). During the battle against the Philistines, both Hophni and Phinehas were killed (1 Samuel 4:11), while the ark was captured — which caused Eli to die of grief upon hearing the news (1 Samuel 4:17).
H2652.origine: The name Hophni literally means "pugilist" or "fighter," evoking someone violent or aggressive — a bitter irony since he was supposed to serve the God of peace. This name likely reflects the fiery and aggressive character of the individual, traits that will manifest in his priestly corruption.
H2652.emploi: Hophni appears five times in the first book of Samuel, always alongside his brother Phinehas. He embodies, along with the latter, the contrast between priestly responsibility and personal sin: while priests are called to serve the Lord faithfully, Hophni and Phinehas abuse their religious authority. Their death on the battlefield (1 Samuel 4:11) becomes a sign of divine judgment announced in 1 Samuel 2:34 — a punishment that affirms that God does not tolerate religious corruption, even among those who bear His sacred orders.
H2652.portee: The story of Hophni warns believers about the dangers of spiritual corruption and the misuse of religious authority for personal gain. It shows that religious status or heritage (being Eli's son, priest of Israel) does not protect one from God's judgment: only sincere faith and obedience matter. The contrast between the divine calling and Hophni's conduct invites each generation to examine its own spiritual integrity.

sens: To protect by enveloping
To shelter, to keep safe
To surround with divine protection
H2653.detail:
1. The Hebrew verb חׇפַף first evokes the concrete idea of covering something or someone by enveloping it, as one would cover an object to protect it. The image is that of a protective layer that encloses and preserves.

2. From this arises the meaning of sheltering or keeping safe: the one who is covered is also sheltered from danger, like a child kept safe under the care of a parent. In Deuteronomy 33:12, Moses blesses Benjamin by saying that "the Lord will always cover him" — meaning he will remain constantly under divine protection, "will dwell between his shoulders," an image of maternal closeness and care.

3. Finally, the word extends to the theological idea of divine protection: God covers His people or His elect with His presence and power, keeping them safe amid threats. It is less a one-time act than a lasting state of being enveloped and guarded by God.
H2653.origine: The root חׇפַף carries the fundamental image of enveloping or covering. It belongs to a family of Hebrew words that revolve around the idea of covering, protection, and enclosing. The verb expresses a continuous act: the one who covers maintains their covering in a stable manner, hence the idea of lasting and reliable protection.
H2653.emploi: The verb חׇפַף appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Deuteronomy 33:12, in the prophetic blessing of Moses upon the tribe of Benjamin. In this solemn context, it describes the privileged relationship between the Lord and Benjamin: God will always cover him with His protection, remaining close to him like a parent watching over a child. The uniqueness of this usage underscores the importance of this promise for Benjamin, and confers to the verb a high, almost liturgical significance of permanent divine grace.
H2653.portee: This word reveals a profound biblical promise: that of active and personal divine protection. For the believer, discovering that God "covers" means that one is never left alone to insecurity or threat — one is constantly enveloped by the protective presence of the Lord. It is a word of comfort that invites trust and peace, knowing that one remains "between the shoulders" of God, that is, in absolute safety under His care.

sens: To take pleasure in, to rejoice in
To desire, to wish fervently
To consent to, to accept willingly
To be satisfied with, to approve
To take satisfaction in, to delight in
H2654A.detail:
1. To take pleasure in, to rejoice in: this means to experience genuine joy at the sight or thought of something. Shechem "loved" Jacob's daughter (Genesis 34:19), meaning she deeply pleased him. God says He "takes pleasure" in justice (Isaiah 42:21), He rejoices in it.
2. To desire, to wish fervently: this means to feel an urge within oneself toward something one wants to obtain or do. Job "wants" to speak to the Almighty (Job 13:3): he has a burning desire for it. The one who does not "want" to respond to God's call (Isaiah 65:12) deliberately refuses to do so.
3. To consent to, to accept willingly: this means to say yes, to give one's agreement with satisfaction. The one who "wants" to let his wife go (Deuteronomy 21:14) agrees to free her. God "wants" to forgive us (Isaiah 55:11), He consents to it and accomplishes it.
4. To be satisfied with, to approve: this means to judge something good and worthy of keeping. What you "want" to do is what pleases you to do (2 Samuel 20:11). God "disapproves" of what is evil in His eyes (Isaiah 65:12).
5. To take satisfaction in, to delight in: this means to find one's contentment in something. The wicked take "pleasure" in fighting (Psalms 68:31). God "delights" in the one who fears Him (Psalms 112:1).
H2654A.origine: The Hebrew verb חָפֵץ (chaphéts) comes from a root that evokes the idea of attraction, of inclination. It is related to other Hebrew words denoting desire and will. Its basic image is that of an inclination of the heart, a movement toward what attracts us. The word is used for both man and God, which shows that it describes a profound phenomenon: the orientation of the will toward what one considers good.
H2654A.emploi: This verb appears 69 times in the Hebrew Bible, very often in the Psalms, in the Prophets, and in the Wisdom literature. It describes sometimes the desires of men (Shechem loves Jacob's daughter, Job wants to plead before God), and sometimes the will of God (God delights in justice, He approves or disapproves of actions). Sometimes it takes a lighter nuance: to accept, to consent to a particular thing (to let a woman go, to follow a leader). The context determines whether the emphasis is on deep feeling (to take pleasure, to rejoice), on intention (to want, to desire), or on the act of consenting. Isaiah 65:12 shows the negative: God says that one has "chosen what [displeases] Him," meaning what He does not approve.
H2654A.portee: This word teaches the reader that will is never an abstract force, but always the expression of a deep attraction, a preference of the heart. When the Bible says that God "wants" to forgive us or "takes pleasure" in the one who fears Him, it reveals that God acts not out of compulsion, but from a benevolent inclination toward us. For the believer, understanding what God truly wants—His justice, His mercy—helps to align one's own will with His. Finally, this verb shows us that our free will holds us accountable: we choose what pleases God or what displeases Him.

sens: To curve, to flex the body or a part of the body downward
To incline as in a gesture of humility or submission
H2654B.detail:
1. To bend means to curve or flex a part of the body. In Job 40:12, the crocodile "bends" its tail as one would bend a flexible branch: it is a movement of flexion, a curvature of the body downward.
2. In a figurative sense, to bend can evoke humility or submission—the idea that the one who bends is bowing before something stronger. Although this usage is rare in the provided text, the root carries this nuance of yielding or voluntary inclination.
H2654B.origine: The Hebrew verb חָפַץ (chaphatz) comes from a root expressing the movement of bending or curving. The word paints the image of a part of the body that inclines, that bends. The same root can also denote pleasure or desire—two ideas linked in ancient thought: what one bends toward, what one brings close to oneself, is what one desires.
H2654B.emploi: The verb appears only once in the Hebrew Bible with this precise meaning. In Job 40:12, it describes the crocodile (Behemoth) bending its tail with remarkable power, a symbol of its indomitable strength. The author uses the image of flexible movement to show the mastery and superiority of this creature in the face of human questions about divine justice.
H2654B.portee: This word invites the reader to contemplate creation with wonder. In Job, the question is not theoretical: God shows Job the powerful and flexible creatures that man cannot master or judge. Understanding this simple gesture—bending its tail—is to recognize the humility that befits the creature before the Creator.

sens: To want something, to covet it
To take pleasure in something, to delight in it
To be willing, to be inclined
To find contentment, satisfaction
H2655.detail:
1. To want something, to have a desire to obtain it: this means to experience a desire, an attraction toward an object or a goal. Naboth refuses to give up his vineyard because he does not want to, despite King Ahab's offer (1 Kings 21:6).
2. To take pleasure in something, to rejoice in it internally: this means to find joy, satisfaction in what is presented. God does not take pleasure in evil (Psalms 5:5): this means He does not delight in it, He rejects it.
3. To be willing, to show good will: this means to be ready, with a well-oriented heart. Solomon must serve God with a willing heart (1 Chronicles 28:9), meaning with a heart fully turned toward Him.
4. To experience contentment, satisfaction in a situation or expectation. The one who loves life desires to prolong his days (Psalms 34:13), he wishes to enjoy it for a long time.
H2655.origine: The Hebrew word חָפֵץ (cha.phets) comes from a root that expresses the idea of experiencing attraction, of leaning toward something. In the Hebrew Old Testament, it describes both simple wanting and deep pleasure, the delight of one who finds joy in something. The word can qualify both human desire and that of God, revealing what one truly loves.
H2655.emploi: This word appears eleven times in the historical and poetic books of the Old Testament. It primarily expresses ordinary human desire—wanting a vineyard, wanting to accomplish something (1 Kings 21:6, Nehemiah 1:11)—but also, notably, the pleasure of God. God does not take pleasure in wickedness (Psalms 5:5), and it is earnestly requested that He rejoice in the happiness of His servants (Psalms 35:27). The word always emphasizes an inclination of the heart, an inner orientation, not a mere intellectual decision.
H2655.portee: Understanding this word helps to grasp that in the Bible, desire is never neutral: it reveals what we love, what truly attracts us. Knowing that God has pleasure or displeasure (that He desires or refuses) shows us a God who is not indifferent, but who loves or rejects according to His justice. For the believer, this invites examination of one's own desires: what do we truly want? Does this change our heart and our actions?

sens: What pleases, what brings joy or satisfaction
Desire, what one wishes or loves
Someone's will, what they want
A particular object or thing
H2656.detail:
1. The word primarily expresses pleasure in the sense of contentment: that which makes someone happy or satisfied. When Samuel asks if the Lord finds "pleasure" in sacrifices (1 Samuel 15:22), it means that God prefers obedience, which gives Him more satisfaction than rituals.
2. Desire is the second meaning: it is what someone strongly wishes for, that which they covet. When Solomon gives the queen of Sheba "everything she desired" (1 Kings 10:13), he fulfills her innermost wishes.
3. The will of a person, especially of a sovereign or God, also comes from this word: it is what they have decided to do or see accomplished. Isaiah says that Cyrus "will fulfill all my will" (Isaiah 44:28), meaning the plans that God has set.
4. By extension, the word also designates a thing, a concrete object that one possesses or speaks of: "for every thing and for every work" (Ecclesiastes 3:17) has the sense of "business" or "enterprise."
H2656.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of leaning towards, of desiring. It is frequently used in the poetic and wisdom literature of the Bible to express both the pleasure of God (His "goodwill") and human desire (the thirst for what one wants). The same root produces other forms for "to want" or "to take pleasure in." It is a fundamental word for discussing satisfaction, divine or human.
H2656.emploi: This word appears 38 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the poetic books (Psalms, Proverbs), wisdom literature (Ecclesiastes, Job), and prophetic books (Isaiah, Jeremiah). It has several main uses: the pleasure of God (what pleases Him or depends on His goodwill; 1 Samuel 15:22, Isaiah 53:10 where the Lord desires the servant to accomplish His purpose), human desire (what someone strongly wants; 1 Kings 10:13), divine will as purpose (Isaiah 44:28, 46:10), and things or affairs in a general sense (Ecclesiastes 3:17). The word also nuances between personal pleasure, a determined intention, and the good pleasure of a monarch or God.
H2656.portee: This word invites the believer to ask a central question: what truly pleases God? The Bible answers: obedience, justice, and not the multiplication of empty religious gestures (1 Samuel 15:22). It is also a call to align our personal will with that of God: recognizing His "wills" and accepting them is to enter into His peace. Finally, the word reminds us that pleasure and desire are normal forces within us, to be directed towards good and holiness.

sens: wife of King Hezekiah and mother of King Manasseh
symbolic name for Jerusalem in messianic prophecy
H2657G.detail: 1. Hephzibah is the queen, wife of King Hezekiah (2 Kings 21:1), and she is the mother of King Manasseh who reigned for a long time in Jerusalem. She is mentioned only once by name in the history of the kings, at the time of her son's accession to the throne. 2. The name Hephzibah means "my pleasure is in her" in Hebrew; it expresses joy and satisfaction towards the person so named. This name was also symbolically given to Jerusalem in the prophecy of Isaiah, evoking God's favor and blessing towards His city.
H2657G.origine: The name Hephzibah comes from the Hebrew חֶפְצִי־בָהּ, composed of חֵפֶץ (chephets, "pleasure", "delight") and the pronoun "in her". Its literal meaning is "my pleasure is in her", expressing affection and satisfaction. This symbolic name was attributed to Jerusalem in the prophecies, signifying that the city was the object of divine favor.
H2657G.emploi: Hephzibah is mentioned only once in the historical Bible, in 2 Kings 21:1, where she is identified as the mother of King Manasseh. She represents a figure of Davidic royalty, but no personal details about her are provided in the accounts. The name Hephzibah holds particular theological significance in the book of Isaiah, where it becomes a prophetic name for Jerusalem, symbolizing God's favor and pleasure towards His people.
H2657G.portee: The name Hephzibah reminds us that the kings of Israel, even in the line of David, depended on women and mothers playing a role in the transmission of royal power. More broadly, the use of this name for Jerusalem in prophecy invites the reader to meditate on God's favor towards His people and His city, and on the restoration of the divine heart towards those who belong to Him.

sens: Name given to Jerusalem to express God's favor and joy towards her
H2657H.detail: 1. It is a symbolic name attributed to Jerusalem. The name literally means "my delight is in her" or "my pleasure is in her". It expresses how God views the city with satisfaction and affection, as a possession He cherishes particularly. In Isaiah 62:4, the prophet announces that Jerusalem will no longer be called "Forsaken" but will bear this new name, marking a radical change in God's relationship with the city.
H2657H.origine: The name is composed of two Hebrew elements: "chephets" (חֶפְצִי) which means "my desire, my pleasure, my delight", and "bah" (בָהּ) which means "in her". It is a theophoric name, meaning it directly expresses God's feeling or decision. In Hebrew, names like this served to proclaim a spiritual truth or a change of status.
H2657H.emploi: This name appears only once in the provided biblical usages, in Isaiah 62:4. It is used by the prophet in an oracle of consolation addressed to Jerusalem after the exile. The context shows that God restores the city and changes its identity: it will no longer be known by names of humiliation ("Forsaken", "Desolate"), but by names of glory that reflect its restored status and importance in God's eyes.
H2657H.portee: This name reminds the people of God that Jerusalem is not just a political or geographical city, but a place of covenant where God manifests His love and favor. For Christians, it illustrates how God can transform a situation of desolation into joy, and how He views His people not by what they have done, but by the grace and pleasure He takes in them.

sens: to make a hole in the ground by removing material
to explore a place by traversing or inspecting it
to actively seek something hidden
H2658.detail:
1. Dig means to make a hole in the earth or rock by removing material: it is a concrete physical task. Isaac and his servants dug wells to find water in the desert (Genesis 26:19); it is an act of creation and possession, as Abraham dug wells that marked his establishment in the land.
2. To explore is to dig a place in a figurative sense: one traverses it to know it, one scrutinizes it. Moses tells Israel to send men to "explore the land" (Deuteronomy 1:22) and the spies of Rahab came to "explore the whole land" (Joshua 2:3): they sought to know its strengths, resources, and weaknesses.
3. To seek is to dig with intention: one digs, one probes to find what is hidden or desired. The context broadens: in a moral or metaphorical sense, one can "dig" a project or dig after someone (to spy on them, to set a trap for them).
H2658.origine: The Hebrew verb charphar comes from a root that evokes the idea of making a hollow, of penetrating beneath the surface. The word is linked to the image of depth and secrecy: what one seeks is often what is buried or hidden. In biblical Hebrew, this verb is quite common to describe practical and metaphorical search activities.
H2658.emploi: The verb appears 21 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in the narratives of the Pentateuch (Genesis, Exodus, Deuteronomy, Numbers) and in the Psalms and wisdom literature (Job, Ecclesiastes). Its simplest and most frequent meaning is "to dig" (14 occurrences), notably for digging wells (Genesis 21:30; 26:19, 32). The usage "to explore" (3 times) appears in military or reconnaissance contexts: the Israelites explore Canaan before conquering it. A few rare usages show nuances: to covet, to spy, to tread the ground, always with the underlying idea of penetration or intentional search.
H2658.portee: This word reminds us that faith sometimes requires persistent work: Abraham and Isaac "dug" wells, meaning they rooted themselves in the promised land through work and trust. For the believer, "exploring" the Word of God is also digging, seeking its hidden treasures. The word also invites vigilance: one should not dig traps for others (Psalms 7:16; 35:7), but seek truth and establishment rather than evil.

sens: to feel confusion, embarrassment in the face of failure or affront
to be covered with shame, to lose honor
to blush, to show humiliation externally
to cause someone shame, to cover them with confusion
H2659.detail: 1. The fundamental meaning is to experience deep shame, an inner confusion in the face of disappointment or an affront to honor: this is what those who place their trust in something that collapses feel (Job 6:20, where hopeful travelers become "ashamed" upon discovering the desert). 2. Here, shame is less a simple discomfort than a loss of public honor: one who blushes with shame is humiliated before the eyes of others, dishonored (Psalms 35:4 and 71:24 describe enemies who will be "ashamed and confused"). 3. The word paints the physical image of shame: to blush, to become scarlet, to show humiliation on one's face (Isaiah 1:29, where the people will "blush" for their idols). 4. In its active form, the verb can mean to cause shame, to cover someone with infamy: the wicked "covers himself with shame" through his own actions (Proverbs 13:5).
H2659.origine: The root חפר (chaf) evokes the idea of hollow, of void — hence the image of someone collapsing inwardly. The word belongs to the family of Hebrew terms expressing humiliation and loss of dignity. In the Greek Old Testament, it often translates the Greek word aïschynomaï (to be ashamed, to be confused).
H2659.emploi: The verb appears 17 times mainly in the Psalms and among the prophets. It is frequently used in prayers, where the psalmist asks that his enemies be covered with shame (Psalms 35:4, 40:15, 71:24) — it is a prayer for God to reverse the situation, honor His servant, and confound those who persecute him. Isaiah uses it in announcing divine judgments: nations will be ashamed in the light of God (Isaiah 24:23, 54:4). Jeremiah uses it to depict the desolation of Israel covered with shame (Jeremiah 50:12).
H2659.portee: This word reminds us that God sees injustice and dishonesty, and that they ultimately cover their authors with confusion. For the praying believer, it is assurance: God vindicates the humiliated righteous and exposes the shame of the wicked. It is also a warning: building one's life on lies, idolatry, or pride inevitably leads to humiliation.

sens: Man of the tribe of Manasseh
Son of Gilead
Father of Zelophehad
Eponymous ancestor of the Hepherites
H2660A.detail: Hepher is a man of the tribe of Manasseh, son of Gilead and brother of Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, and Shemida (Joshua 17:2). He is best known as the father of Zelophehad, whose daughters play an important role in the distribution of the lands of Canaan: since Zelophehad had no sons, his daughters Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah ask for and receive the inheritance that would have belonged to their father (Numbers 27:1-11). His descendants give rise to the family of the Hepherites, one of the branches of Manasseh mentioned during the census in the wilderness (Numbers 26:32).
H2660A.origine: The name Hepher means "a well" in Hebrew, an image of stability and resource. It is a common name in ancient Israel, borne by several personalities, but this entry concerns the son of Gilead, ancestor of the lineage of Zelophehad. Three different men bear this name in the Bible, but this one is the most significant due to his descendants.
H2660A.emploi: Hepher appears 5 times in the Bible, only in the books of Numbers and Joshua, all passages concerning tribal organization and the distribution of lands after the conquest of Canaan. The first two usages (Numbers 26:32-33) mention him during the census of the families of Manasseh in the wilderness; the next three (Numbers 27:1 and Joshua 17:2-3) place him in the genealogy of Zelophehad, establishing the lineage by which Hepher becomes the founding father of a line whose members inherit lands in Canaan. His role is primarily genealogical: he serves as an anchor point in the chain of generations of Manasseh.
H2660A.portee: The story of Hepher and his descendants, particularly the daughters of Zelophehad, shows how God honors faithfulness across generations and how He ensures that each family receives its inheritance. The repeated mention of his name in genealogical lists reminds us that God knows each person and each lineage, and that none are forgotten in His plan.

sens: City of Canaan, west of the Jordan
Region or administrative territory under Israelite control
H2660B.detail: 1. Hépher is a city of Canaan located west of the Jordan, conquered by Joshua during the taking of possession of the land. It is listed among the defeated Canaanite kingdoms, whose king is enumerated alongside that of Tappuah (Joshua 12:17). 2. During the established monarchy under Solomon, Hépher becomes an administrative region: a governor named "son of Hessed" oversees this area, which includes the city of Soco and all the surrounding territory (1 Kings 4:10). This shows that Hépher extends beyond a simple fortress to form an organized territorial unit of royal administration.
H2660B.origine: The name Hépher means "a well" in Hebrew. This etymology reflects the vital importance of water in the semi-arid regions of Canaan: a fortified city around a spring or major well could become a strategic and commercial crossroads. The name thus describes the geographical feature that likely attracted human settlement to this location.
H2660B.emploi: Hépher appears twice in the Bible, both in contexts of political geography. First, it is included in the list of Canaanite kings that Joshua defeated (Joshua 12:17), establishing it as an important urban center of Canaan before the conquest. Then, it reappears centuries later as an administrative center of the kingdom of Israel under Solomon (1 Kings 4:10), showing that its strategic position kept it important throughout Israel's history. These two mentions thus frame the transition period of Canaan under Israelite control.

sens: Man of the tribe of Judah during the time of the Divided Monarchy
H2660G.detail: 1. Hépher is a man of the tribe of Judah, mentioned only once in Chronicles. He is the son of Ashhur and Naarah, and he has brothers Ahuzzam, Temeni, and Haahashtari (and half-brothers Zereth, Izhar, Ethnan, and Koz). The Bible does not recount anything else about him: his name appears in a simple family genealogy, where he is presented as one of the children of Naara.
H2660G.origine: The name Hépher literally means "a well" in Hebrew. This likely evokes a source of water or an important place, although the Bible does not provide any explanation for this choice of name. It is a personal name among the descendants of Judah.
H2660G.emploi: Hépher is mentioned only once in the entire Bible, in 1 Chronicles 4:6, in the list of descendants of Judah. He is presented there as one of the sons of Naara, the wife of Ashhur. This passage is part of a long genealogical enumeration of the tribes of Israel, where many ancestors' names are found, with no further details about their lives or deeds.

sens: Warrior of the time of the Divided Monarchy
Locality in Canaan west of the Jordan
H2660H.detail:
1. Hépher is a man mentioned only once in the Bible, in the list of mighty warriors of King David. He is presented as the father of Mekira, one of these valiant men (1 Chronicles 11:36).
2. The name Hépher also designates an ancient city of Canaan, located west of the Jordan, which was conquered by Joshua during Israel's entry into the Promised Land. It is probably the same place that gave its name to the warrior mentioned above.
H2660H.origine: The name Hépher comes from a Hebrew root meaning "well." This meaning fits well with an ancient place, as access to water was essential for the establishment of cities in Canaan. The well as a source of life was a strong symbol in Israelite culture.
H2660H.emploi: Hépher appears only once in the Bible, in 1 Chronicles 11:36, where he is cited as the father of Mekira among the thirty elite warriors of King David. This text enumerates the most valiant and loyal men who surrounded David during the time of the united monarchy. His inclusion in this list of "mighty men" shows that Hépher came from a family of renowned warriors.

sens: small burrowing rodent
unclean animal according to Mosaic law
symbol of the vain and worthless nature of idols
H2661.detail:
1. The word designates a small rodent that lives underground and digs tunnels — which the Hebrew emphasizes by highlighting its burrowing activity. It is a common animal in the Holy Land, harmful as it devastates crops and provisions.
2. According to the law of Moses, the rat is classified among unclean animals (Leviticus 11:29), meaning that the Israelites could not consume it or touch it without becoming unclean. This prohibition marks it with a strong negative connotation in the minds of the people.
3. In Isaiah 2:20, the prophet imagines men throwing their gold and silver idols to the rats and bats: a striking image of a future where these precious objects, foolishly worshiped, will end up eaten and defiled by filthy beasts, revealing the absurdity of idolatry.
H2661.origine: The Hebrew word חֲפֹר (chabor) comes from a root meaning "to dig," "to burrow." It is a name for the animal constructed from the verb that describes its characteristic behavior: the rat is primarily the one who digs. The same word appears in its verbal form in the Old Testament to describe the action of digging.
H2661.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 2:20, in a prophetic vision of the day of judgment and renewal. It is the only usage, but it is highly significant: the prophet places the rats alongside the bats, other unclean creatures of darkness, as recipients of the final contempt reserved for idols. The eschatological context ("In that day") gives the word an ultimate significance: these ignoble animals embody the unworthy fate that awaits false gods.
H2661.portee: This word reminds the reader that idols, while they may shine with precious material here on earth, are fundamentally vain and worthless before God. The image of rats gnawing at gold invites reflection on the futility of what we devote our worship to outside of God: what seems precious ultimately faces destruction and contempt.

sens: descendants of Hépher, man of the tribe of Manasseh
H2662.detail: The Héphrites are the descendants of Hépher, a man of the tribe of Manasseh who lived during the time of Egypt and the desert. This family name appears in the census of the families of Manasseh: "Shemida, the family of the Shemidaites; Hépher, the family of the Héphrites" (Numbers 26:32). Hépher was the son of Gilead and the father of Zelophehad, whose daughters made a famous request to inherit their father's land since they had no brothers.
H2662.origine: The word comes from the proper name Hépher (חֵפֶר), which literally means "pit" or "shame." It is a Hebrew patronymic formed according to the customs of Israel to designate a family lineage. Hépher was the son of Gilead and gave his name to all his descendants.
H2662.emploi: The Héphrites are mentioned only once in the Bible, in Numbers 26:32, during the second census of Israel in the desert, after the rebellion of Korah. They are listed among the families of Manasseh to whom the promised land was to be distributed according to their number. It is through this genealogy that the text establishes the link between Hépher and his son Zelophehad, whose daughters' story is recounted shortly after (Numbers 27).

sens: City of the tribe of Issachar in Canaan
H2663.detail: Hapharaïm is a locality mentioned only once in the Bible, during the division of the Promised Land among the twelve tribes of Israel. It appears in the list of cities allocated to the tribe of Issachar, alongside Shion and Anacharath (Joshua 19:19). The name literally means "two pits" or "two holes," probably referring to geographical features of the place. This city is not further described in the biblical text.
H2663.origine: The name Hapharaïm comes from the Hebrew חֲפָרַיִם, formed from the root חפר (to dig, to burrow) and the dual suffix יִם which designates two paired things. The basic image is that of diggings or pits in the ground, two natural or constructed formations that would have marked the landscape of the place.
H2663.emploi: Hapharaïm appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 19:19. It is cited in the enumeration of the cities that Joshua distributes to the tribe of Issachar after the conquest of Canaan. No particular event is reported at Hapharaïm, and no story involves it: it is simply a locality of the Israelite territory, identified by its name in the tribal cadastre.

sens: To actively search for something or someone
To examine carefully, to rummage through a place or one's thoughts
To reflect, to meditate internally
To disguise oneself, to change appearance to avoid being recognized
H2664.detail:
1. To seek means to undertake a search to discover something hidden or lost. It is a voluntary and often repeated action: one seeks until finding. Saul sought the teraphim (idols) at Laban's, without success (Genesis 31:35), just as one rummages through a house (2 Kings 10:23) to locate what one desires.
2. To rummage or examine in detail means to probe deeply, to scrutinize a place or situation. The heart of the righteous (Proverbs 20:27) is thus examined, like a lamp that illuminates secret corners. It is to look beyond appearances.
3. To meditate or reflect within oneself refers to the inner work of thought: the psalmist "meditates" during the night, leading to inner reflection (Psalms 77:7). This is no longer seeking outwardly, but inwardly.
4. To disguise oneself means to intentionally change one's appearance or identity. Saul disguised himself before the battle (1 Kings 22:30): he put on other clothes to avoid being recognized as king and to be spared by the enemy.
H2664.origine: The Hebrew verb חָפַשׂ (chavash) expresses the fundamental idea of turning, returning, or scrutinizing carefully. The root evokes the action of rummaging by turning things over to examine them. The word can also mean to transform oneself (hence the meaning "to disguise"). This family of words reflects the image of a search that requires time and energy, turning over each element until the truth is discovered.
H2664.emploi: The verb chavash appears about 20 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical narratives and poetic books. It primarily describes the practical search for objects or people (Genesis 44:12, 1 Samuel 23:23), then the careful examination of a situation or hidden intention. In the Psalms and Proverbs, it expands to the inner realm: meditating on one's ways (Lamentations 3:40), examining the heart (Proverbs 20:27). The meaning "to disguise oneself" appears in war scenes, where disguising was a military strategy (1 Kings 22:30, 2 Chronicles 35:22). The verb thus expresses a movement from the visible to the invisible, from physical searching to spiritual reflection.
H2664.portee: This word speaks to us of a vital reality: God sees all that is hidden, He "searches" our hearts. We too are called to examine our ways and intentions (Lamentations 3:40), to seek wisdom as one seeks treasure. The verb invites us to inner honesty: nothing escapes divine scrutiny, and we cannot "disguise" ourselves before Him.

sens: Calculated and malevolent scheme
Evil stratagem
Ruse
Secret intrigue
H2665.detail:
1. Malevolent plot: this word designates a project conceived with the intention to harm. In Psalms 64:7, the enemies "meditate crimes" and their "plot" is carefully crafted: they think, they prepare in advance what they want to do wrong.
2. Cunning stratagem: the word evokes a strategy, a calculation: the plot is not a simple impulsive act, but a thought carried out with cunning and premeditation. It is moral mechanics — one stirs in their head to fabricate something harmful.
3. Secret intrigue: this plot is hidden. That is why the psalmist calls on God to know the hidden details — because those who concoct it keep it to themselves, like a secret weapon.
H2665.origine: The Hebrew root is uncertain regarding its exact etymology, but the word evokes a thought directed towards a goal, a calculated intention. The Hebrew language often links this concept to the idea of intense meditation — a thought that digs, that unfolds its intentions like one unfolds a war strategy. It is a rare word in the Bible, and its strength comes from its context: it is used to describe how God's enemies plot against the righteous.
H2665.emploi: The word appears only once in Psalms 64:7, at the heart of a complaint from the psalmist against those who persecute him. In this context, the plot is clearly hostile: these men conspire, they "meditate crimes" before letting out their hurtful arrows and words. The psalmist calls on God to thwart this secret plot — to show that what is being devised in the darkness of their hearts does not escape His justice. It is a word of conflict, always negative in the Bible.
H2665.portee: This word calls the believer to be wary of hidden intentions — both those recognized in enemies and those that must be monitored in one's own heart. But it also calls for trust: no evil plot hatched in secret escapes God. The psalmist teaches us to entrust to God the judgment of these hidden intrigues, rather than wear ourselves out fighting them alone.

sens: To obtain freedom, to no longer be a slave
To be liberated from an obligation or dependence
H2666.detail:
1. This verb describes the state of one who regains freedom after having been a slave or in bondage. In Leviticus 19:20, it refers to a female slave who has not yet been freed — that is, she remains under the yoke of servitude and has not acquired her status as a free woman.
2. More broadly, the word can evoke liberation from any form of dependence or binding link: to be freed means to escape what hinders freedom.
H2666.origine: The verb חָפַשׁ (chaphash) comes from a root that carries the idea of unblocking, of clearing. The word evokes the image of shaking off chains, of letting go of one who was held. It is a technical term in Israelite law regarding the condition of slaves: moving from the state of servitude to that of freedom.
H2666.emploi: This verb appears only once in the provided biblical text, in Leviticus 19:20. The Law of Moses uses it to specify the legal status: a female slave engaged to another who has not yet been freed remains under the yoke of servitude. The context is judicial: the non-affirmation of legal freedom has consequences on the punishments applicable in case of fault. The word thus designates an official and recognized change of condition.
H2666.portee: For the believer, this word reminds us that freedom is not a natural state of the slave, but an act that must be accomplished — it must be granted and legally recognized. Spiritually, this evokes the necessity of true liberation, not by our own strength, but by an act of deliverance that pulls us from sin.

sens: Fabric used as a saddle or covering for riding a horse
Cloth or cover for equipping horses
H2667.detail:
1. This word designates a fabric used to sit on a horse during travel or a journey. It was a prized possession in antiquity, a sign of wealth and status. In Ezekiel 27:20, Dedan traded in horse blankets — an important trade item in exchanges between ancient merchant cities.
2. More broadly, the word evokes the fabrics that equipped and adorned horses: fine textiles, often richly worked, that served both as practical equipment and as a mark of social status or luxury.
H2667.origine: The Hebrew word חֹפֶשׁ (chopesh) has a root whose basic meaning remains uncertain, but it describes something widespread or extended — a natural image for a fabric spread over the back of an animal. The context of ancient commercial exchanges in the East suggests a garment or cover of large size, likely a fine and sought-after textile product.
H2667.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible: in Ezekiel 27:20, in the description of Tyre's trade during the time of the prophet. Dedan, a prosperous region of Arabia, is among the peoples who traded with Tyre, the great merchant city. This unique mention indicates that saddle blankets or horse equipment were luxury and trade items in the ancient world, exchanged between great commercial powers.
H2667.portee: This detail of ancient commerce reminds us that wealth and prestige came through material goods — fine clothing, animal equipment — and that the prophet Ezekiel lists all trade items to show the extent of Tyre's prosperity before its judgment. This invites us to see how God notices even the details of our material life and our exchanges.

sens: State of one who has been released from slavery or subjugation
Condition of one who is not under the power or authority of a master
Legal freedom or status of a free person
H2668.detail: 1. The word properly designates the condition of a person who has been released from slavery. In Leviticus 19:20, it refers to a slave who has not yet obtained her freedom, meaning she has not been formally released; she therefore remains under the authority of her master, which affects the legal consequences of certain actions. 2. It also more broadly evokes the status of one who is no longer subject to a power or obligation: the freed person enjoys a legal freedom that the slave does not have. 3. Thus, it is a word that speaks of breaking bonds and accessing a new condition, that of the free person recognized by the law.
H2668.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of breaking or separation. It belongs to the family of biblical terms that express liberation, particularly important in Israelite law since the Law of Moses provided specific modalities for the emancipation of slaves. It is a rare word in biblical Hebrew, used only once, but it summarizes a key notion of Israelite civil law.
H2668.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Leviticus 19:20. It designates the state of a slave who has not yet obtained her legal freedom. The context is that of criminal law: the Law distinguishes punishments based on whether the woman is freed or not, as her legal status changes the severity of the offense. This word fits into the system of Old Testament law, where a person's status — free or slave, freed or not — determines their rights and the extent of legal protection.
H2668.portee: This word reminds us that the Bible acknowledges the reality of slavery in ancient societies while regulating it through the Law. It also shows that in God's plan, slavery was not permanent: the possibility of emancipation was inscribed in the legislation. For the Christian reader, it is an opportunity to contemplate how God regulates human institutions and how He aspires to the dignity and freedom of each individual.

sens: Set apart, isolated from the rest
Physically removed, distanced
Withdrawn from the community, excluded
H2669.detail:
1. The word describes something or someone that is set aside, placed at a distance from the group or the usual place. It conveys the idea of a clear and deliberate separation. In 2 Kings 15:5, King Uzziah, having become leprous, "remained in a separate house": his illness forces him to live in isolation, away from the palace and normal life.

2. This separation can be imposed by law or medical and religious necessity. It creates a barrier between the sick person and those who might be contaminated. The separate house of the leprous king kept him away from the temple and his royal duties, which 2 Chronicles 26:21 explicitly recalls: "he was excluded from the house of the Lord".

3. The word also expresses the state of a person rejected or excluded from community and religious life for reasons of purity. It was a form of protective and purifying confinement according to the Law.
H2669.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that means "to be free" in the sense of "released, separated," hence "set apart." The physical freedom of lepers was that of separation: free to move alone, but separated from all. The primary idea is one of clear distinction, like something that detaches or moves away from the group.
H2669.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible, in two parallel accounts of the same event: the leprosy of King Uzziah (2 Kings 15:5 and 2 Chronicles 26:21). In both cases, it qualifies the house where the king lived after his contamination, emphasizing his forced isolation and separation from the structures of power and worship. It is both a historical and medical term: it designates both the physical place of separation and the social status of exclusion of the leper.
H2669.portee: This word reminds us of the radical nature of leprosy in the Old Testament: a disease that separates not only the body but the sick person from worship, from their responsibilities, and from their community. It illustrates the weight of ritual purity in the Law and invites the reader to understand how Jesus, by healing lepers (Mark 1:40-45), restores them to the community and reintegrates them into normal life.

sens: Freed from slavery, no longer belonging to a master
Exempt from taxes, duties, or obligations to someone
Released, not held or imprisoned
H2670.detail:
1. The primary meaning is that of a slave who regains his freedom. According to the Law of Moses, a Hebrew slave was to serve only six years: in the seventh year, he was to be sent away "free," that is, emancipated without owing anything to his master (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12). This is a legal and complete liberation.
2. The word also applies to one who is released from a financial obligation or subjugation. A master who caused the eye of his slave to be injured had to "set him free," meaning to release him without demanding any compensation (Exodus 21:26). This includes the idea of no longer being subject to a burden.
3. In a broader sense, the word describes the state of one who is not under domination. Job refers to the slave who is no longer "subject" to his master in the realm of the dead (Job 3:19), where all human hierarchy disappears. It is the absence of constraint or dependency.
H2670.origine: The Hebrew word חׇפְשִׁי (chophshi) likely comes from a root expressing the idea of "to release" or "to set apart." It is related to other Hebrew words meaning "free space" or "not bound." In the Old Testament, the related verb describes the action of releasing someone or letting them go. The concept reflects Israel's laws on emancipation and the jubilee, where the freedom of Hebrew slaves was a fundamental principle of justice.
H2670.emploi: The word appears 17 times in the Old Testament, primarily in the laws of the Pentateuch (Exodus and Deuteronomy). It is almost exclusively used to describe the emancipation of Hebrew slaves according to legal prescriptions: after six years of servitude, they were to be sent away free (Exodus 21:2; Deuteronomy 15:12). The same term applies to complete liberation during the jubilee (Jeremiah 34). It is also found in Job and the Psalms, where it takes on a more existential hue: the absence of domination or slavery. In Job 3:19, it is the equality of all in the realm of the dead, where masters and slaves lose their distinct status.
H2670.portee: This word reminds Christians that true freedom comes from God and is a right of the weak against the powerful. In Israel's law, the periodic emancipation of slaves was an institution of mercy that protected the poor from perpetual servitude. For the New Testament reader, this word sheds light on the profound meaning of salvation: just as the Hebrew slave was sent away free, the believer in Christ receives true freedom — no longer a slave to sin, but freed to serve God (John 8:36).

sens: sharp projectile shot from a bow, weapon of war and hunting
wound or pain, especially moral or spiritual
cutting word, lie or accusation that hurts
judgment or anger of God
H2671.detail:
1. An arrow is a sharp projectile, equipped with a point and a shaft, that is shot from a bow: it is the weapon of archers in battle or hunting. In 1 Samuel 20:38, Jonathan's boy collects his master's arrows. Genesis 49:23 mentions archers who "shoot arrows" against the one they persecute.
2. By extension, the arrow also refers to the wound itself or the pain it causes, particularly moral suffering. Job 6:4 says: "The arrows of the Almighty are within me; my soul drinks in their poison" — it is the wound of trial that pierces the whole being.
3. Arrows also symbolize false words or accusations that strike like a dart. Proverbs 25:18 compares one who lies to a weapon: "A man who bears false witness against his neighbor is like a club, a sword, and a sharp arrow."
4. Finally, arrows represent the punishment or anger of God directed against His enemies or those who disobey Him. Deuteronomy 32:23 says: "I will heap disasters upon them; I will spend My arrows against them," an image of divine justice that strikes.
H2671.origine: The Hebrew word chets (חֵץ) refers to the material object from ancient times: it is the sharp, cut projectile designed to fly. Like many weapon words, it has taken on figurative meanings: the wound, the word that hurts, and finally the manifestation of divine anger. Arrows are mentioned in ancient Egypt and Mesopotamia; it was an essential weapon for war and hunting.
H2671.emploi: The word chets appears about 50 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in narrative texts (1 Samuel, 2 Kings), poetic texts (Psalms, Proverbs), and prophetic texts (Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Zechariah). In the concrete sense, it refers to the projectile of the archer: 1 Samuel 20 recounts a scene where Jonathan shoots arrows to communicate with David. In the sense of wound or suffering, the word appears in Job and in the Psalms (Psalms 38:3: "Your arrows have pierced me"). In the sense of hurtful word or lie, it is used in Proverbs (Proverbs 7:23, Proverbs 26:18). Finally, God's arrows represent His judgment or vengeance: Deuteronomy 32:42 states that God will fill His arrows with vengeance, and Ezekiel 5:16 mentions the arrows of famine shot against Jerusalem.
H2671.portee: Understanding the word "arrow" helps grasp the strength of biblical imagery: when the psalmist says "Your arrows have pierced me," he expresses a deep, real suffering, not abstract. It is a weapon that wounds the soul. It also reminds us that our words can be "arrows" — they may seem light until they strike someone. Finally, seeing God as the one who "shoots His arrows" against evil shows us that His justice is not passive: it acts, it strikes, it restores order.

sens: Extract stone, wood, or earth by working with tools
Shape stone or wood to make a useful form
Excavate the ground to create a hole
Engrave or inscribe characters in rock
Divide or split something into pieces
In a figurative sense: strike, cut deeply
H2672.detail:
1. Extract stone, wood, or earth by working with tools — this is the work of the miner or quarryman who detaches raw material. In 2 Chronicles 2:2, Solomon gathers eighty thousand men to "cut stones in the mountain": these are workers digging into the rock to extract blocks for the temple.
2. Shape stone or wood to make a useful form — this is giving shape to the extracted material, preparing it for construction. In 2 Kings 12:12, "stone cutters" are mentioned who receive money for the temple: these are artisans working the raw material.
3. Excavate the ground to create a hole or a well — this is removing earth to create a cavity. In Deuteronomy 6:11, God gives the Israelites "hewn cisterns" already prepared: these water reservoirs were excavated from the rock.
4. Engrave or inscribe characters in rock — this is a fine work that requires precision. In Job 19:24, Job wishes that his words be "engraved in the rock" with an iron tool, engraved forever.
5. Divide or split something into pieces — the verb can have a more brutal sense of separation. It is to tear, cut, cleave.
6. In a figurative sense: strike, cut deeply — In Hosea 6:5, the prophet says "I have struck them by the prophets," where the verb evokes an action that penetrates and divides, separating the just from the unjust.
H2672.origine: The Hebrew root חצב (ḥatsav) evokes the idea of digging, shaping, cleaving. It is related to other words that describe actions of working on hard material. The verb has forms: in the simple mode (Qal) it means "to dig, to shape, hewer"; in the passive (Niphal) "to be dug, to be shaped"; in the intensive mode (Hiphil) "to cut into pieces." The starting image is that of the tool striking the rock or wood to modify its shape.
H2672.emploi: The verb ḥatsav appears 22 times in the Hebrew Bible, mainly in historical books and construction narratives. It is used to describe the extraction and preparation of materials: hewn cisterns (Deuteronomy 6:11, 2 Chronicles 26:10), stones cut for the temple and palace (2 Chronicles 2:2, 2 Kings 12:12). It is also found in more serious contexts: Job uses it to express his desire that his words be engraved forever (Job 19:24), and Hosea uses it figuratively to describe the striking of the prophet that divides and instructs (Hosea 6:5). In Isaiah, the word characterizes the action of one who digs the winepress (Isaiah 5:2) and the work of the carpenter's tools (Isaiah 10:15).
H2672.portee: This verb reminds us that God provides for our concrete needs — He gives houses, cisterns, vineyards "all hewn and planted" (Deuteronomy 6:11). It also honors manual labor and craftsmanship: stone cutters, carpenters are recognized as important workers in God's projects. Finally, it invites depth: may our words, like those of Job, be engraved not on the surface but in the heart of the rock, and may the Word of God work deeply within us, shaping us with the energy of the chisel.

sens: Divide something into two or more parts
Distribute among people
Cut through (a barrier, a body of water)
Consume half, live half (of the expected time)
H2673.detail:
1. The primary meaning is to divide something into two or more portions: it is the concrete act of sharing. Jacob "shares" his people and livestock into two camps for protection (Genesis 32:7), or two owners "share" the price of a dead ox (Exodus 21:35).
2. Often sharing implies distribution among people or groups: Moses "divides" the spoils of war among the fighters and the other Israelites (Numbers 31:42), or a leader "shares" his troops into three divisions (Judges 9:43).
3. The verb can also mean to cut through an obstacle: when Elisha strikes the waters of the Jordan, they "part" before him, opening on either side, and he crosses (2 Kings 2:14). It is the image of a radical separation, a cut that creates a passage.
4. Figuratively, the word takes on the meaning of "living half of one's days" or only "reaching" half of one's lifespan: violent men will not fulfill the normal duration of their existence (Psalms 55:24).
H2673.origine: The Hebrew verb חָצָה comes from a root that evokes the idea of "cutting" or "dividing" in the middle. Its basic image is that of a line or separation in the sense of length. In Hebrew, the noun חֵצִי ("half") is found, which clearly shows the connection with the idea of division into two equal parts. The root expresses both the physical act of dividing and the abstract idea of sharing or distribution.
H2673.emploi: The verb appears about 14 times in the Old Testament, mainly in historical and poetic narratives. It primarily denotes the concrete sharing of goods (spoils, price of an animal, territory) among several people or groups. It is also used to describe the organization of a troop into tactical divisions (Judges 7:16, Judges 9:43). A remarkable usage is in miracles: the Red Sea and the Jordan "part" before God's servants (2 Kings 2:8, 2 Kings 2:14), symbolizing divine intervention that creates a passage. Figuratively, the verb can express the idea of living only half of the expected duration, as a divine judgment (Psalms 55:24). The context determines whether the sharing is equal or unequal, voluntary or imposed.
H2673.portee: This word reminds us that God governs goods and lives, and that He can open a way through the most insurmountable obstacles. Just sharing is an act of wise management; the ability to "part the waters" symbolizes the divine power that intervenes to save His people. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize that everything comes from God and to distribute without fear, knowing that God Himself shares and protects His own.

sens: Fortified city in northern Palestine, capital of an important league of Canaanite kingdoms
Royal city allotted to the tribe of Naphtali during the conquest of the promised land
H2674G.detail:
1. Hazor was a major fortress in the northern Canaanite territory, the seat of power of a coalition of Canaanite kings who opposed Israel. Joshua 11:10 describes it as "the chief city of all these kingdoms," highlighting its strategic and political importance.
2. After the conquest, Hazor was integrated into the territory of the tribe of Naphtali (Joshua 19:36). It then became an Israelite possession, although the city had a tumultuous history, notably being taken by Jabin (Judges 4:2) before being subdued again.
H2674G.origine: The name means "enclosure" or "castle" in Hebrew, evoking a fortified stronghold. Hazor represents the image of a strong city, protected by walls and ramparts, capable of serving as a base of power and resistance.
H2674G.emploi: Hazor appears about a dozen times in the Bible, mainly concentrated in the account of the conquest (Joshua 11, 12, and 19). At the time Joshua conquers the Promised Land, Hazor is the capital of the royal league led by Jabin, its king. Joshua takes it, kills its king, and burns the city (Joshua 11:10-11), confirming its unique status among Canaanite cities as it is the only one burned during this campaign (Joshua 11:13). Hazor resurfaces several centuries later: the same Jabin reigns there during the time of the Judges (Judges 4:2), reminding us that the subjugation of Canaan was never definitive. The city also appears as a fortified place under Solomon (1 Kings 9:15).
H2674G.portee: Hazor symbolizes the resistance of the Canaanite world to the establishment of God's people in their promised land, and its destruction shows the decisive nature of the divine victory granted to Joshua. It is also a reminder that possession of the land requires vigilance: Hazor, though defeated, remains a center of resistance during the period of the Judges, illustrating the ongoing challenges Israel faces in its faithfulness to God.

sens: City in southern Judah
H2674H.detail: Hazor is a fortified city (the name means "castle" or "enclosure") located in the extreme south of the territory of Judah. It appears in the list of cities that Joshua assigns to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of the promised land (Joshua 15:23), listed among the cities of the Negev (the desert south of Israel), alongside Kadesh and Ithnan.
H2674H.origine: The Hebrew name חָצוֹר (Hazor) comes from the root חצר (hatzar), which means "enclosure" or "fortified courtyard." It is a term that evokes a closed, defended place, a castle or fortress — a city capable of protecting itself, which was essential in the arid region of the Negev.
H2674H.emploi: Hazor appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:23, in the context of the enumeration of the cities in southern Judah after the conquest. This passage lists the territorial possessions assigned to the tribe of Judah by Joshua, establishing the boundaries of the divine territory granted to God's people.

sens: City in southern Judah
H2674I.detail: Hazor is a small city in the extreme south of the territory of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible. It appears in the list of cities assigned to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:25), where it is also called Hazor-Hadathta ("Hazor the new"), suggesting that it received this nickname to distinguish it from another more famous Hazor, probably the one in northern Israel.
H2674I.origine: The name Hazor means "castle" or "fortified enclosure" in Hebrew. It is a common place name in the Old Testament, borne by several different cities, always located in strategically important regions. The same name appears to designate the great fortress in the north, the capital of Galilee.
H2674I.emploi: Hazor of the south is mentioned only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:25, in the enumeration of the cities belonging to the tribe of Judah. This list delineates the borders and extent of the territory of Judah after the conquest of Canaan. Unlike the famous Hazor in the north, this small city in the south holds no significant place in the biblical narrative.

sens: City in Judea where the Benjamites settled after the exile
H2674J.detail: Hazor is a locality in the region of Judea, mentioned in the Bible as one of the places where the Benjamites resettled after their return from captivity in Babylon (Nehemiah 11:33). Its name means "castle" or "fortress" in Hebrew, evoking a fortified place. It was located north of Jerusalem and was part of the territory where the inhabitants of Benjamin rebuilt their communities.
H2674J.origine: The name Hazor comes from the Hebrew חָצוֹר (ḥâṣôr), derived from the root חָצַר (ḥâṣar) meaning "to enclose" or "to fence in." The word thus evokes a fortified place, a defended enclosure, or a castle — the image of a space protected by walls.
H2674J.emploi: Hazor appears only once in the Bible, in the book of Nehemiah in chapter 11, verse 33. This passage enumerates the cities and villages where the Benjamites established themselves after their return from exile, likely in the fifth century B.C. It is mentioned among other localities in the Benjamin region, situating its geographical position within the territory of the tribe of Benjamin, north of Jerusalem.

sens: region or settlement in Arabia, populated by nomadic tribes
H2674K.detail: 1. Hatsor is a region or settlement located in Arabia, inhabited by nomadic tribes. The prophet Jeremiah announces that it will be attacked by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, and that its inhabitants will have to flee (Jeremiah 49:28-30).
H2674K.origine: The name Hatsor literally means "castle" or "enclosure" in Hebrew, evoking a fortified place or a defined settlement. This region of Arabia was probably a trading center or a gathering of fortified tents where the tribes of the East lived.
H2674K.emploi: Hatsor appears three times in the Bible, all in the prophetic passage of Jeremiah 49:28-33. The prophet announces divine judgment against this region: it will be destroyed by Nebuchadnezzar (Jeremiah 49:28), its inhabitants must flee (Jeremiah 49:30), and it will become a permanent desert, a haunt for jackals, where no one will live anymore (Jeremiah 49:33). These three verses form a unit and describe the fulfillment of the word of the Lord against this Arab region.

sens: Fortified city in the south of Judah
H2675.detail: Hatsor-Hadattha is a city in the south of Judah, mentioned only once in the Bible. The name means "the new Hatsor": it is a distinction from another older Hatsor located in the north of the country. It appears in the list of cities in the territory assigned to the tribe of Judah (Joshua 15:25).
H2675.origine: The name consists of two Hebrew parts: Hatsor, which literally means "enclosure" or "fortress" (from the verb meaning "to enclose"), and Hadattha, which means "new." It is a descriptive name that clearly indicates the status of this locality in relation to another Hatsor. There are several cities named Hatsor in the Old Testament, with the northern one being the most famous.
H2675.emploi: Hatsor-Hadattha appears only once in the Bible, in the book of Joshua in chapter 15, where it is listed among the cities assigned to the tribe of Judah during the division of the territory after the conquest of Canaan. It is also referred to by another name: Kerijoth-Hetsron. This dual designation suggests that it was an important locality in the southern part of the territory of Judah, although we know little biblical detail about it.

sens: the heart of the night, the moment when it is most advanced
a precise and dramatic moment when God acts
a time of watchfulness and prayer, separate from ordinary rest
H2676.detail:
1. The word designates the central point, the heart of the night: it is when the night is the deepest. In Exodus 11:4, Moses announces that the Lord will pass "in the middle of the night" to strike the firstborn of Egypt — it is the critical moment, the darkest, when everything is asleep.
2. It is a moment of divine intervention that changes the course of events. In Job 34:20, the people stagger and perish "in the middle of the night," an image of a sudden catastrophe coming from heaven, without visible deadly blow.
3. It is also a time of spiritual watchfulness, detached from ordinary life. The psalmist rises "in the middle of the night" to praise the Lord (Psalms 119:62), a moment of solitude and intimacy with God, when the world sleeps.
H2676.origine: The Hebrew word comes from a root meaning "to be in the middle, to divide." The form חָצוֹת evokes the division of the night into two: on one side the first half, on the other the second. It is a moment of division between before and after, between rest and vigilance. The same root produces other Hebrew words of sharing or division.
H2676.emploi: The word appears only three times in the Bible according to these references, always in the sense of "middle of the night." Exodus 11:4 places it in the crucial moment of the tenth plague, when God manifests most drastically. Job 34:20 uses it for a sudden catastrophe. Psalms 119:62 places it in a context of personal piety and praise. Each context uses this deep hour of the night to mark either a spectacular divine intervention or an act of devotion. It is always a charged moment, never ordinary.
H2676.portee: The middle of the night in Scripture is rarely a banal time: it is when God acts decisively and when the heart opens to Him away from the noise of the day. For the reader, this invites recognition that even in darkness — that of sleeping Egypt as well as that of the silent room — God is active and deserves praise.

sens: Each of the two equal parts of a whole divided in two
Quantity, measure, or number that is half of a whole
Intermediate part, center or middle of a duration or distance
One of the two tribes or groups that form a division
Moment that separates the two halves of a night
H2677.detail:
1. The half is each of the two parts when something is cut in two: in 1 Kings 3:25, King Solomon orders that the living child be divided into two halves, which means cutting it into two equal parts. This is the most concrete and harsh meaning of the word.
2. A half can also be a measured quantity: "a half-hin of wine" (Numbers 28:14) or "a quarter of a hin" designate determined portions, half of a unit of measure.
3. The word also designates the middle or center of a duration or extent: "in the middle of the night" (Exodus 12:29) means at midnight, when the night is halfway between its beginning and end.
4. When speaking of the "half-tribe of Manasseh" (Joshua 22:21), it refers to half of a tribe that settled alone on one side of the Jordan, while the other half settled on the other side.
5. The half of a night is the peak point of the middle of the night, as when God struck all the firstborn "in the middle of the night" of Egypt.
H2677.origine: The Hebrew word חֲצִי (he-tsi) comes from a root meaning "to cut" or "to divide." It is a simple and ancient word, which the Old Testament uses over a hundred times to speak of divisions, portions, and middles. The word evokes the very concrete action of cutting something into two equal parts.
H2677.emploi: The word appears 103 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in the historical and Law books. It primarily designates territorial divisions: half of Gilead (Joshua 13:25), the half-tribe of Manasseh that settled east of the Jordan (Numbers 32:33, Deuteronomy 3:12). It also measures precise quantities in worship: half-hin of wine, measures of oil or flour in offerings (Numbers 28:14). It finally indicates a moment or a point in the middle: the middle of the night (Exodus 12:29), the middle of the day, half of a distance traveled. In Nehemiah 4:16, half of the servants worked while the other half was armed, showing how the word structures a division of labor. Its use is concrete and unambiguous: it always states a separation or a position at the center.
H2677.portee: This word reminds us that God knows the divisions of our life and time: the moment of midnight when He struck the firstborn of Egypt marks a decisive act of judgment and deliverance. It also teaches us the justice of fair shares: when the Law prescribes determined portions, it reminds us that the Lord loves equity. For the believer, knowing that God divides and measures can reassure: nothing escapes His will, even the moments we go through and the resources we share.

sens: Pointed projectile shot from a bow
Message or signal agreed upon between two people
Quick and precise strike that hits its target
H2678.detail:
1. The arrow is the projectile shot with a bow: a shaft equipped with a sharp point. In the story of Jonathan and David (1 Samuel 20:36-37), Jonathan shoots arrows as a secret signal to his young servant, shouting where they fall so that David, hidden, understands his message. It is a formidable weapon: in 2 Kings 9:24, Jehu shoots an arrow so precisely that it pierces the heart of Joram and comes out his back.
2. By extension, the arrow refers to the message or signal agreed upon between allies. Jonathan uses the arrows not to kill, but to communicate with David: he arranges for the boy to act as a "living signal" who will carry the message by seeing where the arrows fall. The weapon becomes language.
3. Figuratively, an arrow represents a strike that reaches its objective with speed and certainty, like the sudden death it brings to Joram.
H2678.origine: The Hebrew word חֵצִי comes from a root that expresses the idea of "to cut" or "to divide." The arrow is primarily the object that divides air and flesh. It is a simple and ancient word, regularly found in the war and hunting narratives of the Old Testament to designate this basic yet formidable military equipment.
H2678.emploi: The word appears three times in the provided translations, always in the concrete sense: first in the episode of the secret signal between Jonathan and David (1 Samuel 20), where the arrows serve as a silent language to communicate a vital message that will determine whether David should flee or stay. Then in 2 Kings 9:24, as a precise and deadly instrument of execution. The arrow is always an object of concrete and dramatic use: it kills or signifies, never is it neutral.
H2678.portee: For the Christian reader, the arrow reminds us that God controls even the most ordinary actions of men. Jonathan uses a common arrow as a means to deliver David from danger: God uses the ingenuity and courage of believers to protect them. It also symbolizes the swiftness of death or judgment, and the importance of faithful communication between allies of the Lord.

sens: place where wild animals usually live
refuge or shelter
fixed dwelling
haunt or dark shelter
H2681.detail: 1. The word primarily designates the natural den of wild animals — the place where they rest and establish their daily lives. In Isaiah 34:13, it is the den of ostriches in the ruins of the palace of the defeated enemy, a place now abandoned by humans and become the habitat of beasts. 2. By extension, it is a refuge, a shelter where one withdraws to remain safe. The idea is of a fixed, established place where one finds protection and rest. 3. More broadly, it expresses the idea of a dwelling or a regularly and durably inhabited place. 4. In a context of ruin and desolation, it evokes a dark and desolate den, related to judgment or abandonment.
H2681.origine: The word comes from a Hebrew root that expresses the idea of dwelling or establishing oneself. It is constructed with a sense of shelter or habitat — the place where one rests, to which one regularly returns to inhabit. The same family of words in Hebrew refers to the arranged and inhabited space, whether human or animal.
H2681.emploi: The word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Isaiah 34:13. It describes the desolate future of Edom after God's judgment: the palaces and fortresses, once dwellings of power, will become the den of wild creatures. This context emphasizes the reversal of divine judgment: the place of civilization and human power transforms into a habitat for beasts. The word thus intensifies the image of desolation and total abandonment.
H2681.portee: This passage shows that all human power that ignores God is destined for complete ruin. The contrast between the past palace and the den of ostriches reveals the futility of any fortress erected against the Lord. For the believer, it is a call not to place trust in earthly edifices of power, which will not last.

sens: Herbaceous plant that covers fields and pastures
Food for livestock
Image of the fragility and brevity of human life
What is momentary and perishable in contrast to the eternity of God
H2682A.detail:
1. Grass primarily refers to the herbaceous vegetation that covers the land: it is the greenery of fields and pastures. In 1 Kings 18:5, Ahab sends Obadiah to seek grass to feed the horses and mules during the drought, showing that it is a vital resource for livestock.
2. Grass is the natural fodder for cattle: Job 40:10 describes the hippopotamus that "eats grass like an ox." It is the ordinary food of herds, essential for their survival.
3. The Bible uses grass as a striking image of human fragility. In Psalms 103:15, the psalmist compares man's days to grass that flourishes and then disappears: "Man! His days are like grass, he flourishes like the flower of the field."
4. More broadly, grass symbolizes everything that is ephemeral and mortal in the face of God's eternal power. Isaiah 40:7-8 describes the grass that withers when the breath of the Lord blows, while His word endures forever. This image reminds the reader of the vanity of earthly life and the necessity of clinging to God alone.
H2682A.origine: The Hebrew word חָצִיר (cha.tsir) literally denotes the green grass that grows and withers. Its basic image is that of fragile and transient vegetation. In the Old Testament, this word regularly characterizes what is momentary and without duration in contrast to eternity, particularly in the wisdom poems and prophetic oracles. The comparison between grass and human life runs throughout the Scriptures to express the humility of the mortal condition.
H2682A.emploi: The word appears 19 times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly in Psalms and Isaiah. It is used literally to denote vegetation and food for herds (1 Kings 18:5; Job 40:10; Psalms 147:8). But its primary use is figurative: it expresses the brevity of life (Psalms 103:15), the powerlessness of kings and peoples before God (Isaiah 40:6-8; Isaiah 37:27), and the vanity of human plans (Psalms 37:2; Psalms 90:5). Isaiah particularly returns to this image to show that everything not founded on the eternal word of God is destined to perish like withered grass.
H2682A.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the fragility of human existence and the importance of not placing trust in transient things. In the face of challenges and trials, it reminds us that only the word and grace of God endure forever. It also encourages humility and trust: by recognizing that we are like grass, we turn to the One who lasts forever and whose promise will never fail.

sens: Vegetable plant of the Middle East, with long leaves and a white bulb
Common food in ancient Egypt
Modest food, evoking nostalgia for material goods
H2682B.detail:
1. The leek is a vegetable plant cultivated in the Middle East and ancient Egypt, recognizable by its long green leaves and edible white bulb. It is a simple yet appreciated vegetable.
2. In biblical usage, the leek appears as ordinary food in Egypt, consumed by the people (Numbers 11:5): the Israelites, during their journey through the desert, lament the vegetables they ate in abundance during their slavery in Egypt, alongside fish and melons.
3. Figuratively, the leek symbolizes nostalgia for earthly and material comforts: the Israelites, freed from Egypt but hungry in the desert, covet the foods of the past rather than trusting in God who was guiding them.
H2682B.origine: The Hebrew word חָצִיר (tsir) comes from a root meaning "that which grows" or "greenery."
