It designates the leek, a characteristic plant of Egyptian gardens and vegetable patches that the Hebrews were well acquainted with during their captivity. In Hebrew, several words express different forms of greenery: this term specifically applies to the leek, a cultivated and appreciated vegetable.
H2682B.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Numbers 11:5. The Israelites, camped in the desert after their departure from Egypt, complain about the manna and long for the meals of Egypt: fish, cucumbers, melons, leeks, onions, and garlic. These very simple and accessible vegetables symbolize the material comfort and satiety that slavery provided them, contrasting with the trials of the desert. This regret reveals a spiritual tension between the freedom gained and the carnal needs.
H2682B.portee: This humble mention of the leek speaks to a deep human reality: the temptation to regret the past, even when oppressive, when the present is difficult. It invites us to reflect on our own nostalgia for lost comforts and to rediscover where our true trust lies — in divine provision rather than in our memories of comfort.

sens: Gather and tie bundles of grain for transport
Make a tight package of elongated things
H2683.detail:
1. To bind sheaves means to gather several sheaves (the cut stalks of wheat or barley) and tie them together for carrying or storage. It is the work of the reaper who, after the harvest, creates tight bundles. In Psalms 129:7, "he who binds the sheaves" refers to the worker who takes the scattered sheaves and ties them: it is an act of labor and gathering.
2. More generally, the word can refer to the action of making a bundle or a sheaf of any elongated object — stalks, reeds, branches — by tightly binding them together.
H2683.origine: The Hebrew word חֵצֶן comes from a root that expresses the idea of tightening, binding firmly. Its basic image is that of the farmer taking stalks in his hands and tying them to make a compact and transportable unit. This type of agricultural vocabulary is common in Hebrew: the Bible often speaks of the concrete gestures of harvesting and gathering.
H2683.emploi: The word appears only once in the Bible, in Psalms 129:7. It is a poem about the harvest, where the psalmist describes the actions of the workers. He says that the reaper does not fill his hand with sheaves, and he who "binds" the sheaves does not load his arm — in other words, the harvests are meager, the work unfruitful. This context shows that "binding the sheaves" is a normal and expected act of the farmer, but that drought or divine curse here prevents sufficient harvest to accomplish this act.
H2683.portee: This verse reminds us that all agricultural work depends on God's blessing: even an act as natural as binding sheaves can become impossible if God withdraws His favor. For the believer, it is an invitation to recognize divine providence in the harvests and not to place trust solely in the strength of one's own arm, but in the generous hand of the Creator.

sens: The space between a person's arms and chest, where one carries something or someone
The lap, the space of the garment folded over the chest and belly
By extension, a position of tenderness or protection
H2684.detail:
1. The bosom primarily refers to the hollow formed by the arms and chest. It is the part of the body where one can carry an object or a child close to oneself, as seen in Isaiah 49:22 where the nations will bring back the sons "in their arms" — literally, in this hollow of the body which is the bosom.
2. The word also refers to the lap, that space of the cloak or garment that is folded over oneself. In Nehemiah 5:13, Nehemiah shakes his "garment" (literally: his bosom) to signify that he is separating from the one who breaks his commitment — the garment folded over the chest is shaken to pour out what was carried within.
3. Figuratively, the bosom represents a place of intimacy, protection, or care: it is where one holds dear what one loves or possesses.
H2684.origine: The Hebrew word חֹצֶן (hotsen) likely comes from a root expressing the idea of "holding" or "containing." The bosom is the hollow of the body and garment that naturally contains. In Greek, the corresponding word is κόλπος (kolpos, "bosom" or "lap"), which appears in several translations of the Old Testament into Greek (the Septuagint).
H2684.emploi: The word appears twice in the Hebrew Bible according to our sources. In Nehemiah 5:13, it is translated as "garment": it refers to Nehemiah's gesture of shaking the folded edge of his garment to signify rejection or rupture. In Isaiah 49:22, it is translated as "arms": the context speaks of the nations who will bring back the children of Israel, carrying them in their bosom, that is, tenderly and securely. In both cases, the word evokes a relationship between the body (or garment) and what is contained within: either one shakes it off to rid oneself of it, or one carries someone with care.
H2684.portee: This word reminds us that the body of one who loves — whether God or man — is a place of refuge and tenderness. When the nations bring back the children of Israel "in their arms," the text expresses maternal protection and kindness. For the Christian, this image of the bosom speaks of intimacy with God, of the security of one who is carried and loved.

sens: Who exercises authority with rigor, without gentleness
Who imposes with urgency and force
Who manifests insolence or contempt
H2685.detail:
1. The word describes an authority or decision that does not tolerate dissent and is applied with rigor. In Daniel 2:15, Arjoc acknowledges that the king's order is "severe" — it is a harsh sentence, uncompromising, demanding swift and unquestioned execution.
2. The word also evokes pressing urgency, tyrannical impatience: in Daniel 3:22, "the king's order was severe" means that it imposed immediate and irrevocable execution, so urgent that the extreme heat killed even those who had thrown the three young men in.
3. Underlying the previous meaning, the word contains the idea of insolence from the one commanding: he does not ask, he imposes with disdain for objections.
H2685.origine: The root evokes the idea of haste and brutal audacity. The word belongs to a family that expresses what is prompt, impatient, even insolent — the image is that of a will that rushes without delay, trampling over obstacles.
H2685.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both times in Daniel and always concerning the orders of King Nebuchadnezzar. In Daniel 2:15, it qualifies a death sentence (the king's word must cause the wise men of Babylon to perish). In Daniel 3:22, it qualifies the order to heat the furnace to a deadly point. In both cases, it is characteristic of an absolute power that commands without appeal and expects no mercy.
H2685.portee: This word shows how the orders of the tyrant impose with a brutality that leaves no way out. For the reader, it reveals the injustice and violence of regimes that reject God: they command without wisdom, without mercy. It is in this atmosphere of ruthless severity that God protects His faithful servants.

sens: Terminer, mener à sa fin
Diviser, séparer en parties
Être coupé net, prendre fin
H2686A.detail:
1. This verb primarily means to complete or finish: to bring something to its full term. In Job 21:21, it speaks of the number of months that comes to an end — in other words, life that flows and concludes. It conveys the idea of a limit reached, an end that occurs.

2. The verb can also mean to divide or separate into distinct portions, like cutting something. In Proverbs 30:27, the locusts come out in divisions — that is, they unfold in separate and organized groups, each forming a distinct unit.

3. In the passive form, the word expresses the idea of being cut off, being completed or abruptly interrupted, as if a cord were to snap. It describes the state of something that has reached its definitive limit.
H2686A.origine: This verb comes from a Hebrew root evoking the action of cutting, separating, or slicing. The central idea is one of a clear division or demarcation: something complete that comes to an end, or that divides into distinct parts. The root refers to the concrete image of separating, delimiting, or finishing.
H2686A.emploi: The verb חָצַץ (cha.tsats) is rare in the Bible: it appears only twice in the translations we have. It expresses two closely related but distinct nuances. In Job 21:21, it describes completion: the months of life are counted and come to an irrevocable end. In Proverbs 30:27, it denotes organized division: the locusts advance in formation, divided into coherent groups. In both cases, the word evokes a clear limit or separation, whether temporal or spatial.
H2686A.portee: This word confronts us with the reality of our limits: our life has a determined number of days that flow and come to an end. It invites the believer to wisdom and not to postpone eternity, as highlighted in the context of the passage from Job. The image of the locusts organized in divisions also reminds us that order and structure come from God, even in the smallest creatures.

sens: Celui qui tire des flèches avec un arc
H2686B.detail: 1. The archer is a fighter who wields the bow and arrows. He is a warrior specialized in projectile shooting. In the Song of Deborah (Judges 5:11), archers are mentioned as part of the people of the Lord who go down to battle, celebrating the victories of the Lord.
H2686B.origine: The Hebrew verb חָצַץ (chatsats) expresses the action of shooting or sifting with arrows. The form used here is the participle of the Piel, which denotes one who actively or habitually performs this action. The word refers to the image of the warrior whose specialty is archery, a formidable weapon in ancient battles.
H2686B.emploi: This word appears only once in the Hebrew Bible, in Judges 5:11, in the Song of Deborah. It designates the archers of the people of Israel who participate in the victory against Sisera. The context shows the archers as warriors of God's people, praising the Lord for His intervention on their behalf. Although rare, this term emphasizes the military role and solidarity of the people in celebrating the acts of the Lord.
H2686B.portee: This word reminds us that Israel's victory comes from the Lord and not solely from its military strength. The archers who sing of the Lord's blessings illustrate how each fighter must remember that it is God who acts, and how true strength lies in trust in Him rather than in weapons.

sens: Petites pierres ou cailloux
Élément dur qui remplit la bouche et symbolise l'amertume
Châtiment ou souffrance physique
H2687.detail:
1. Gravel is primarily a concrete material: small stones, pebbles that litter the ground or a path. It is a hard and unpleasant material.
2. In Proverbs 20:17, gravel symbolically fills the mouth: after the deceptive pleasure of lying (‘sweet bread’), a man discovers bitterness, as if he were crunching on gravel instead of eating. The image expresses the brutal contrast between the seductive appearance of a lie and its destructive reality.
3. In Lamentations 3:16, the psalmist describes the suffering of divine punishment: his teeth are broken by gravel, his body crushed under ashes. Here, gravel embodies the relentless harshness of God's judgment on Jerusalem.
H2687.origine: The Hebrew word חָצָץ (ḥatsats) designates small stones, gravels. It evokes the image of hard and brittle mineral fragments. The word belongs to a semantic field of hardness and rupture. It is a simple and concrete term that depicts the material as found in nature.
H2687.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Hebrew Bible. In Proverbs 20:17, it expresses the hidden bitterness of a lie under a culinary image: what seemed good turns out to be destructive and painful. In Lamentations 3:16, it describes the violence of divine punishment on destroyed Jerusalem, where the body of the suffering righteous is broken like gravel breaks teeth. In both cases, gravel symbolizes the inevitable suffering that follows sin or judgment, with a flavor of irony or tragedy.
H2687.portee: This word invites the reader to meditate on the hidden consequences of lies and evil: what seems pleasant may hide a destructive reality. It also reminds us that divine discipline, though difficult to bear, is real and serious. For those who listen to the Word, biblical gravel becomes a warning not to be seduced by deceptive appearances.

sens: Brass wind instrument, elongated in shape, that produces a bright sound
Signal or call given by this instrument
Assembly or event announced by the sound of the trumpet
The bright and powerful sound of a trumpet
H2689.detail:
1. The trumpet is a metal instrument, forged and hammered, that produces a piercing and powerful sound. Moses is commanded to make two silver trumpets for summoning the assembly of Israel (Numbers 10:2). This instrument serves both as a practical means of communication and as a symbol of ritual solemnity.

2. The trumpet emits precise signals: the sound of the trumpet calls people to gather or gives the order to set out (Numbers 10:8-10). Each type of sound has a different meaning — a simple call does not have the same effect as a prolonged fanfare.

3. The trumpet accompanies important moments in the religious and political life of Israel: the procession of the Ark (1 Chronicles 15:24), the coronation of the king (2 Kings 11:14), the solemn offering (2 Chronicles 29:27). It marks these public and serious events.

4. The sound of the trumpet is described as resounding, brilliant, producing an impressive and audible effect from afar (Numbers 31:6). It is a sound of celebration and victory: the priests sound trumpets at the dedication of the temple, at the shout of joy (2 Chronicles 5:12-13).
H2689.origine: The Hebrew word חֲצֹצְרָה (ḥatsotserah) likely comes from a root evoking a high or piercing sound. It is a cultic instrument typically used by Israelites: the two trumpets made under Moses become sacred objects, preserved and used by the priests throughout the ages. The term is specific to Israel and does not simply refer to an object, but to the instrument of worship of the true God.
H2689.emploi: The word trumpet appears 27 times in the Old Testament, almost exclusively in the historical and cultic books (Numbers, Kings, Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah) and twice in the Psalms. The trumpets are always in the hands of the priests or Levites: they are never weapons of war, but instruments of worship and religious communication. They are sounded at the consecration of the temple (2 Chronicles 5:12), during solemn feasts (2 Chronicles 15:14), at the offering of burnt offerings (2 Chronicles 29:27), or to call the people to assemble (Numbers 10:2). The context is always solemn and religious: never profane or merely entertaining.
H2689.portee: The trumpet reminds the people of God that they are summoned by the Lord and must gather to fulfill His will. It symbolizes the voice of God that calls and commands. For the Christian, it evokes the importance of listening to the divine call and responding with obedience and respect, knowing that God communicates with His people in a clear and powerful way.

sens: to produce a sound with a trumpet or brass instrument
to sound a musical call or signal
to accompany an action or ceremony with the sound of trumpets
H2690.detail:
1. The word designates the action of producing a sound by blowing into a trumpet or a similar instrument. It is a concrete and musical gesture: the priests "sounded trumpets" before the Ark of God during solemn processions (1 Chronicles 15:24).
2. The sound of the trumpet is a signal or a call that can be heard. In 2 Chronicles 5:13, those who sounded the trumpets join with those who sang to celebrate the Lord, and their harmony produces a powerful effect: the house of the Lord is filled with a cloud.
3. The action of sounding the trumpet accompanies important moments in religious life: dedication of the temple (2 Chronicles 5:12), praise (2 Chronicles 7:6), call to prayer in times of distress (2 Chronicles 13:14). The sound thus becomes an integral part of worship and communication with God.
H2690.origine: The Hebrew root חצר (tsar) primarily evokes the idea of producing a high or piercing sound. The verb in the intensive (Piel) or causative (Hiphil) form expresses the action of making an instrument sound. This word is specific to the Scriptures and particularly characterizes the activity of the priests in the temple.
H2690.emploi: The verb appears 6 times in the Bible, exclusively in 1 and 2 Chronicles, in contexts of temple liturgy. The priests are its typical agents: they sound trumpets during processions, dedications, praises, and calls to God. The word always expresses an organized and significant action, never trivial or incidental. Its use reflects the importance of the sound of trumpets as a central element of Israelite worship: it is a means of glorifying God and marking solemn moments.
H2690.portee: The sounding trumpet is a biblical symbol of proclamation and divine signal. For the believer, this word reminds that true worship is not limited to inner silence: it is also expressed through visible and audible acts. The trumpets sound to celebrate, to call to prayer, to invoke God's help. This invites the reader to consider how they express their faith, not only in thought but also through acts and words that shine forth.

sens: Open space surrounded by a fence or wall, inner courtyard
Court of the tabernacle or temple, sacred space reserved for worship
Courtyard of a prison or palace
Open space in front of a house
Public passage or waiting area
H2691A.detail:
1. The courtyard is primarily an open space, enclosed by a barrier or wall, where one can enter and move around: it is a court (Exodus 8:9, the frogs perish "in the courts").

2. In the tabernacle and the temple, the courtyard is the sacred space surrounded by curtains or walls that encloses the altar and the sanctuary, where the Israelites can approach God for worship and sacrifices (Exodus 40:33, "he erected the courtyard around the tabernacle").

3. The courtyard can also refer to a detention or prison yard, a closed place where someone is confined or kept (Jeremiah 38:13, Jeremiah remains "in the court of the prison").

4. In royal palaces, the courtyard refers to the open area where guards stand and where one waits to be received (Esther 5:1).

5. By extension, it is any open public space where people can gather, or even the surroundings of a dwelling (Exodus 8:9).
H2691A.origine: The Hebrew word חָצֵר comes from a root that expresses the idea of being enclosed or limited. It fundamentally designates a closed space, whether enclosed by walls, curtains, or a fence. The word relates to the idea of delimitation and protection: a courtyard is a separate space, distinct from the outside world.
H2691A.emploi: The word courtyard (or court) appears more than 120 times in the Bible, especially in descriptions of the tabernacle and the temple. It is very frequent in Exodus (construction of the tabernacle), in Kings and Chronicles (temple of Jerusalem), and in the Psalms (approaching the temple). In the religious context, the courtyard is the space where the Israelites gather to pray and offer sacrifices, sanctified by the presence of God. In the secular context, it is a prison yard (Jeremiah), a palace courtyard (1 Kings, Esther), or simply a closed space adjacent to a house. The word always carries the idea of a defined space, distinct from what surrounds it.
H2691A.portee: The courtyard reminds the reader that access to God is not anarchic: there is a path, an organized and designated space where one can meet Him. The Psalms express the believer's desire to cross the courtyard of the temple, an image of their aspiration to approach God (Psalms 84:3). For the Christian, this notion invites consideration that the presence of God is accessible, but in a conscious and respectful manner, with the awareness that one enters a separate, sanctified space.

sens: Small inhabited settlement, grouping of houses without fortifications
Set of dwellings that depend on a fortified city
Camp or enclosure for livestock and herds
Refuge or hiding place
H2691B.detail:
1. The word primarily designates a small human settlement, a modest agglomeration of houses, without walls or defenses — unlike a fortified city. It is a permanent but open habitat, vulnerable. In Genesis 25:16, the "camps" of Ishmael refer to these semi-nomadic establishments.
2. Very often, the word refers to the villages that revolve around a fortified city and depend on it: the lists in Joshua (15:41, 15:57, 19:6) systematically enumerate "sixteen cities, and their villages," "ten cities, and their villages." These villages constitute the urban hinterland.
3. The word can also denote a park or enclosure for livestock, a closed space but without houses: this is the pastoral image of the term. Genesis 25:16 uses it for the encampments of Ishmael's nomadic peoples.
4. Rarely, it takes on a figurative sense of refuge or hiding place: the psalmist describes one who "secretly [sets] his traps" (Psalms 10:8), suggesting a hidden lair.
H2691B.origine: The Hebrew word חָצֵר (cha.tser) literally means "fence" or "enclosure," derived from a root that evokes the idea of closing, enclosing. It first appears to designate a delimited space — a park for animals. Then it came to refer to small groupings of houses enclosed by low walls or fences. The word has also given rise in Hebrew to "hasar" (the course of a house) and various derivatives expressing the idea of enclosure.
H2691B.emploi: The word appears 44 times in the Hebrew Bible, primarily in geographical and administrative lists: especially in Joshua (29 occurrences), where it enumerates the villages dependent on each tribe and each city (Joshua 15, 18, 19). It also appears in 1 Chronicles (5 occurrences) and in Nehemiah (4 occurrences) for residences of the Levites. A notable occurrence in Leviticus 25:31 regulates the right of redemption of houses in the villages — which is not subject to the jubilee release like that of fortified urban houses. The meaning stabilizes: the village is always the minor, dependent, unfortified establishment, in contrast to the "city" (עִיר, ir).
H2691B.portee: This word reminds us of the actual structure of biblical society: ancient Near Eastern Israel primarily lived in agricultural and pastoral villages, with a few fortified centers. Understanding that the land was organized into cities and villages helps the reader to concretely imagine the living environment of the biblical narratives and to grasp the administrative and economic functioning of Israel during the monarchical period.

sens: Location in the Negev, at the southern edge of the Promised Land
H2692.detail: Hatsar-Addar is a place located on the southern border of the territory that God promises to Israel. The name literally means "enclosure of glory" or "splendid enclosure" — hatsar evokes a closed or surrounded space, addar the magnificence. In the only biblical passage that mentions it (Numbers 34:4), it marks a stopping point in the description of this southern boundary: after Kadesh-Barnea, the border passes through Hatsar-Addar before continuing to Atsmon. This site, whose exact geographical location eludes us today, was a known landmark for the Israelites to delineate their inheritance.
H2692.origine: The name combines two Hebrew elements: hatsar ("enclosure," "court") and addar ("glory," "splendor"). Hatsar shares its root with other words designating spaces surrounded by walls or fences; addar evokes divine majesty. Although the site is identified by this name alone in the Hebrew Bible, it represents a concrete territorial landmark in the Palestinian Negev.
H2692.emploi: Hatsar-Addar appears only once in the Bible, in the context of Numbers 34, where God dictates to Moses the exact borders of the territory that Israel will occupy. This passage methodically enumerates the northern, eastern, southern, and western boundaries of the Promised Land. The role of Hatsar-Addar is purely geographical: it is a relay on the southern border, between Kadesh-Barnea (the great sanctuary of the desert where Israel stayed for forty years) and Atsmon. The mention of the place in this official context confirms its importance as a territorial landmark at the time of the text.

sens: Location in Judea mentioned only once in the list of cities in southern Judah
H2693.detail: Heschmon (called Hatsar-Gadda in the Hebrew text) is a small town in southern Judea. It appears in the enumeration of localities assigned to the tribe of Judah after the conquest of Canaan (Joshua 15:27). It is one of the many border towns in the southern territory of Judah, in an arid and sparsely populated region.
H2693.origine: The Hebrew name חֲצַר גַּדָּה (Hatsar-Gadda) literally means "village (or enclosure) of good fortune." חֲצַר (hatsar) means enclosure or fortified village; גַּדָּה (gaddah) evokes prosperity or wealth. The Greek translation of the Bible (Septuagint) rendered this name as Ἐσεμών (Esemon), from which the French form Heschmon derives. The original name reflects a place thought to be prosperous or favored.
H2693.emploi: Heschmon appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:27, in the detailed list of cities in the Negev (southern Judah) that Joshua assigns to the tribe of Judah after the conquest. It is cited between Hatsar-Gadda and Beth-Paleth, with no other historical or narrative information. Like many localities in this region, its exact location has not been clearly identified by archaeology.

sens: Place in Palestine, probably east of Hermon
H2694.detail: Hatzer-Hatthicon is a place mentioned only once in the Bible, in the prophetic description of the future borders of Israel. The name literally means "court of the middle" in Hebrew. According to the context of Ezekiel 47:16, it is located in the mountainous region of the east, between Damascus and Hamath, probably near Hermon or on its eastern slopes. It is a geographical landmark that the prophet uses to outline the territory that God promises to His people at the time of their final restoration.
H2694.origine: The Hebrew name חֲצַר הַתִּיכוֹן (Ḥatsar hat-Tīkhōn) comes from חֲצַר (ḥatsar, "court" or "enclosure") and from תִּיכוֹן (tīkhōn, "of the middle"). The image evokes a closed or delimited space at the heart of a region. Although this place is mentioned only once in Ezekiel 47:16, its precise name suggests that it was known as a local landmark at the time of the prophet.
H2694.emploi: Hatzer-Hatthicon appears only in the prophetic vision of Ezekiel 47, where the prophet describes the new borders of the promised land after the restoration of Israel. This passage enumerates a series of cities and places that mark the territory, from north to south and east to west. Hatzer-Hatthicon is among these landmarks, specifically located between Damascus and Hamath, in the eastern heights. This unique mention shows that the prophet uses real and recognizable localities to make his vision tangible and credible to his listeners.

sens: One of David's elite warriors
Warrior from Carmel
H2695.detail: Hetsraï is one of the thirty most powerful warriors who formed the personal guard of King David. He appears in two lists: in 2 Samuel 23:35 he is called "Hetsraï, of Carmel," and in 1 Chronicles 11:37 he is listed as "Hetsro, of Carmel." These lists enumerate the bravest men of the united kingdom, those in whom David trusted to protect him and lead his battles. His connection to Carmel, a region of Judah, indicates his origin.
H2695.origine: The name Hetsraï (or Hetsro) literally means "enclosed" or "enclosure," perhaps evoking a form of refuge or fortress. It is a typical Hebrew name from the time of the Israelite monarchy. The spelling variations between 2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles (Hetsraï/Hetsro) are common for Hebrew proper names transmitted in writing.
H2695.emploi: Hetsraï is mentioned twice in the Bible, always in identical contexts: the lists of David's elite warriors. In 2 Samuel 23:35, he is among David's thirty mighty men. In 1 Chronicles 11:37, the same list names him again. These two passages likely reflect the same event or tradition of famous warriors. No particular narrative is attached to Hetsraï: he is known only for being a trusted warrior in the immediate entourage of the king.

sens: son of Reuben
clan or family descended from Hetsron
H2696G.detail:
1. Hetsron is one of the four sons of Reuben, the firstborn of Jacob, mentioned when the family descends into Egypt (Genesis 46:9). He appears in the genealogical lists of Exodus and 1 Chronicles, always alongside his brothers Henoch, Pallu, and Carmi.
2. From his name comes a family, the Hetsronites, which forms a recognized unit during the census of the Israelites in the wilderness (Numbers 26:6). Thus, his name also designates the group of his descendants, as is common in biblical genealogies.
H2696G.origine: The name literally means "surrounded by a wall" (Hebrew root evoking a fortified enclosure). It is a name among the ancestors of the tribe of Reuben, mentioned in the ancient lineages of Israel transmitted through genealogical documents.
H2696G.emploi: Hetsron is mentioned four times in the Bible, always in a genealogical context: three times in the lists of the sons of Reuben (Genesis 46:9; Exodus 6:14; 1 Chronicles 5:3), which enumerate the descendants of Jacob's firstborn during the entry into Egypt and after the exodus from Egypt. He also appears in Numbers 26:6, where the family of the Hetsronites is mentioned, showing that his descendants formed an established and countable clan during the wilderness journey. These usages are purely genealogical: Hetsron himself does not intervene in the narrative action; he simply serves to anchor the genealogies of Israel.

sens: son of Perez and grandson of Judah
ancestor of King David and Jesus through the lineage of Judah
patriarch founder of an important family in Israel
H2696H.detail:
1. Hetsron is a man of the tribe of Judah who lived at the time of the exodus from Egypt and the wilderness journey. He is the son of Perez and the grandson of Judah. He first appears in Genesis 46:12 when Jacob and his family descend into Egypt to meet Joseph.
2. Hetsron is especially known as the starting point of a major genealogy in the Bible. From him are born several important sons: Ram, Jerachmeel, Kelubaï, Caleb, and Segub (1 Chronicles 2:9). Ram, in particular, is the direct ancestor of King David, making Hetsron an essential link in the genealogical chain leading to Jesus.
3. He is recognized as the head of the family from which the Hetsronites descend, an important division of the sons of Judah (Numbers 26:21).
H2696H.origine: The name Hetsron means "surrounded by a wall" or "enclosed by an enclosure." It comes from a Hebrew root that evokes the idea of closure or enclosure. It is a name that suggests protection and the delimitation of a space.
H2696H.emploi: Hetsron appears in the genealogy of Judah starting from Genesis 46:12, where he is mentioned as one of the sons of Perez. He regularly reappears in the genealogical lists of the book of Numbers (26:21) and Chronicles (2:5, 2:9, 2:18, 2:21, 2:24, 2:25, 4:1), always in the context of the descendants of Judah. His historical and theological importance comes from his place in the genealogy of David: in Ruth 4:18-19, we see the chain Perez → Hetsron → Ram → Amminadab, which leads directly to David a few generations later. Chronicles delve into his descendants and confirm his role as a founding patriarch.
H2696H.portee: Hetsron represents a living link in God's promise to David: from him will come an unbroken royal lineage that will culminate in the Messiah. For the reader of the Gospels, Hetsron is a name in the genealogy of Jesus (Matthew 1:3 cites him as an ancestor of the Lord). It reminds us that God works through ordinary human generations and that the story of salvation is woven slowly, from father to son, from the Exodus to the Messiah.

sens: city in southern Judah
H2696I.detail: Hetsron is a locality in the extreme south of the territory of Judah. Its name literally means "surrounded by a wall" in Hebrew, reflecting the image of a fortified city. It is mentioned in Joshua 15:25 in the list of cities that were assigned to the tribe of Judah during the conquest of the land.
H2696I.origine: The name comes from the Hebrew root חצר (khatsár), which means "enclosure" or "courtyard," and the suffix -ôn forming place names. The word evokes the image of a place surrounded by walls or fortifications, which was common for cities in biblical times.
H2696I.emploi: Hetsron appears only once in the Bible, in Joshua 15:25, where it is included in the detailed enumeration of the cities in southern Judah (the Negev). It is designated there as one of the fortified localities in the territory assigned to Judah. Its full name was apparently Qerioth-Hetsron, combining two elements (Qerioth meaning "villages").

sens: Locality in southern Judea, at the edge of the Negev desert
H2696J.detail: 1. Hetsron is a city located in the extreme south of the territory of Judah, in the desert region of the Negev. It appears in the description of the southern borders of Judah (Joshua 15:3), where it marks a passage point between garrison locations: it is situated after the pass of Akrabbim and before Karkaa, in an arid and sparsely populated area, on the fringes of the desert.
H2696J.origine: The Hebrew name חֶצְרוֹן (chetsron) derives from a root meaning "to enclose" or "to fortify": it evokes a locality closed or protected by walls. It is related to the word חָצֵר (chaTser, courtyard or enclosure) and to חָצוֹר (Chazor, Hazor), another fortified city in southern Judah. The primary meaning thus refers to the idea of a "place surrounded by walls."
H2696J.emploi: Hetsron appears only once in the Old Testament, in Joshua 15:3, during the enumeration of the border cities of the southern tribe of Judah. It is listed there as a topographical landmark in the southern boundary route, between Kadesh-Barnea and Karkaa. It was a locality well-known enough to serve as a reference point for the delimitation of tribal lands.

sens: Descendant de Hetsron, homme de la tribu de Juda
H2697.detail: 1. The term designates a member of the family clan descended from Hetsron, an ancestor of the Hetsronites. Hetsron was a man of the tribe of Judah, the son of Perez, who lived during the time of Egypt and the desert. The people of Israel were organized into families and clans: each clan bore the name of its founding ancestor. In Numbers 26:6 and 26:21, during the census in the desert, Moses lists the clans of Judah, and the Hetsronites are mentioned as one of the major families of this tribe, alongside the Carmites and the Hamulites.
H2697.origine: The word comes from the proper name Hetsron (חֶצְרוֹן), which likely meant "enclosure" or "division of song." It is a typical name in Hebrew: the suffix -ite (in Hebrew -ni) is added to the name of the ancestor to form the name of the clan. The members of the clan then bear the patronymic name that connects them to their founding ancestor and their genealogy.
H2697.emploi: The word appears only twice in the Bible, both in Numbers 26, in the chapter of the census of the tribes of Israel in the desert. Each time it is used to count the clans of Judah: Hetsron, from which the family of the Hetsronites descends (Numbers 26:6 and 26:21). These two mentions enumerate the same clans in an administrative and genealogical context: the establishment of the register of men of fighting age for the conquest of the Promised Land.
H2697.portee: For the believer, this term reminds us that God knows each family, each clan, each person by name. The genealogical enumeration in the Bible shows that the Lord does not lose sight of any of His children: even an apparently ordinary patronymic like that of the Hetsronites is recorded in the divine register. This is a source of certainty: the Lord knows those who belong to Him.
